question: An analyst has refined the wording she uses for supplier reviews across many rounds, using the same supplier's file throughout. She now wants to adopt it as her team's standard wording. What should she do before that?
options: A) Record the reasoning behind each instruction, so that colleagues understand why the wording is written this way.
B) Shorten the wording so that colleagues who have not followed the refinement can still take it in quickly.
C) Ask colleagues to read the wording through and confirm that they find the instructions in it clear enough.
D) Try it on two or three other suppliers' files, since it may have been shaped to fit the one file she used.
correct_answers: D) Try it on two or three other suppliers' files, since it may have been shaped to fit the one file she used.
explanations: Documenting the reasoning helps the team maintain the wording later, but it assumes the wording already generalises.
Shortening improves how approachable the wording is, and it may remove instructions whose value has not been established.
A readability check confirms colleagues can follow the instructions, not that the instructions work on a supplier file she never tested.

Correct. Wording refined against a single example tends to encode that example's quirks, such as its headings or its level of detail. Trying it on other files is what separates a genuine improvement from one that only fits the case it was built on.

correct_answers: C) As a useful prompt for her own checking, since a review of its own work is not independent confirmation.
explanations: Three corrections in a draft are unremarkable, and discarding otherwise usable work is an overreaction to a normal review result.

Reviewing only the flagged sections trusts the same judgement that produced the draft to decide where checking is needed.

question: A marketing operations specialist has built a workflow that will send Claude-drafted emails automatically to a fifty-thousand-person customer list at six tomorrow morning. Nobody has read any of the drafts yet. What should she do first?
options: A) Read the first and last few drafts as a sample, and let the send run if those ones look fine.
B) Turn off the automatic send, so that nothing reaches the list until it has been reviewed.
C) Read as many of the drafts as she can before six, and let the rest of them go out unread.
D) Ask Claude to check its own drafts overnight and correct any problems that it finds in them.
correct_answers: B) Turn off the automatic send, so that nothing reaches the list until it has been reviewed.
explanations: A sample of the first and last few tells her nothing about the drafts in between, and every one of them still goes to a real customer. Sampling is reasonable for low-stakes internal work, not for an irreversible mass send.

Correct. The output is externally visible, irreversible once sent and has a very wide blast radius, so the first move is to remove the deadline pressure by stopping the automatic send. Review can then happen properly rather than against a clock she does not control.
This accepts that unreviewed messages will reach customers anyway. Once an email is sent to fifty thousand people it cannot be recalled, so partial review under a running clock is not enough.
Leaving the model to check itself keeps the unreviewed send in place. No human has looked at anything, which is precisely the risk here.

question: After four rounds, an internal newsletter item is accurate and well structured, but two headings use the wrong department names. The item is due in ten minutes. What should the editor do?

correct_answers: B) Correct the two headings herself, since the remaining gap is smaller than the effort of another full round.
explanations: Regenerating the item risks the accuracy and structure that four rounds established, with ten minutes left to verify them.

Publishing known errors and correcting them later costs the team credibility over a fix that takes moments.
Another round can fix two words, but it returns a whole document that has to be re-read to confirm nothing else moved.

question: An analyst is unhappy with a Claude output and wants to diagnose the cause properly rather than guess. Which sequence is correct?
options: A) Compare the output with what the request actually asked for; check whether the source material was ever supplied; rewrite the request with the missing specifics; consider a different model or a fresh chat.

B) Consider a different model or a fresh chat; rewrite the request with the missing specifics; compare the output with what the request actually asked for; check whether the source material was ever supplied.

C) Check whether the source material was ever supplied; consider a different model or a fresh chat; compare the output with what the request actually asked for; rewrite the request with the missing specifics.

D) Rewrite the request with the missing specifics; consider a different model or a fresh chat; check whether the source material was ever supplied; compare the output with what the request actually asked for.
correct_answers: A) Compare the output with what the request actually asked for; check whether the source material was ever supplied; rewrite the request with the missing specifics; consider a different model or a fresh chat.
explanations: Correct. Diagnosis comes before action: establish what is actually missing, check whether the material was ever provided, fix the request, and only then change the model or the conversation.
Changing the model first treats the most expensive lever as the first resort, before anyone knows what is wrong.
Checking the source material first is reasonable, but switching models before reading the output leaves the diagnosis half done.
Rewriting before comparing means guessing at what was missing rather than establishing it.

There is no rule that limits a connection to newly created files.
Connecting does not grant access beyond what the person can already open, and weekly re-approval is not how the control works.

question: A sponsor wants to deploy a new Claude-powered feature to all users in every region simultaneously on day one. What rollout approach should be recommended instead, and why?
options: A) Recommend delaying the launch indefinitely, since no rollout strategy can reduce risk for AI-powered features.
B) Recommend the simultaneous global launch as proposed, since phased rollouts add no measurable risk-reduction benefit.
C) Recommend a phased rollout to a small user segment first, so issues can be caught and addressed before scaling to everyone.
D) Recommend launching only in the region with the least usage data, since regional differences do not affect quality.
correct_answers: C) Recommend a phased rollout to a small user segment first, so issues can be caught and addressed before scaling to everyone.
explanations: Incorrect. Indefinite delay is unnecessary; a phased approach allows launch to proceed while managing risk.
Incorrect. Phased rollouts are a standard risk-reduction practice; claiming no benefit contradicts common deployment guidance.
Correct. A phased or pilot rollout to a limited audience lets the team observe real-world performance and fix issues before exposing the full user base to them, reducing overall risk.
Incorrect. Regional usage patterns and data characteristics can affect performance, so ignoring them is not sound rollout planning.

question: An Enterprise owner decides to shorten the organisation's data retention period substantially. What is the greatest concern before saving the change?
options: A) Shortening retention disables project sharing, because shared projects require indefinite retention.
B) Data falling outside the new window is deleted immediately, so work still in progress can be lost.
C) The change applies only to new chats, so nothing older is affected and the setting has no real effect.

correct_answers: B) Data falling outside the new window is deleted immediately, so work still in progress can be lost.
explanations: Retention settings and project sharing are unrelated.
Correct. Shortening retention deletes anything already older than the new window as soon as it is saved.
The setting is not limited to new conversations; existing data is in scope.
Retention changes do not require connectors to be reconnected.

question: A manager challenges a claim in a Claude answer, Claude replies that it is confident the claim is correct, and the manager accepts it. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The manager's challenge is recorded in the chat, which makes the exchange harder to audit.
B) A restated assurance is not evidence, and a fabricated claim is defended just as readily.
C) Repeating the question uses allowance that could have been spent on the rest of the review.
D) Claude will always reverse its position when challenged, so its second answer is unreliable.
correct_answers: B) A restated assurance is not evidence, and a fabricated claim is defended just as readily.
explanations: Incorrect. A recorded exchange helps an audit rather than hindering it; the problem is that no external source was consulted.
Correct. Confidence is produced by the same process that produced the claim, so a challenge answered from inside the conversation adds nothing independent.
Incorrect. The cost of one follow-up message is trivial next to acting on a claim that was never actually checked.
Incorrect. It does not always reverse, and the manager's error is treating either response as evidence about the outside world.

question: A researcher has fifteen sets of interview notes and must produce a findings section for a report. Which sequence of stages should she follow?
options: A) Check each theme against the notes; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; write the findings section; group the extracts into themes.
B) Group the extracts into themes; check each theme against the notes; write the findings section; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes.
C) Pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; group the extracts into themes; check each theme against the notes; write the findings section.
D) Write the findings section; group the extracts into themes; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; check each theme against the notes.
correct_answers: C) Pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; group the extracts into themes; check each theme against the notes; write the findings section.
explanations: Checking themes that have not yet been formed is not possible, and grouping after the section is written leaves the writing unsupported.
Themes cannot be grouped before the extracts have been pulled, so this ordering starts from material that has not been gathered.

Correct. Extracts come out of the notes first, grouping turns them into themes, the check confirms each theme is genuinely supported before it becomes a claim, and the section is written last from verified material.
Findings written before the extracts exist are assertions in search of evidence, and the checking stage arrives after the section is already written.

question: A team lead must brief a sceptical director on a new Claude-assisted reporting arrangement. Which framing is most appropriate?
options: A) Say that results will improve automatically as newer models become available
B) Say that the pilot's best output shows what every report will look like now
C) Say that the arrangement removes the need for the team's current review step
D) Say what it does reliably, what needs checking, and who does the checking
correct_answers: D) Say what it does reliably, what needs checking, and who does the checking
explanations: Promising automatic future improvement asks the director to accept an outcome nobody can commit to.
Presenting the best single output as typical sets an expectation the arrangement will not meet in ordinary use.
Claiming the review step is unnecessary oversells the arrangement and removes the safeguard the director is most likely to ask about.
Correct. Honest communication pairs capability with limitation and names where human review stays in the loop. That is what lets a sceptical stakeholder judge the arrangement rather than the pitch.

question: An events team has redesigned its exhibitor-liaison workflow so that Claude carries a request from first enquiry through to a confirmed booking slot. Where does an approval checkpoint most clearly belong?
options: A) Only if an exhibitor complains about the slot they were allocated
B) After the exhibitor has replied to the confirmation that was sent
C) At the end of each month, when all bookings are reviewed together
D) Before anything is sent to the exhibitor on the team's behalf
correct_answers: D) Before anything is sent to the exhibitor on the team's behalf
explanations: Waiting for a complaint makes the exhibitor the quality control, which is precisely what a checkpoint is meant to avoid.
A check after the exhibitor has replied comes after the commitment, so it can only manage the consequences.
A monthly review catches patterns but arrives long after individual bookings have gone out.
Correct. The checkpoint belongs at the last moment where a person can still prevent an external, hard-to-retract action. Once the exhibitor has been contacted, the commitment has been made.

Incorrect. Claude does support image input and can reason about visual content, so manual transcription into text is not required; this understates its actual capabilities.

question: A product team is brainstorming new feature ideas and wants Claude to generate a wide range of genuinely different concepts rather than several variations on the same idea. What should the team do when providing example ideas in the prompt?

B) Include a small set of deliberately varied examples so Claude avoids one narrow pattern
C) Include just one example and ask Claude to generate close variations of it
D) Include many examples that all follow the exact same structure as just one clear pattern
correct_answers: B) Include a small set of deliberately varied examples so Claude avoids one narrow pattern
explanations: Incorrect. While examples aren't required, omitting them does not itself guarantee variety; well-chosen diverse examples are the recommended way to actively support a broad range of ideas.
Correct. Examples should be diverse, covering edge cases and varying enough that Claude does not pick up an unintended narrow pattern, which supports a wide range of brainstormed ideas.
Incorrect. Asking for close variations of one example directly narrows the output to minor tweaks instead of a wide range of distinct ideas.
Incorrect. Uniform examples that all share the same structure and theme encourage Claude to converge on that single pattern rather than exploring genuinely different concepts.

question: A consultancy team on an Enterprise plan wants Claude's research on a client sector to draw on the firm's own past engagement reports, not only on public material. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: A) Paste the single most relevant engagement report into each new chat whenever it seems likely to be needed.
B) Put the past engagement reports into the project so every research chat in it works from that material.
C) Ask Claude to describe what a firm like this one would probably have learned in past engagements.
D) Summarise the past engagement reports into a single page and rely on that page from then onwards.
correct_answers: B) Put the past engagement reports into the project so every research chat in it works from that material.
explanations: Relying on someone to notice the right report and paste it in means the internal evidence is used inconsistently. It also limits each piece of research to one report when the value lies in the pattern across many.

Correct. Project knowledge is durable background for every chat in that project, so the firm's own engagement history informs each piece of research without anyone re-pasting it. That makes the internal evidence a standing input rather than something remembered on a good day.

Asking Claude what such a firm would probably have learned invites it to invent the firm's experience. The reports exist and can be supplied, so guessing at their contents is the one option that produces confident fiction.

A single summary page discards the detail that makes past engagements useful, and it becomes stale the moment new work is completed. The team would be researching against a snapshot rather than the record.

question: A support team must triage several thousand incoming messages a week, of which a small proportion involve genuinely difficult judgment. What is the most sensible arrangement?
options: A) Run the bulk on the fastest tier and send the cases it flags as difficult to the deepest tier.
B) Run everything on the deepest tier, so that the difficult cases are never handled by a lighter one.
C) Run everything on the fastest tier, since the difficult cases are only a small proportion.
D) Alternate between tiers message by message, so that the allowance is spread evenly over time.
correct_answers: A) Run the bulk on the fastest tier and send the cases it flags as difficult to the deepest tier.
explanations: Correct. A two-stage arrangement matches each message to the depth it needs, so volume is handled cheaply and the small hard tail still gets proper reasoning.
Incorrect. Paying the deepest tier's allowance cost on thousands of routine messages to protect a handful of hard ones is a poor trade.
Incorrect. The hard cases are usually where the cost of a mistake sits, so treating them as negligible is the expensive error.
Incorrect. Alternating assigns depth at random, which means some hard cases get the lightest treatment.

question: A fintech company built a product that uses Claude to automatically approve or deny small business loan applications without human involvement. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, what must the company do to comply with the high-risk use case requirements for financial services?
options: A) The company should route every denial through a separate rules engine so only approvals originate from Claude, removing any human review requirement.
B) The company may skip disclosure to applicants as long as it retains complete logs of every underwriting input and output that Claude produces for compliance audit.
C) The company should reduce how long loan application records are stored so AI-generated decisions cannot later be inspected during compliance audits.
D) The company must disclose Claude's involvement to applicants and have a qualified human review the model's output before any adverse lending decision is finalized.
correct_answers: D) The company must disclose Claude's involvement to applicants and have a qualified human review the model's output before any adverse lending decision is finalized.
explanations: Incorrect. Routing denials away from Claude does not eliminate the requirement for disclosure and human review. High-risk financial decisions still demand human oversight regardless of which system generates the outcome.

Incorrect. Retaining logs does not exempt the company from disclosing AI involvement or providing human review. The Usage Policy requires both disclosure and human review for high-risk financial decisions.

Incorrect. Reducing how long records are kept impairs the ability to conduct compliance audits. Moreover, it does not fulfill the Usage Policy's requirements for disclosure and human review of high-risk decisions.

Correct. The Usage Policy classifies automated lending decisions as high-risk. Therefore, the company must disclose Claude's involvement to applicants and ensure a qualified human reviews the output before any adverse lending decision is finalized.

explanations: Incorrect. Batch processing helps with running many separate requests asynchronously; it does not let a single request hold more content than the context window allows.

question: Within a single response, Claude states in the first paragraph that a company was founded in 1998, then states in the closing paragraph that the same company celebrated its 30th anniversary last year, which would imply a different founding year. correct_answers: D) An internal inconsistency, since the two statements within one response contradict each other
explanations: Incorrect. Bias involves systematic skew toward a group or viewpoint, not a single self-contradictory pair of dates.
Incorrect. The problem described is a factual contradiction between two claims, not merely a difference in date formatting style.
Incorrect. The scenario does not establish that the founding date is unverifiable or invented; the issue is that the response contradicts itself.
Correct. When two statements within the same response conflict with each other, this is an internal inconsistency, regardless of whether either individual fact can be verified externally.

question: An analyst wants to upload a partner company's forecast data, shared under a non-disclosure agreement, into a Claude project. What should she do first?

question: A project manager reviews a risk register that Claude built from incident logs. Every risk attributed to one supplier is rated high and every risk attributed to the other is rated low, although both suppliers had comparable incidents. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to redo the register and use the second version if it gives a more balanced split.
B) Compare the incident records behind several of the ratings to see whether the pattern is supported.
C) Ask Claude to raise the ratings for the second supplier so that both suppliers are treated more evenly.
D) Accept the register, because a consistent pattern within a supplier suggests a genuine difference.
correct_answers: B) Compare the incident records behind several of the ratings to see whether the pattern is supported.
explanations: Incorrect. Choosing whichever regeneration looks more comfortable selects on appearance rather than on what the incident records actually show.
Correct. A systematic split like this is either a real signal in the data or a skew introduced in the response, and only the underlying records can tell her which.
Incorrect. Forcing an even split assumes the answer. If the second supplier really does carry more risk, she has now hidden it.
Incorrect. Consistency is exactly what a skewed response looks like. A uniform pattern is a reason to check the evidence, not a substitute for checking it.

question: A market analyst must produce a competitor briefing drawn from many public sources, and the team will keep editing that briefing for weeks afterwards. Which two Claude features fit this job? Select two.
options: A) Open a separate chat for each competitor so that no single conversation ever grows long.
B) Ask for the briefing as an artifact, so the team can edit and reuse it outside the chat.
C) Use Research mode, so the briefing is built by multi-step searching and returns citations.
D) Turn on a mail connector first so that the competitor facts are drawn from the team inbox.
E) Keep the briefing inline in the chat and re-paste the newest version whenever an edit lands.
correct_answers: B) Ask for the briefing as an artifact, so the team can edit and reuse it outside the chat.
C) Use Research mode, so the briefing is built by multi-step searching and returns citations.
explanations: Incorrect. Splitting by competitor fragments the briefing and does nothing about sourcing or about the editing the team has ahead of it.
Correct. An artifact is the durable, editable deliverable format, so weeks of later editing happen on one object rather than in chat replies.
Correct. Research mode runs an agentic, multi-step search and returns citations, which is exactly what a sourced competitor briefing needs.
Incorrect. An internal mailbox is not the source of public competitor information, and connecting one does not answer the sourcing need here.
Incorrect. Re-pasting an inline answer for every edit is precisely the friction artifacts exist to remove, and versions drift apart quickly.

question: A logistics company processes a very high volume of straightforward shipment-status classifications per day and has tight per-request latency requirements, but still wants strong reasoning quality for edge cases. Which model tier is the best fit?
options: A) Claude Sonnet, since high-volume straightforward tasks are always better served by a mid-tier model
B) A model chosen at random each request, since reasoning quality does not depend on which tier handles the request
C) Claude Opus, since strong reasoning on edge cases requires the most capable and expensive tier regardless of volume
D) Claude Haiku, since it offers near-frontier performance with the fastest speed at the most economical price point
correct_answers: D) Claude Haiku, since it offers near-frontier performance with the fastest speed at the most economical price point
explanations: While Claude Sonnet offers a balance of intelligence and speed, Anthropic specifically designates Claude Haiku for straightforward classifications. There is no universal rule that mid-tier models are always better for such tasks; the choice depends on the specific requirements for latency, cost, and capability.

Reasoning quality varies significantly across model tiers, and randomly selecting a model would lead to inconsistent performance and unpredictable costs. Best practice is to select the most appropriate model based on the task's requirements.

Claude Opus is the most capable model, but using it for every request in a high-volume scenario would be extremely costly and introduce higher latency, making it unsuitable for straightforward classification tasks. The documentation advises using the appropriate model tier based on task complexity and budget.

Anthropic documentation recommends Claude Haiku for straightforward classification tasks like routing and intent detection, emphasizing its speed and cost-efficiency. It provides near-frontier performance at the most economical price, making it ideal for high-volume, low-latency requirements. For edge cases requiring deeper reasoning, a multi-model architecture can escalate requests to more capable models.

question: A records team reclassifies several thousand short archive descriptions overnight, and an archivist spot-checks a sample of the results each morning before anything is published. Which consideration should carry most weight in the team's tier choice?
options: A) The preference of the archivist who runs the morning check, since she is the person most familiar with how the descriptions read.
B) The overall importance of the archive to the organisation, since anything touching the permanent record deserves the best available.
C) Whichever tier the rest of the organisation has settled on, so that the records team's results stay comparable with everyone else's.
D) The volume and routine nature of the descriptions, together with the fact that a person already reviews a sample before publication.
correct_answers: D) The volume and routine nature of the descriptions, together with the fact that a person already reviews a sample before publication.
explanations: The archivist's familiarity makes her a good reviewer, but personal preference is not a basis for a decision about throughput and allowance across thousands of items processed overnight.

General importance is too blunt to guide the choice. It would justify the deepest tier for every task the team ever runs, including thousands of short, formulaic descriptions that do not need that depth.
Matching what others use ignores the specifics that actually matter here: this is high-volume, repetitive work with a human check already in place, which is not the shape of most colleagues' tasks.
Correct. High volume, short and repetitive items, and an existing human spot-check together point to speed and allowance as the deciding factors rather than the deepest available reasoning.

question: Four analysts on an Enterprise plan are running separate chats to analyse requirements for the same programme, and each keeps re-pasting the same brief, glossary and stakeholder map. What is the most appropriate improvement?
options: A) Ask each analyst to paste a shortened summary of the documents rather than the full versions each time.
B) Agree that a single analyst holds the source documents and answers the other three analysts on request each time.
C) Merge the four conversations into one long chat so the shared material has to be pasted only once.
D) Put the brief, glossary and stakeholder map into a shared project so every analysis chat starts from them.
correct_answers: D) Put the brief, glossary and stakeholder map into a shared project so every analysis chat starts from them.
explanations: Shortened summaries mean each analyst works from a different reduction of the same material, which is how definitions quietly diverge. Requirements analysis depends on everyone reading the same glossary, not four paraphrases of it.

Funnelling the documents through one person creates a bottleneck and leaves the other three analysts analysing from second-hand descriptions. It solves the duplication by removing access rather than by sharing context.

One very long shared conversation mixes four unrelated lines of analysis, becomes hard to follow, and pushes against the limits of a single chat. It also gives no way to start a fresh piece of analysis from the same background.

Correct. Recurring work over a stable set of source material is exactly what a project is for: the brief, glossary and stakeholder map become durable background for every chat in that project, so all four analysts work from the same current version instead of from whatever each last pasted.

question: A team's breakdown of a supplier review ends with a stage described as 'format the findings and add the recommended supplier to the summary page'. What is the greatest concern with this stage?
options: A) Formatting and writing in the same stage makes the stage take longer than the other stages in the breakdown.
B) The recommended supplier will appear on the summary page before it appears in the body of the review itself.
C) The summary page may end up formatted differently from the rest of the review, which readers will find jarring.
D) A decision that should be made and reviewed on its own is folded into a step everyone treats as presentation.
correct_answers: D) A decision that should be made and reviewed on its own is folded into a step everyone treats as presentation.
explanations: Uneven stage durations are a planning detail rather than a risk to the integrity of the review.
Ordering within the document is an editorial choice, and the recommendation appearing early is normal in a review of this kind.
Inconsistent formatting is a cosmetic defect that a single pass fixes, and it does not affect which supplier is chosen.

Correct. Naming the recommendation is the consequential act of the whole review, and burying it in a formatting step means nobody schedules a review of it. Decisions should sit in stages of their own, where they can be challenged.

question: A grants team is designing a new way of working in which Claude prepares the first draft of each funding decision summary. Nothing has been built yet. What should the team do first?
options: A) Agree what an acceptable summary contains, so drafts can be judged against it
B) Announce the new arrangement so that people begin sending their cases through
C) Write the longest and most detailed instruction the team can manage in one go
D) Ask every member of the team to try their own approach and compare next month
correct_answers: A) Agree what an acceptable summary contains, so drafts can be judged against it
explanations: Correct. Defining what "good" looks like before delegating is what makes every later round of iteration meaningful; without it, nobody can say whether a draft is acceptable or whether a change helped.
Announcing an arrangement that has not been designed pushes unfinished work onto colleagues and makes problems harder to withdraw from.
Instruction length is not the design. A long instruction written before the team knows what it wants encodes guesses at scale.
Four private approaches produce four private standards, and a month later there is still no agreed standard to compare them against.

question: A business analyst is deciding whether to send one large request or break it into stages. Which two features of a request are the strongest signals that it should be decomposed? Select two.
options: A) Later parts are only worth producing if the earlier factual work is correct.
B) It runs to a long prompt because a good deal of background has been pasted in with it.
C) It bundles several distinct deliverables that are meant for different audiences and uses.
D) It asks for the final answer to be presented as a table rather than as flowing paragraphs.
E) It concerns a subject area the analyst has not personally worked in for several years.
correct_answers: A) Later parts are only worth producing if the earlier factual work is correct.
C) It bundles several distinct deliverables that are meant for different audiences and uses.
explanations: Correct. Dependency is a separate signal from bundling: when step two builds on step one, a single pass propagates any early error into everything downstream unchecked.
A long prompt is not the same as an overloaded one. Pasting rich source material is good practice and often makes a single-step request work better.
Correct. Multiple deliverables with different readers pull the output in different directions, and one response has to compromise. Splitting lets each part be specified properly.
Output format is a presentation choice. A table can be produced in one step just as easily as prose, so it is not a reason to break the work up.
Unfamiliarity affects how carefully the analyst must review the result, but it says nothing about whether the request itself is structurally overloaded.

question: A manager asks whether the new Claude-assisted process means the team can cut its review budget. Which two responses are honest and useful? Select two.
options: A) Share what the pilot actually changed in the cycle time, and what it did not change at all.
B) Confirm that the review budget can be cut right now, since the pilot produced no visible errors.
C) Say that the process is fully reliable, so the manager's confidence in it is not undermined.
D) Explain that review is still needed, because outputs continue to need checking before release.
E) Avoid the question, since discussing limitations now would weaken support for the rollout.
correct_answers: A) Share what the pilot actually changed in the cycle time, and what it did not change at all.
D) Explain that review is still needed, because outputs continue to need checking before release.
explanations: Correct. Reporting both what improved and what did not is what sets an expectation the rollout can actually meet.
Incorrect. Absence of visible errors in a short pilot is weak evidence, and cutting review on it removes the safeguard.
Incorrect. Claiming full reliability is an overstatement, and confidence built on it collapses at the first real error.
Correct. Review remains part of the design, and saying so plainly is the honest answer to a budget question.
Incorrect. Withholding limitations to protect support is exactly the communication failure this competency warns against.

question: An operations team wants Claude to help find where a twelve-step expense reimbursement process loses time. Which input will produce the most useful analysis?
options: A) The actual step list with who does each step, the handoffs between them, and typical waiting times.
B) A summary of the process written for new starters, which explains its purpose and the policy behind it.
C) A description of how the team feels the process performs, written by the team's most experienced approver.
D) A list of the complaints employees have raised about reimbursement over the past two reporting quarters.
correct_answers: A) The actual step list with who does each step, the handoffs between them, and typical waiting times.
explanations: Correct. Delay in a multi-step process almost always sits in the handoffs and the waiting between steps, so the analysis is only as good as the map it is given. Supplying the real steps, owners and typical waits lets Claude point at specific queues instead of generalising.

A new-starter summary explains why the process exists and what policy governs it. That is the wrong level of detail for finding delay, because it deliberately omits the handoffs and waiting that create it.
An experienced approver's impression is a useful hypothesis but not evidence. Perceived slowness usually clusters around visible effort rather than around the queues where time is genuinely lost.

Complaints record where employees felt the pain, which is often the last step before an outcome rather than the step that caused the wait. They are a helpful cross-check but a poor primary input for locating a bottleneck.

question: A project manager asked for a risk register covering five workstreams and received a neat table of eleven risks. Which two checks best establish that the output is accurate and complete? Select two.
options: A) Check that the table renders properly and that the columns line up as they should.
B) Check that the wording matches the tone the sponsor prefers in written reporting.
C) Confirm that all five of the named workstreams are actually represented in the table.
D) Judge whether eleven risks is about the number a project of this size usually has.
E) Trace the dates and owners in the table back to the project plan they came from.
correct_answers: C) Confirm that all five of the named workstreams are actually represented in the table.
E) Trace the dates and owners in the table back to the project plan they came from.
explanations: Rendering is a presentation matter. A perfectly formatted table can carry wrong owners and missing workstreams without any visual sign of a problem.
Tone affects how the register reads, not whether its content is right. Editing for the sponsor comes after accuracy has been established.
Correct. Completeness is measured against the request. A polished table can silently cover four workstreams, and only checking coverage item by item exposes that.
A plausible count is not evidence. Eleven risks can look reasonable while omitting an entire workstream or duplicating two entries from another one.
Correct. This tests accuracy rather than coverage: the entries must match the source plan, and a risk with an invented owner is wrong even if the scope is complete.

question: A finance team is designing a way of working in which Claude prepares the monthly variance commentary. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Write the instruction for the rest; try it on last month's figures; decide which parts a person must own; adjust one thing and try again
B) Try it on last month's figures; decide which parts a person must own; write the instruction for the rest; adjust one thing and try again
C) Decide which parts a person must own; write the instruction for the rest; try it on last month's figures; adjust one thing and try again
D) Write the instruction for the rest; decide which parts a person must own; adjust one thing and try again; try it on last month's figures
correct_answers: C) Decide which parts a person must own; write the instruction for the rest; try it on last month's figures; adjust one thing and try again
explanations: Writing instructions before deciding what stays human means the instruction may quietly cover work that should never have been handed over.
Testing before the boundary or the instruction exists gives a result nobody can interpret, and the design decisions come too late to shape it.
Correct. Delegation boundaries come first: decide what a person must own, write instructions for the remainder, test on real past figures, then adjust one thing at a time.
Adjusting before the arrangement has been tried at all means the first adjustment is made blind, and the test arrives after the changes.

question: Explanation
options: A) The examples are causing Claude to ignore the instructions entirely and rely solely on memorized training data instead.
B) Ten examples is too many; Anthropic caps effective examples at two, and anything beyond that causes overfitting.
C) The examples are not diverse enough, so Claude picked up the unintended pattern that taglines must always be puns.
D) The issue is unrelated to the examples; it stems from an implicit temperature default that favors humorous phrasing.
correct_answers: C) The examples are not diverse enough, so Claude picked up the unintended pattern that taglines must always be puns.
explanations: Incorrect. There's no basis for claiming the examples cause instructions to be ignored in favor of training data; the documented issue with narrow examples is pattern overfitting to the examples themselves.
Incorrect. Anthropic recommends 3-5 examples for best results as a general guideline, not a hard cap of two, and the core problem here is lack of diversity, not raw example count.

Correct. Anthropic's guidance on using examples effectively specifies they should be diverse, varying enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns; a set of examples that are uniformly puns teaches the model that puns are required, not just one possible style.
Incorrect. This misattributes a documented examples-diversity issue to an unrelated sampling parameter with no such documented default behavior.

question: A facilities project still has last year's contractor safety standard uploaded as project knowledge, and Claude keeps quoting its old inspection interval with complete confidence. Which two actions actually resolve this? Select two.
options: A) Move the project onto a more capable model tier, which will state the inspection interval more accurately.
B) Replace the uploaded file with the current standard so the outdated interval cannot be retrieved again.
C) Add an instruction telling Claude to take particular care whenever any inspection interval is mentioned.
D) Open a fresh conversation and put the same question to Claude once again, this time much more firmly worded.
E) Re-check the inspection dates already issued on the strength of answers quoting the superseded figure.
correct_answers: B) Replace the uploaded file with the current standard so the outdated interval cannot be retrieved again.
E) Re-check the inspection dates already issued on the strength of answers quoting the superseded figure.
explanations: A stronger model reads the same outdated file and repeats the same wrong interval just as confidently.
Correct. The knowledge source is wrong, not the model, so nothing improves until the superseded document is replaced.
An instruction to be careful cannot compensate for a source that is authoritative-looking and out of date.
Rewording or insisting changes nothing when the retrieved document itself contains the wrong number.
Correct for a separate reason: fixing the source does not undo the decisions already taken on bad information, which still need remediation.

question: A team asks for 'a polished two-page write-up explaining why our regional sales fell'. They receive a confident, elegantly written explanation. What is the greatest risk in how they framed this?
options: A) The write-up may cover several causes at once when the audience would prefer one clear headline reason.
B) The write-up may be longer than the audience for a regional sales question is realistically willing to read.
C) The write-up may use vocabulary the regional sales team does not share, which slows down their response.
D) They asked for a finished piece of writing about a question that first needs working out from the figures.
correct_answers: D) They asked for a finished piece of writing about a question that first needs working out from the figures.
explanations: Several causes may well be the honest answer, and choosing a single headline reason is an editorial decision rather than a hazard.
Two pages is a modest length for this kind of question, and length can be adjusted without changing whether the explanation is sound.
Unshared vocabulary is a presentation problem, and it is corrected by naming the audience rather than by changing the task.

Correct. The request is shaped as a drafting task when the underlying work is analysis. Because polish was what was asked for, polish is what arrives, and a fluent explanation of an unexamined cause is very hard for a reader to tell apart from a real finding.

question: A team lead is writing a short internal guide on what to do when Claude returns an answer that looks incorrect or misleading. Which two actions does Claude's own guidance recommend? Select two.
options: A) Turn off web search so that answers come from the model alone and stay consistent.
B) Use the thumbs-down control on the reply so the problem is reported as feedback.
C) Regenerate the answer several times and keep whichever version the team likes most.
D) Ask Claude to score its own confidence and only accept answers above a chosen level.
E) Open the sources Claude cited and read them, since the originals reveal misreadings.
correct_answers: B) Use the thumbs-down control on the reply so the problem is reported as feedback.
E) Open the sources Claude cited and read them, since the originals reveal misreadings.
explanations: Removing web search removes the citations that make checking possible. Consistency is not accuracy, and this makes verification harder rather than easier.
Correct. The feedback control is the documented route for flagging an unhelpful or incorrect response, and it is the step users most often skip.
Choosing the version the team prefers selects for appeal rather than truth, and repeated generations can repeat the same underlying error.
A self-reported confidence score is produced in the same way as the answer, so it cannot serve as independent evidence that the answer is sound.
Correct. Reviewing cited sources is a distinct recommendation from giving feedback: checking the original content is what reveals anything that was misinterpreted.

question: A shared services group wants to take a Claude-assisted purchase-request triage from an idea to everyday use across eight teams. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed.

B) Run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary.

C) Pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary.

D) Compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary; run it alongside the existing process for a month.
correct_answers: C) Pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary.
explanations: Extending to every team first is a full rollout before any evidence exists, which makes the later pilot and comparison pointless because the risk has already been taken.
Running alongside the existing process before choosing a team and a slice means the trial has no defined scope, and the scoping decision arrives after the comparison it was supposed to make possible.

Correct. A bounded slice on one team keeps early mistakes cheap, running alongside the existing process gives a fair comparison rather than an impression, fixing what failed happens while the scope is still small, and the wider rollout then carries the human checks the comparison showed were needed.
There are no results to compare at the start, and the parallel run that would have produced them is left until after the arrangement has already been extended to all eight teams.

question: An operations manager has deliberately kept one chat alive for months, letting Claude condense earlier messages rather than ever starting fresh. What is the biggest concern with this habit?
options: A) A conversation that has been condensed can no longer be exported or shared, so her team is unable to review the thread once it passes the length limit
B) Condensing earlier messages deletes them from her chat history for good, so nobody on the team is able to go back and reread what was originally agreed
C) Automatic condensing is offered only on free accounts, so a paid plan will refuse to shorten the conversation and will simply stop accepting further messages
D) The decisions her team relies on exist only inside one conversation, and Claude now works from a condensed version rather than what was originally agreed
correct_answers: D) The decisions her team relies on exist only inside one conversation, and Claude now works from a condensed version rather than what was originally agreed
explanations: Condensing does not restrict exporting or sharing a conversation; that is unrelated to how context is managed as a chat grows.
Condensing affects what Claude carries forward as working context; the full chat history remains accessible for her to scroll back and read.
Automatic context management is not a free-account-only behaviour, and a conversation reaching its length limit does not simply refuse further messages in the way described.

Correct. Two things go wrong at once: the durable decisions are trapped in a single fragile conversation instead of being persisted somewhere reusable, and once earlier messages are condensed Claude is reasoning from a summary rather than the original wording. Moving what must survive into a Project fixes both.

question: Explanation
options: A) Publish the priority list so that residents can see how the ordering was arrived at.
B) Ask Claude to state whether its own priority list contains any unfair bias in it.
C) Use the list for this year and then compare the outcomes against last year's decisions.
D) Examine whether the historical records under-represent groups who applied less often.
correct_answers: D) Examine whether the historical records under-represent groups who applied less often.
explanations: Transparency about the ordering is worth having, but publishing a list that may embed historical inequity makes it visible rather than fair, and residents are affected either way.
Claude cannot audit the representativeness of records it was given, and a reassuring self-assessment would give the team false confidence about exactly the risk they need to investigate.
Using the list and reviewing afterwards means a year of residents receive grants in an order that may be skewed, and the comparison arrives long after the decisions have been made.

Correct. A priority list derived from past cases inherits whatever unevenness is in those cases, and residents who historically applied less often will be under-served by it. Because the output drives a decision about people, checking the data for that skew comes before the list is used at all.

question: A content team wants Claude to draft a press release, have the draft checked against their style guide, and then produce a revised version based on that check, with each stage logged separately for review. How should this drafting workflow be set up?
options: A) Ask Claude to draft the release ten different ways and pick the best one
B) Ask for the draft, the style review, and the revision all together in a single response
C) Chain three calls: draft the release, review it against the style guide, then refine it
D) Skip the review step and have Claude produce only a final polished draft
correct_answers: C) Chain three calls: draft the release, review it against the style guide, then refine it
explanations: Incorrect. Generating many parallel drafts without a review step against the style guide does not fulfill the requirement to check drafts against specific criteria before revising.
Incorrect. Bundling all three stages into one response does not give the team separately logged and inspectable outputs at each stage.
Correct. This is the self-correction chaining pattern for drafting tasks: generate a draft, review it against criteria, then refine, with each step as a separate, inspectable call.
Incorrect. Skipping the style guide review removes the criteria check the team explicitly wants applied before finalizing the draft.

question: A technical writer generates two drafts of an API integration guide, one for experienced developers and one for low-code platform users, and needs to check them for consistency before publishing. What should the writer confirm?
options: A) Both drafts must describe the same steps and results, varying only in terminology and depth.
B) The writer should check that both drafts have identical code samples to ensure uniformity.
C) The low-code draft should omit authentication, as low-code users only need the base URL.
D) The developer draft should simply be essentially a condensed version of the low-code guide.
correct_answers: A) Both drafts must describe the same steps and results, varying only in terminology and depth.
explanations: Correct. Both drafts should describe the same underlying steps and outcomes, ensuring consistency across audiences. The only acceptable differences are in terminology and level of detail appropriate for each user group.

Incorrect. Requiring identical code samples overlooks the fact that experienced developers and low-code platform users interact with the API differently. Low-code users may not use code samples at all, or they might need platform-specific snippets that differ from the developer draft.

Incorrect. Low-code users still need authentication information to use the API securely. Omitting authentication entirely and providing only a base URL would leave them with incomplete setup instructions.

Incorrect. The developer draft should not be a condensed version of the low-code guide; each audience requires distinct structure and depth. Developers need in-depth technical details and code examples, while low-code users need simplified configuration steps.

question: A manager tells his team to 'use common sense' with Claude rather than writing anything down. What is the most useful thing to recommend he add?

B) A monthly report of how many messages each person sent, to show that Claude is being used enough.

correct_answers: D) A short written standard naming approved plans, permitted data, disclosure rules and who to ask.
explanations: Collecting every conversation creates a large store of sensitive material without telling anyone what is allowed.
Volume statistics measure activity, not whether the activity complied with anything.
Restricting use to two people avoids the question rather than answering it, and does not guide their judgment either.
Correct. A short, concrete standard is what makes a policy usable day to day: what plan, what data, what must be disclosed, and who decides the ambiguous cases.

question: A policy writer expects roughly nine rounds of ordinary wording and structure changes on a report, with one genuinely hard judgement in the middle about how to reconcile two conflicting evidence bases. How should she spread the work across tiers?
options: A) Run every round on the fastest and cheapest tier, and accept whatever it produces for the reconciliation to keep the process simple.
B) Do the wording rounds on the default tier and reserve the deepest-reasoning tier for the one hard reconciliation in the middle.
C) Run every round on the deepest-reasoning tier, so that the hard judgement benefits from all the context built up in earlier rounds.
D) Alternate between the tiers round by round, so that the report gets a mix of perspectives as the drafting work progresses.
correct_answers: B) Do the wording rounds on the default tier and reserve the deepest-reasoning tier for the one hard reconciliation in the middle.
explanations: Simplicity is bought at the cost of the one step that matters. The reconciliation of conflicting evidence is precisely the task where shallower reasoning is most likely to produce a weak result.

Correct. The default tier is fast, capable and right for routine drafting and wording iterations, while the extra allowance cost of the deepest tier is worth paying only for the single step where reasoning depth genuinely decides the outcome.

Running nine wording rounds on the most expensive tier spends heavily on work the default tier handles well, and the accumulated context does not require every earlier round to have used the deeper tier.
Alternating by round bears no relation to what each round demands, so the hard judgement may land on a lighter tier by chance while routine wording changes consume the deeper one.

options: A) Rewriting a prompt after a weak result is the wrong response, because the first output should always be accepted as given

question: An operations manager compares two drafts of a policy announcement, one for headquarters staff and one adapted for a regional office, to confirm both convey the same policy without confusing readers. What should the manager check for?
options: A) Only the headquarters draft should be used, since any rewrite risks altering policy's meaning.
B) Verify both drafts have the same number of words so neither office feels treated differently.
C) Check that the regional draft uses more formal language than headquarters to convey authority.
D) That the drafts convey identical rules and deadlines but use wording tailored to each audience.
correct_answers: D) That the drafts convey identical rules and deadlines but use wording tailored to each audience.
explanations: Incorrect. While rewriting carries some risk, careful adaptation ensures the policy is clear to each audience without changing meaning. Using only the headquarters draft ignores the regional office's needs and may lead to misinterpretation.

question: An analyst has condensed a twenty-page Claude-produced analysis into a one-page version for an executive committee that will act on it directly. Which check matters most before she circulates the shorter version?
options: A) That the one-page version reads in the same house style as the committee papers her team has circulated in previous quarters.
B) That the one-page version comes in under the length the committee asked for, since executive committee papers are capped at a single side.
C) That the one-page version is worded differently enough from the long analysis for the two documents to be told apart easily.
D) That nothing removed in the condensing changes the recommendation, particularly any condition on which that recommendation depends.
correct_answers: D) That nothing removed in the condensing changes the recommendation, particularly any condition on which that recommendation depends.
explanations: House style helps a paper land well with a familiar audience, but it is a presentation concern. A perfectly styled summary can still have lost the qualification that made the recommendation safe.
Meeting the length limit is a formatting requirement that must be satisfied anyway, and it is easy to check. It says nothing about whether the shortened paper still supports the decision being made.

Distinguishing the two documents is a filing convenience at best. Deliberately rewording for difference risks introducing changes of meaning rather than protecting the committee from acting on a distorted summary.

Correct. Adapting for an audience must not change what the audience will do. A caveat or condition dropped in the interests of brevity turns a qualified recommendation into an unqualified one for the people acting on it.

question: A charity is scoping a use case in which Claude would decide which grant applications are rejected at first screening, removing the review panel's initial pass entirely. What is the greatest concern with this use case?
options: A) The screening criteria may be worded differently across the charity's several grant programmes.
B) The number of applications in each round may be larger than one conversation can work through.
C) Panel members may need extra training before they can interpret the reasoning given for each decision.
D) Rejection at first screening is not seen or appealed by anyone, so no person owns the decision made.
correct_answers: D) Rejection at first screening is not seen or appealed by anyone, so no person owns the decision made.
explanations: Inconsistent criteria across programmes is a real quality problem, and it is worth fixing, but it can be corrected by harmonising the wording. It does not touch the question of who is answerable for a rejection.
Volume is a workload constraint that can be handled by processing applications in batches. It affects how the screening would be run rather than whether the decision should be delegated at all.

Training panel members to read the reasoning would help, but it assumes the panel still reviews the decisions. In the use case as described the panel's initial pass has been removed, so there is nothing left for them to interpret.

Correct. A first-pass rejection is effectively final for the applicant and no human sees it, so an error is neither visible nor recoverable and nobody is accountable for it. Work carrying that kind of consequence should keep a person in the decision, with Claude preparing the assessment instead.

question: A consultant set account-wide instructions two years ago describing a role they no longer hold, and answers now carry the wrong framing. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A) Mention the correct role at the start of each conversation and accept the extra step as normal.
B) Update the account-wide instructions so they describe the consultant's current role and the work they do now.
C) Create a brand-new account so that the outdated preferences are all left behind with the previous configuration.
D) Add a line to every project's instructions telling Claude to disregard the account-wide instructions.
correct_answers: B) Update the account-wide instructions so they describe the consultant's current role and the work they do now.
explanations: Repeating a correction forever is the manual overhead durable configuration exists to remove.
Correct. Personal configuration needs the same periodic refresh as any other durable direction.
Abandoning an account to escape a stale setting loses all the history and other configuration with it.
This is a workaround that leaves the outdated configuration in place for all work outside projects.

question: A charity's operations analyst asks Claude to produce a requirements list for a new volunteer scheduling process, giving it only the notes from the two coordinators who happened to be available that week. The list reads as thorough and is circulated as the agreed requirements. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Claude will refuse to produce a requirements list from notes covering part of the service
B) The two coordinators will be named in the list, exposing internal comments to everyone
C) The list will present gaps in the source notes as settled requirements nobody stated
D) The list will be too long for the sponsor to read before the decision has to be made
correct_answers: C) The list will present gaps in the source notes as settled requirements nobody stated
explanations: Claude will work with whatever it is given; it does not withhold an answer because the input covers only part of the service.
Attribution is a housekeeping matter and easily corrected; it does not affect whether the requirements themselves are real.

Correct. Claude will fill an incomplete picture with plausible, well-written material. Circulated as "the agreed requirements", inferred content becomes indistinguishable from what stakeholders actually asked for.
Length is a presentation problem. A concise list built on the same partial input would carry exactly the same defect.

question: A recruiting team answers similar candidate questions every week and re-pastes the same rubric and tone rules into every new chat. Which two moves fit the available features? Select two.
options: A) Ask Claude at the end of each chat to remember the rubric for whichever chat opens next.
B) Move the rubric and the tone rules into a Project, so each chat starts from that context.
C) Run every one of the candidate questions through Research mode so answers arrive with citations.
D) Keep the reusable reply template as an artifact the team can open and edit between chats.
E) Keep one very long running chat open so the rubric stays somewhere in the history above.
correct_answers: B) Move the rubric and the tone rules into a Project, so each chat starts from that context.
D) Keep the reusable reply template as an artifact the team can open and edit between chats.
explanations: Incorrect. A request made inside one chat does not durably carry team context into the next one; that is what a Project is for.
Correct. A Project is the feature for recurring work that needs shared context, so the rubric and tone rules stop being re-pasted every week.
Incorrect. Research mode is for agentic multi-step investigation of open questions, not for applying a known internal rubric.
Correct. The reply template is self-contained content the team returns to and edits, which is what an artifact is for.
Incorrect. One ever-growing chat pushes against the context limit and still leaves the rubric buried instead of durably configured.

question: A financial analyst asks a Claude-powered assistant, "What was Acme Corp's closing stock price yesterday?" The assistant has no tools enabled and answers with a specific dollar figure stated confidently. What is the most likely validation concern with this response?
options: A) The figure is unreliable because stock prices are personal financial data that Claude is restricted from ever discussing
B) The response is untrustworthy because Claude always declines to answer any question that involves specific numbers
C) Without a tool that retrieves external data, the figure is likely fabricated since Claude cannot know yesterday's actual price
D) The response cannot be trusted because Claude's training data updates in real time and may include conflicting price figures
correct_answers: C) Without a tool that retrieves external data, the figure is likely fabricated since Claude cannot know yesterday's actual price
explanations: Public stock prices are not restricted personal data, so this is not the relevant validation issue.
Claude does not categorically refuse numeric answers; the concern here is factual grounding, not refusal behavior.

Correct. Claude's knowledge comes from training data with a cutoff and does not include live market data. Without a tool like web search to fetch current information, a specific recent stock price is likely a hallucination and should be treated as unverified.
Claude's training data has a fixed cutoff and is not updated in real time, which is precisely why an ungrounded answer about yesterday's price is risky.

question: What is the most effective way to use Claude to analyze and categorize a list of requirements?
options: A) Ask Claude to design a new spreadsheet layout for organizing the requirements, including columns for type and priority.
B) Ask Claude to review each requirement for completeness, clarity, and testability without performing classification.
C) Ask Claude to remove fifty percent of the requirements at random to reduce workload, simplifying the review process.
D) Ask Claude to classify each requirement as functional, non-functional, or constraint with explanations.
correct_answers: D) Ask Claude to classify each requirement as functional, non-functional, or constraint with explanations.
explanations: Incorrect. Designing a spreadsheet layout focuses on formatting rather than analyzing or categorizing requirements. It does not leverage Claude's ability to classify requirements but instead adds a workflow artifact that doesn't directly address the need for analysis.

Incorrect. This approach only evaluates quality attributes but does not categorize requirements, which is the primary goal of analysis. It fails to leverage Claude's classification capabilities, missing the chance to organize and understand requirements effectively.

Incorrect. Randomly removing requirements is not a valid analysis or categorization technique and risks losing essential information. It compromises the completeness of the requirements set and fails to achieve proper classification.

Correct. This directly uses Claude's strength in analysis and classification by categorizing requirements into functional, non-functional, or constraint, along with explanations. It enhances clarity, traceability, and follows best practices for requirements analysis.

question: A team judges its Claude-assisted research notes purely by whether colleagues say they enjoy reading them. What is the greatest risk in using this as the measure?
options: A) Positive ratings may encourage the team to produce more notes than colleagues have time to read.
B) Fluent, confident notes can be well liked while carrying errors nobody checked against sources.
C) Colleagues who read quickly may rate the notes higher than colleagues who read them thoroughly.
D) Preferences drift over time, which makes this quarter's ratings hard to compare with last quarter's.
correct_answers: B) Fluent, confident notes can be well liked while carrying errors nobody checked against sources.
explanations: Producing more notes is a workload effect rather than a risk to the reliability of the notes.
Correct. Reader satisfaction measures how the notes read, not whether they are right, so a confident and wrong note scores as well as a correct one and the error is adopted.
Variation between readers adds noise to the measure, but the deeper problem is what it measures at all.
Drift makes comparison harder over time; it does not explain why accuracy goes unmeasured.

question: A team wants Claude to brainstorm names for a new product from the perspective of a branding specialist, aiming for tone and instincts consistent with that professional background throughout the session. What is a simple, effective way to set this up?

question: A teacher pastes a whole term of student feedback into a single chat and keeps asking Claude to summarise themes as the conversation grows very long. What is the greatest risk to the quality of her summaries?
options: A) The chat will refuse to accept any further messages until she upgrades to a higher-priced plan tier.
B) Every answer will be produced by a weaker model once the conversation has passed the context window limit.
C) Claude will delete the earlier messages from the chat history, leaving her nothing at all to check.
D) Detail from early in the chat may be condensed away, so her theme counts can quietly omit some feedback.
correct_answers: D) Detail from early in the chat may be condensed away, so her theme counts can quietly omit some feedback.
explanations: Incorrect. Reaching a length limit does not force a plan upgrade; she can continue in a new chat or move the material into a Project.
Incorrect. The model in use does not change because a conversation is long. Approaching the limit affects available working memory, not model quality.
Incorrect. Condensing earlier messages does not erase them. The full chat history stays readable, so she can still go back and check.
Correct. As a conversation approaches the context limit, earlier messages are condensed to make room. The summary still reads confidently, but it may no longer rest on every comment she pasted in.

question: A product manager is using Claude to help define the minimum viable product (MVP) for a new feature. Which approach should they use?
options: A) Ask Claude to prioritize features considering business value, feasibility, and strategic alignment.
B) Ask Claude to randomly pick features to include in the MVP without any criteria, by random selection from the list.
C) Ask Claude to generate even more feature ideas to expand the list for the MVP, then pick the most requested ones.
D) Ask Claude to keep only features endorsed by the most senior stakeholder, using their approval as the deciding factor.
correct_answers: A) Ask Claude to prioritize features considering business value, feasibility, and strategic alignment.
explanations: Correct. Prioritizing features based on business value, feasibility, and strategic alignment ensures the MVP delivers the most impact with the least risk. This structured approach helps define a lean, focused product that addresses key user needs while remaining realistic to build.

question: An e-commerce operator wants Claude to auto-generate customer support replies containing fabricated tracking numbers and fake refund confirmation emails to delay legitimate refund requests. Is this an appropriate use of Claude?
options: A) Yes, because automating customer support, including generating tracking and confirmation messages, is a common and encouraged use case.
B) Yes, as long as a human support agent reviews each fabricated tracking number and confirmation email to verify accuracy before sending.
C) No, because the Usage Policy requires outgoing emails to use approved services, and using an unapproved vendor violates the policy.
D) No because the Usage Policy bans generating fraudulent documents such as fake confirmations to deceive customers.
correct_answers: D) No because the Usage Policy bans generating fraudulent documents such as fake confirmations to deceive customers.
explanations: Incorrect. Automating customer support is a common and encouraged use case, but this scenario involves generating fabricated tracking numbers and fake refund confirmations to deliberately deceive customers. The Usage Policy prohibits such deceptive content regardless of the general use case.

Incorrect. Having a human review fabricated information does not make it legitimate; the content remains deceptive by design. The Usage Policy prohibits fraudulent content irrespective of any review process.

Incorrect. The violation stems from the fabricated content intended to deceive customers, not from using an unapproved email service. The Usage Policy focuses on the deceptive nature of the communication, not the delivery method.

Correct. The Usage Policy explicitly bans generating fraudulent documents, including fake confirmations and deceptive communications intended to mislead customers. This scenario directly violates that prohibition.

question: A team adds Claude to the middle of a workflow that already produces frequent rework, without changing anything else about it. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Claude will refuse to take part in a workflow that has not first been documented
B) The team will need a different plan tier before Claude can join an existing flow
C) Colleagues downstream will receive their work later than the old workflow gave it
D) The same faults now appear faster and in greater volume than they did before
correct_answers: D) The same faults now appear faster and in greater volume than they did before
explanations: Claude does not require a workflow to be documented before it will contribute to a step.
Plan tier is not what determines whether an existing process can be augmented, and it would not cause rework.
The likely effect is faster delivery, not slower; the problem is what is being delivered, not when.
Correct. Speeding up a broken process scales its defects. The rework was caused by the workflow's design, and inserting Claude without addressing that simply produces more of it, sooner.

question: A procurement lead asks Claude to recommend one of three suppliers, giving it only the brochures and web copy that each supplier provided. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The comparison can only reflect what each supplier says about itself, with no independent evidence.
B) Comparing three suppliers at once may produce an answer that is too long for the committee pack.
C) The recommendation may be written in a tone that is too informal for a procurement committee.
D) The brochures may each use different section headings, which makes the comparison harder to lay out neatly.
correct_answers: A) The comparison can only reflect what each supplier says about itself, with no independent evidence.
explanations: Correct. Every input is written by the party being assessed, so the comparison measures marketing quality rather than supplier quality. The output will read as a balanced analysis while containing no reference checks, pricing evidence or performance history at all.
Length can be controlled by asking for a shorter comparison or a summary table. A recommendation that is too long is inconvenient; one built on marketing claims is misleading.
Tone is adjusted by asking for a different register. It affects how the recommendation reads to the committee, not whether the underlying comparison is sound.
Inconsistent headings make the material messier to align and may need a little manual mapping. This is a presentation problem rather than a defect in the evidence base.

question: A membership team must recommend one new member benefit to its board. Which sequence of task types should they work through?
options: A) Write the recommendation; generate candidate benefits; look up what comparable bodies offer; weigh the shortlist against their budget.
B) Look up what comparable bodies offer; write the recommendation; weigh the shortlist against their budget; generate candidate benefits.
C) Generate candidate benefits; look up what comparable bodies offer; weigh the shortlist against their budget; write the recommendation.
D) Weigh the shortlist against their budget; write the recommendation; generate candidate benefits; look up what comparable bodies offer.
correct_answers: C) Generate candidate benefits; look up what comparable bodies offer; weigh the shortlist against their budget; write the recommendation.
explanations: Writing the recommendation first fixes the conclusion, and the generation and research stages then serve to justify a choice already made.
Research before generation is defensible, but the recommendation is written second here, ahead of the weighing and the generation it depends on.

Correct. Each task type feeds the next: open generation widens the field, research grounds the candidates in what others actually do, weighing against the budget narrows them, and only then is there a decision worth writing up.
A shortlist cannot be weighed before any candidates have been generated, so this ordering starts from something that does not yet exist.
