question: A stakeholder has submitted the requirement "make monthly reporting easier." An analyst wants Claude to help prepare for the next stakeholder meeting. Which use of Claude is most appropriate here?
options: A) Ask Claude to rewrite the requirement in formal language so it can be entered into the requirements log.
B) Ask Claude to describe how comparable organisations define easier reporting and adopt that wording.
C) Ask Claude to decide which reading the stakeholder most likely meant, and then build the entire delivery plan on it.
D) Ask Claude to produce several plausible readings of the requirement plus questions to put to the stakeholder.
correct_answers: D) Ask Claude to produce several plausible readings of the requirement plus questions to put to the stakeholder.
explanations: Formalising the language makes a vague requirement look rigorous without adding any information. The log then contains a polished statement that still cannot be built or tested, and the ambiguity survives into design.

Adopting an external definition replaces this stakeholder's need with a generic one. It also produces confident-sounding wording that nobody in the organisation has agreed to, which makes the ambiguity harder to spot later, not easier.

Letting Claude pick the most likely reading converts an open question into a hidden assumption. The stakeholder is available to answer, so guessing on their behalf trades a cheap clarification for an expensive misunderstanding.

Correct. Ambiguity is resolved by the stakeholder, not by the tool. Claude is best used here to widen the analyst's view of what the phrase could mean and to generate the specific questions that will close it, so the meeting produces a decision rather than another vague line.

question: A designer asks Claude to create a company logo as a scalable vector graphic that they can drop directly into their design tool. Which output approach is appropriate?

correct_answers: B) An artifact containing the SVG markup, since SVG images are a supported artifact content type meant for standalone, reusable visual assets
explanations: Incorrect. Design tools do not automatically convert prose descriptions into vector paths, so plain text would not give the designer a usable asset.

Incorrect. Strict tool use validates parameters passed to a defined tool; it is not a mechanism for generating or delivering image assets.
Incorrect. JSON outputs are meant for structured data fields, not for producing renderable vector graphics that a design tool can import directly.

question: A finance team wants Claude to help streamline month-end close, but the process has never been written down and each of the four preparers does parts of it differently. What should the team do first?
options: A) Write down how the close actually runs today, including exceptions and the preparers' own variations.
B) Ask Claude to describe a typical month-end close process and use that description as the starting point.
C) Ask Claude to list the month-end steps that are most often automated in finance teams of a similar size.
D) Ask each preparer to try Claude on their own part of the close and then share whatever improvements they find.
correct_answers: A) Write down how the close actually runs today, including exceptions and the preparers' own variations.
explanations: Correct. There is nothing to optimise until the current process is visible, and the exceptions and per-preparer variations are exactly where the inefficiency lives. Capturing them gives Claude a real process to analyse and gives the team a baseline to improve against.

A typical close describes the average of other organisations, not this one. Optimising against it produces recommendations aimed at steps this team may not perform and misses the variations that are the actual source of friction.

A list of commonly automated steps is a solution catalogue offered before the problem is known. It also encourages the team to chase whichever steps are easy to automate rather than the ones costing them time.

Four uncoordinated experiments deepen the existing problem, which is that four people already do the close differently. Local improvements to inconsistent practice make the overall process harder to reason about.

question: A team is designing an agent that must autonomously produce very long outputs, such as an extensive generated report or a large batch of generated code, and wants the model tier best associated with handling the most demanding, large-scale generation tasks. Which tier should they choose?
options: A) Any tier works equally well, since maximum output length does not differ meaningfully across current models
B) Claude Sonnet, since it is the only tier that supports generating long-form output at all
C) Claude Haiku, since its lower cost per token always outweighs output-length considerations for any task
D) Claude Opus, since it is positioned for the largest-scale, most complex generation and engineering tasks
correct_answers: D) Claude Opus, since it is positioned for the largest-scale, most complex generation and engineering tasks
explanations: Model tiers differ in intelligence, latency, and cost for demanding generation tasks, so the choice of tier is not interchangeable for the most complex, large-scale work described here.
Long-form output generation is supported across the current model lineup, not exclusively by Sonnet, so this option misstates the family's capabilities.
Lower cost per token is a real advantage of Haiku, but for the most demanding, large-scale generation tasks Anthropic points to the most capable tier rather than defaulting to the cheapest one.
Correct. Opus is recommended for the largest-scale, most complex engineering and generation work, matching a scenario centered on demanding, large-scale autonomous output generation.

question: A Claude-drafted notice about a service change is going out to every customer tomorrow. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Have the accountable owner review it; publish the notice to customers; check the facts against the source; obtain the required sign-off.
B) Check the facts against the source; have the accountable owner review it; obtain the required sign-off; publish the notice to customers.
C) Publish the notice to customers; check the facts against the source; have the accountable owner review it; obtain the required sign-off.
D) Obtain the required sign-off; check the facts against the source; publish the notice to customers; have the accountable owner review it.
correct_answers: B) Check the facts against the source; have the accountable owner review it; obtain the required sign-off; publish the notice to customers.
explanations: Incorrect. The owner reviews unverified content, and the notice is published before either the fact check or the sign-off has happened.
Correct. Factual checking comes first because the owner's judgment depends on accurate content, sign-off follows a completed review, and publication is the last irreversible step.
Incorrect. Publication comes before every check, which means any error reaches customers before anyone has looked for it.
Incorrect. Sign-off is given before anything has been checked, and the owner's review lands after customers have already received the notice.

question: A manager has broken a customer-refund policy rewrite into five stages and wants one point at which she personally reviews the work. Where should that review sit?
options: A) After the stage that settles which refund cases are covered, because every later stage is written to that decision.
B) After the first stage, since reviewing early gives her the longest possible time to act on anything she finds.
C) At whichever stage happens to fall in the middle, which keeps the amount of unreviewed work on each side even.
D) At the very end, once all five stages are complete, so that she reviews the finished policy as customers will read it.
correct_answers: A) After the stage that settles which refund cases are covered, because every later stage is written to that decision.
explanations: Correct. A checkpoint is worth most immediately after the decision that constrains everything downstream. If the covered cases are wrong, the wording, the examples and the exceptions are all wrong too, and catching that later means rewriting all of them.
Reviewing the first stage is cheap but often premature, since the first stage may be preparatory and not yet contain the decision that matters.
Splitting by position balances the volume of unreviewed work but ignores which stage actually carries the consequential decision.
A final review catches errors at the point where correcting them means redoing the stages that followed the mistake.

question: Explanation
options: A) Ground responses in verified documentation and route uncertain answers to human agents
B) Instruct the model through the system prompt to always sound highly confident to build trust
C) Accept the current error rate as a normal and unavoidable cost of generative AI in support

correct_answers: A) Ground responses in verified documentation and route uncertain answers to human agents
explanations: Correct. Grounding responses in verified sources and escalating uncertain or high-stakes cases to humans directly addresses the risk of confident hallucinations while keeping the tool useful.
Incorrect. Instructing the model to sound more confident would worsen the ethical problem by making incorrect answers even more convincing.
Incorrect. Treating hallucination risk as unavoidable ignores practical mitigations like retrieval grounding and human escalation that responsible deployments should use.
Incorrect. Disabling all specification discussion removes the tool's core value rather than addressing the accuracy problem responsibly.

question: A programme manager is writing a single request asking Claude to turn a supplier's quarterly report into a short briefing note for her steering group. In what order should she assemble the request?
options: A) State the length and sections needed; name the task and who reads the note; say what to do where the report is silent; paste the supplier report and label it.
B) Say what to do where the report is silent; state the length and sections needed; paste the supplier report and label it; name the task and who reads the note.
C) Name the task and who reads the note; paste the supplier report and label it; state the length and sections needed; say what to do where the report is silent.
D) Paste the supplier report and label it; say what to do where the report is silent; state the length and sections needed; name the task and who reads the note.
correct_answers: C) Name the task and who reads the note; paste the supplier report and label it; state the length and sections needed; say what to do where the report is silent.
explanations: Length and sections are decisions about presentation. Fixing them before the task and the source are on the table means the shape is chosen before the content is known.
Handling for gaps is meaningless until the task and the material are defined, so this ordering asks for edge-case rules before the main case exists.

Correct. The task and audience frame everything that follows, the labelled source supplies the substance, format then shapes it, and the instruction about gaps covers what the source cannot answer. Each step depends on the one before it.
Leading with the pasted report and holding back the task until the end means the material arrives with no stated purpose, and gap handling is decided before anyone knows what the note is for.

question: When a stakeholder provides an ambiguous requirement like 'secure login', what is the best approach when using Claude for requirements analysis?
options: A) Ask Claude to build a login feature from the requirement, assuming it is sufficiently clear.
B) Ask Claude to interpret 'secure login' as two-factor authentication and document that assumption.
C) Ask Claude to generate specific clarifying questions about what 'secure login' entails to stakeholders.
D) Ask Claude to confirm that 'secure login' is clear and does not require further elaboration.
correct_answers: C) Ask Claude to generate specific clarifying questions about what 'secure login' entails to stakeholders.
explanations: Incorrect. Asking Claude to build a login feature from an ambiguous requirement like 'secure login' risks producing a misaligned or incomplete solution. It is better to first clarify the requirement by gathering details about authentication methods, security standards, and user constraints.

Incorrect. Interpreting 'secure login' as two-factor authentication without validation risks making an incorrect assumption. While documenting assumptions can be useful, arbitrarily locking in a design choice like two-factor authentication may introduce a requirement that does not match stakeholder intent.

Correct. Asking Claude to generate specific clarifying questions helps stakeholders define the scope and specifics of 'secure login', reducing assumptions. This aligns with requirements analysis best practices by ensuring the solution addresses actual needs before implementation.

Incorrect. Confirming that 'secure login' is clear without further elaboration overlooks its inherent ambiguity. The phrase is not specific enough to be complete; skipping a discovery step can lead to misunderstandings and a solution that does not meet real needs.

question: A strategy lead is planning a market-entry study and wants Claude to help with the research phase of it. Which two approaches are sound? Select two.

correct_answers: B) Ask Claude to draft the research plan and its open questions, then have the team refine it.

question: Two departments have submitted requirements for the same intake queue that directly contradict each other about who approves exceptions. The analyst is preparing the requirements pack for a decision meeting. What should the analyst do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to set out every point at which the two submissions conflict, so they can be tabled openly.
B) Ask Claude to merge the two submissions into one wording that both departments could plausibly accept.
C) Ask Claude to recommend the approval route that is more common in organisations of a comparable size.
D) Ask Claude to drop the approval requirements from the pack and raise them later during the design phase.
correct_answers: A) Ask Claude to set out every point at which the two submissions conflict, so they can be tabled openly.
explanations: Correct. The analyst's job is to make the conflict visible and decidable, not to remove it. A precise list of where the two submissions diverge turns a vague disagreement into a short agenda that the decision meeting can actually settle.

Merging contradictory statements into agreeable wording hides the disagreement rather than resolving it. The conflict then resurfaces during delivery, when the cost of settling who approves exceptions is far higher.

What comparable organisations do is not evidence about this organisation's accountability for exceptions. It also asks Claude to settle a governance question that belongs to the two departments and their sponsor.

Removing the contested requirement leaves the pack looking complete while the hardest question is unanswered. Deferring it to design guarantees the argument happens later, with a partly built process depending on the outcome.

question: A team lead grants "Can edit" access on a shared project to everyone who might ever open it, rather than giving most people "Can view". What is the greatest risk?

Access levels within a project are not billed individually.
Correct. Broad edit rights let the agreed direction and sources be altered silently by any of the members.

question: A procurement officer will ask Claude to summarise an uploaded framework agreement into about forty points, and a colleague will have to spot-check that summary against the agreement in fifteen minutes. What should she build into the request to make that check practical?
options: A) Ask for each point to name the clause of the agreement it came from, so the colleague can go straight to that clause and compare.
B) Ask for the points to be ordered by how commercially important each one is, so the colleague starts with the points that matter most.
C) Ask for the summary to be kept to short single sentences, so the colleague can read the whole of it well inside the fifteen minutes.
D) Ask for a confidence rating beside each point, so the colleague can concentrate the checking effort on the points rated least certain.
correct_answers: A) Ask for each point to name the clause of the agreement it came from, so the colleague can go straight to that clause and compare.
explanations: Correct. Tying each point to its clause turns verification into a direct comparison at source, which is the only step that shows whether the agreement was represented accurately, and it fits the time available.
Importance ordering helps the colleague choose what to look at, but it does not help him find the corresponding clause in a long agreement, which is where the fifteen minutes would actually be spent.
Brevity makes the summary quicker to read but no quicker to verify. The colleague can read every point and still be unable to locate the clause each one is supposed to rest on.
A self-declared confidence rating is not a reliable guide to which points are wrong, and it can misdirect the check by giving high confidence to a point that was misread from the agreement.

question: Which of the following is the most effective method for using Claude to produce an executive summary of a lengthy market report?
options: A) Break the report into sections, prompt Claude to summarize each section separately, and then manually compile those summaries.
B) Provide the report and ask Claude to produce a single-paragraph executive summary without providing any explicit structure or focus areas.
C) Supply the entire report, specify a desired structure (e.g., key trends, risks, opportunities), and request a concise structured summary.
D) Upload the report and ask Claude to list all action items directly mentioned in the text, ignoring the general market context.
correct_answers: C) Supply the entire report, specify a desired structure (e.g., key trends, risks, opportunities), and request a concise structured summary.
explanations: Incorrect. While breaking the report into sections can help process long documents, manually compiling separate summaries adds extra work and can introduce inconsistency. This approach is less efficient than prompting Claude to generate a structured executive summary directly from the full report.

Incorrect. Providing the report without any explicit structure or focus areas may result in a generic or unfocused single-paragraph summary. Claude benefits from clear guidance to produce a summary that is structured and relevant for an executive audience.

Correct. Supplying the entire report and specifying a desired structure (e.g., key trends, risks, opportunities) ensures a concise, well-organized, and relevant executive summary. This leverages Claude's ability to follow detailed instructions and improves efficiency.

Incorrect. Asking Claude to list only action items directly mentioned in the text is too narrow for an executive summary and ignores broader context such as trends, risks, and opportunities. This makes the output less useful for strategic decision-making.

question: A team asks Claude to draw up options for reorganising its weekly reporting cycle, and Claude returns three credible options. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A) Adopt the option Claude lists first, since it ordered them by likely effectiveness
B) Ask for a fourth option, on the basis that more choices produce a better decision
C) Ask Claude to pick one of the three and put that choice to the sponsor as agreed
D) Test each option against the constraints the team already knows it must satisfy
correct_answers: D) Test each option against the constraints the team already knows it must satisfy
explanations: Order of presentation carries no ranking, and treating it as one substitutes a formatting artefact for analysis.
A fourth option adds volume without resolving anything, because nothing has yet been checked against what the team needs.
Asking Claude to choose hands over the accountable part of the decision while leaving the constraints untested.
Correct. Generating options is delegable; choosing between them against the team's real constraints is the judgement the team has to own, and it is what turns three suggestions into a decision.

question: A team lead is explaining hallucinations to colleagues who are new to using Claude at work. Which two statements should she include because they are accurate? Select two.
options: A) They occur mainly in long responses, so keeping answers short avoids the problem well.
B) They only occur when Claude has no access to the web and must rely on what it knows.
C) They can appear in answers that read fluently and hold together from start to finish.
D) They are a known limit of current frontier models, not a sign of a broken setup.
E) They can be removed entirely by instructing Claude to answer only when it is certain.
correct_answers: C) They can appear in answers that read fluently and hold together from start to finish.
D) They are a known limit of current frontier models, not a sign of a broken setup.
explanations: Brevity does not confer accuracy. A one-line answer can contain an invented figure just as easily as a long one, and offers fewer clues to catch it.
Web access changes where material comes from but does not remove the possibility of a misstatement, including a source being summarised incorrectly.
Correct. Fluency and internal coherence are not evidence of truth, which is exactly why colleagues who judge by readability tend to miss fabricated content.
Correct. Framing this as a known model limitation is a separate and important point: colleagues should not assume a setting was configured wrongly and stop checking.
No instruction eliminates the behaviour. Asking for certainty can suppress useful hedging while leaving confident errors in place.

question: An analyst uses Claude's research capability to produce a market briefing with citations, then pastes the briefing into a board paper without opening any of the cited sources. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The research may have taken several minutes to run and consumed a noticeable share of the monthly usage.
B) A cited claim may not be supported by the source, and the citations make the paper look already checked.

question: A company systematically queries Claude through the API to collect large volumes of model outputs, then uses that data to train a rival large language model that it plans to sell. This activity is:
options: A) Prohibited under the Usage Policy's restrictions on using Claude's outputs to develop competing models.
B) Prohibited only if the company also republishes Anthropic's original training data alongside the generated outputs.
C) Permitted as long as the resulting competing model is not marketed as being built using Claude's technology.
D) Permitted because outputs generated through the API belong entirely to the company that generated them without restriction.
correct_answers: A) Prohibited under the Usage Policy's restrictions on using Claude's outputs to develop competing models.
explanations: Correct. The Usage Policy prohibits model scraping and using Claude's outputs to develop competing models.
Incorrect. The prohibition applies to the scraping and competing-model training itself, not only to republishing Anthropic's original training data.
Incorrect. Omitting attribution does not make the underlying prohibited activity, training a competitor on scraped outputs, acceptable.
Incorrect. Ownership of individual outputs does not exempt systematic scraping used to train a competing model from Usage Policy restrictions.

question: A long strategy chat has drifted off track, and it keeps re-deriving background the team will still need next week. Which two actions are appropriate here? Select two.
options: A) Start a fresh chat that restates the current goal and carries only the material still needed.
B) Switch over to the lightest and fastest tier so that continuing this long conversation costs less.
C) Move the durable background into a Project, so later chats begin from it without redoing it.
D) Carry on in the same chat and restate the goal more forcefully every time answers drift off.
E) Delete earlier messages from the chat so that older material stops shaping the newer replies.
correct_answers: A) Start a fresh chat that restates the current goal and carries only the material still needed.
C) Move the durable background into a Project, so later chats begin from it without redoing it.
explanations: Correct. Restarting with a tight restatement clears accumulated drift and keeps only the context that is still relevant.
Incorrect. A cheaper tier does not fix drift, and it does not persist the background the team will need again.
Correct. Background needed again next week is durable context, and a Project is where durable context belongs.
Incorrect. Repeating the goal more forcefully in a drifting conversation rarely recovers it and adds to an already crowded context.
Incorrect. Pruning messages is not how a drifting chat is repaired, and it does not make the background durable for next week.

question: A staff member realises she has pasted regulated customer records into her personal Claude account rather than the company's managed workspace. Which sequence is correct?
options: A) Redo the work in the managed workspace; delete the affected conversations as the response team directs; stop using the personal account for this work; report the incident through the escalation path the policy names.

B) Delete the affected conversations as the response team directs; stop using the personal account for this work; report the incident through the escalation path the policy names; redo the work in the managed workspace.

C) Stop using the personal account for this work; report the incident through the escalation path the policy names; delete the affected conversations as the response team directs; redo the work in the managed workspace.

D) Report the incident through the escalation path the policy names; redo the work in the managed workspace; delete the affected conversations as the response team directs; stop using the personal account for this work.
correct_answers: C) Stop using the personal account for this work; report the incident through the escalation path the policy names; delete the affected conversations as the response team directs; redo the work in the managed workspace.
explanations: Getting the work done comes ahead of every governance step, and the incident is reported last of all. By then the conversations have already been deleted without direction and the exposure has gone unreported.

Deletion is placed before the incident has been reported, so there is nobody yet to direct it. Destroying the record ahead of the report also removes the evidence the response team needs to scope what was exposed.

Correct. Containment comes first, so no further regulated data is exposed; the incident is then reported through the path the policy names, so the response team can assess it; remediation such as deletion follows their direction rather than preceding it; and the work resumes in the approved workspace.

Reporting comes first here, but the exposure is left running: the work is redone and conversations deleted while the personal account is still in use for regulated material, and it is stopped only at the very end.

question: A budget summary written in prose gives departmental figures and then states a total. The finance officer reads it and finds nothing that looks out of place. What is the greatest risk in accepting it?
options: A) The stated total may not be the sum of the figures given, and prose gives no visual cue that anything is wrong.
B) The summary may express figures in thousands where the finance team's own reports express them in millions.
C) The departments may be listed in a slightly different order from the one that the finance team's reports normally use.
D) The prose format makes the summary harder to move into the reporting spreadsheet the finance team uses.
correct_answers: A) The stated total may not be the sum of the figures given, and prose gives no visual cue that anything is wrong.
explanations: Correct. A total written as a sentence carries no arithmetic behind it, and prose hides the mismatch that a column of figures would make obvious. It has to be re-added by hand before the summary is trusted.
A units mismatch is a real hazard, but it usually shows up as figures that are wildly out of scale and so is caught on reading.
Ordering affects how quickly a reader finds a department and does not change any of the values reported.
Transferring prose into a spreadsheet is inconvenient, but it is handling effort rather than a threat to the numbers themselves.

question: Given a written description of an approvals workflow, Claude suggests removing a second review step that appears redundant. The team plans to remove it next week. What is the greatest concern?
options: A) Removing a step may require retraining the reviewers who currently perform the second review.
B) The description given to Claude may not use the same step names that the workflow tracking tool records.
C) The time saved may be smaller than the team expects once the change has been rolled out fully.
D) The step may exist for a control reason that was never written into the description Claude was given.
correct_answers: D) The step may exist for a control reason that was never written into the description Claude was given.
explanations: Retraining is a normal cost of any process change and is planned for openly. It is a consequence of the decision rather than a reason the decision might be wrong.
Mismatched naming is a mapping nuisance that surfaces quickly and is easy to reconcile. It might make the analysis harder to read, but it does not make removing the step dangerous.
A disappointing saving means the change was not worth much, which is a mild outcome. The team would be no worse off than before, whereas removing a control leaves them exposed.

Correct. Claude can only reason about what the description contains, and the reasons for control steps are usually the part nobody writes down. A step that looks redundant on paper may be the segregation of duties or fraud check an auditor relies on, and removing it is not easily undone.

question: A project lead is finishing a client status pack that Claude helped draft. His firm's AI policy requires AI assistance to be disclosed on external documents, and the client contract says nothing about the subject. What should be his first step?
options: A) Leave the disclosure off, because the contract is silent and the client has not asked for it.
B) Ask the client whether they would rather the pack carried no disclosure line on it at all.
C) Add the disclosure the firm's policy requires, since the contract does not override it.
D) Rewrite enough of Claude's wording that he can argue the disclosure requirement no longer applies.
correct_answers: C) Add the disclosure the firm's policy requires, since the contract does not override it.
explanations: Treating silence in the contract as permission inverts the relationship between the two. The internal policy binds the firm's staff regardless of what a client has thought to ask about.
Inviting the client to waive a rule the firm set for itself puts the obligation in the wrong hands, and it would be awkward to act on a preference that conflicts with the policy.

Correct. The policy applies to external documents and the contract's silence does not create an exception to it. Disclosing is the required action, and it is also the honest one for a pack the client will rely on.
Editing the text in order to escape the disclosure defeats the purpose of the rule and is a deliberate attempt to reach a technicality rather than a good-faith reading of the policy.

question: A bid writer keeps receiving long proposal drafts organised in a way her reviewers dislike, and each rewrite costs a full round. Which sequence should she follow instead?
options: A) Have the draft written to the agreed outline; ask for a section outline; correct the outline with reviewers; check the draft against the outline.
B) Correct the outline with reviewers; ask for a section outline; check the draft against the outline; have the draft written to the agreed outline.
C) Check the draft against the outline; have the draft written to the agreed outline; ask for a section outline; correct the outline with reviewers.
D) Ask for a section outline; correct the outline with reviewers; have the draft written to the agreed outline; check the draft against the outline.
correct_answers: D) Ask for a section outline; correct the outline with reviewers; have the draft written to the agreed outline; check the draft against the outline.
explanations: The draft is written before any outline exists, so the expensive step happens first and the outline is produced after the structure has already been committed to.
Reviewers cannot correct an outline that has not been requested yet, and the draft is written last, after the check that was meant to test it.
Checking a draft that has not been produced is impossible, and the outline work arrives after both the draft and its review.

Correct. The disagreement is about structure, and an outline is the cheapest thing that exposes structure. Reviewers settle the shape in minutes, the full draft is written only once, and the final check confirms it followed the agreed outline.

question: Six weeks in, a team must decide whether to keep a Claude-assisted intake summarising arrangement or return to the previous approach. Which comparison best supports that decision?
options: A) How much faster the summaries are produced now than the team managed before the trial.
B) How the summaries compare with the team's own on the criteria agreed before the trial began.
C) Whether the summaries are entirely free of error, since a wrong summary can misdirect a case.
D) Whether participants say they enjoy the new arrangement more than the approach it replaced.
correct_answers: B) How the summaries compare with the team's own on the criteria agreed before the trial began.
explanations: Speed alone answers half the question. Faster summaries that are less accurate would push cost downstream into misdirected cases, which is why speed has to be weighed against the agreed quality criteria.

Correct. The decision is a comparison against the realistic alternative, measured on criteria fixed in advance so the standard cannot drift to fit the result. That is what turns six weeks of experience into an evidenced choice rather than an impression.
A demand for zero errors sets a standard the previous human process never met either. Judged that way every arrangement fails, so the test cannot distinguish a good option from a bad one.
Enjoyment affects adoption and is worth knowing, but people can prefer an arrangement that produces weaker summaries. Preference is a secondary signal, not the basis for keeping it.

question: A communications officer receives a first draft that is accurate but far too shallow for the intended briefing. Which two follow-up actions are most likely to improve the second attempt? Select two.
options: A) Send the identical prompt again in the hope that the next attempt comes out stronger.
B) Show a passage from last quarter's briefing as an example of the depth wanted.
C) Append the words "be thorough and detailed" to the end of the original request text.
D) Supply the figures and case details the briefing must cover, which were not in the prompt.
E) Reply that the draft was disappointing and ask Claude to try considerably harder now.
correct_answers: B) Show a passage from last quarter's briefing as an example of the depth wanted.
D) Supply the figures and case details the briefing must cover, which were not in the prompt.
explanations: Resending an unchanged prompt is the least productive iteration. The specification is identical, so any improvement is chance rather than something that can be relied on.
Correct. An example communicates a standard that adjectives cannot, and it works even where the officer would struggle to describe the wanted depth in words.
Generic intensifiers are among the weakest edits available. "Thorough" is undefined, so it gives Claude no target it can aim the second draft at.
Correct. Shallowness is usually an information problem. Claude cannot write to a depth the prompt never supplied the material for, so adding the substance is the direct fix.
Negative feedback without specifics tells Claude that something was wrong but not what, so the next draft varies at random rather than converging.

question: Explanation
options: A) Shorten the word problem's wording considerably so there is simply much less text overall for Claude to process carefully before it answers.
B) Have Claude work through the problem step by step before the final answer, separating its reasoning from the answer using structured tags.
C) Repeat the exact same word problem twice within the prompt so Claude effectively gets two separate chances to parse it correctly.
D) Ask Claude to skip any intermediate explanation entirely and output only the final numeric answer so there is less room for error.
correct_answers: B) Have Claude work through the problem step by step before the final answer, separating its reasoning from the answer using structured tags.
explanations: Incorrect. Shortening the wording doesn't address the missing step-by-step reasoning that catches arithmetic mistakes, and could remove necessary problem details.

Correct. Encouraging step-by-step reasoning (chain-of-thought), with structured tags to separate reasoning from the final answer, is Anthropic's documented technique for catching errors reliably, especially in coding and math tasks.
Incorrect. Duplicating the problem statement does not add a reasoning process and is not a documented technique for reducing calculation errors.
Incorrect. Removing the reasoning step is the opposite of the documented fix; skipping intermediate steps tends to increase arithmetic errors on multi-step problems.

question: For six weeks a customer-service lead has typed the same three corrections about tone and terminology into every new chat in her team's project. What should she do about that?

C) Add the three corrections at the end of each chat instead, so they are the most recent thing in the conversation.
D) Ask at the start of each chat whether the three usual corrections are understood before the real work begins.
correct_answers: B) Move the three corrections into the project's standing instructions, so chats there start with them applied.
explanations: A copyable note reduces the typing but keeps the requirement dependent on her remembering, and colleagues in the same project still do without it.

Correct. A correction needed in every chat is standing context rather than a per-chat instruction. Project instructions apply to every conversation in that project, which makes the fix durable and available to the whole team.
Moving corrections to the end of a chat applies them after the work has been produced, so each conversation still starts from the wrong footing.
A confirmation exchange at the start costs a turn and establishes nothing that survives into the next conversation.

question: A grants officer has a draft that is right in structure and evidence, but its second section is too technical for her readers. What is the most efficient next step?
options: A) Rewrite her original request to mention the reader's level, and ask for the whole document to be produced again.
B) Accept the draft as it stands and rewrite the technical section herself before the document goes any further.
C) Ask for three alternative versions of the whole document, and choose whichever of them reads most accessibly.

correct_answers: D) Ask for the second section to be rewritten for a non-specialist reader, leaving the rest of the draft as it is.
explanations: Regenerating everything puts the sections she was happy with back at risk, and she then has to re-review the whole document.
Rewriting it herself is a reasonable fallback, but doing it before asking for a revision gives up the cheapest improvement available.
Producing three full alternatives multiplies the reading and comparison work to fix a problem confined to one section.
Correct. Only one part is wrong, so only that part needs to change. A targeted revision keeps the structure and evidence she has already accepted, and it makes the improvement easy to check.

question: A Project's knowledge base has grown until it approaches the limit of what fits in the context window. Which two statements are accurate? Select two.
options: A) The Project stays in retrieval mode permanently, even if its knowledge is reduced later.
B) The user has to switch retrieval on in the settings once the knowledge passes that threshold.

correct_answers: C) Claude switches over to retrieval automatically, with no configuration needed from the user.
E) Retrieval lets the Project work with roughly ten times more content than it held before.
explanations: Incorrect. The Project reverts to standard processing if the knowledge later drops back below the threshold.
Incorrect. There is no setting to turn on; treating it as manual is the most common misunderstanding of this behaviour.
Correct. Retrieval mode for Projects turns on by itself as the knowledge approaches the limit; there is nothing to configure.
Incorrect. Retrieval works alongside other Claude features, including web search, extended thinking and Research.
Correct. In retrieval mode a Project can hold up to about ten times more content than standard processing allows.

question: A training officer wants a disciplined way to improve the wording she uses for weekly course summaries. Which sequence should she follow on each round?
options: A) Compare the new result against the previous one; name what was wrong with the result; keep the change or undo it; make one change.
B) Make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; name what was wrong with the result; keep the change or undo it.
C) Keep the change or undo it; name what was wrong with the result; compare the new result against the previous one; make one change.
D) Name what was wrong with the result; make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; keep the change or undo it.
correct_answers: D) Name what was wrong with the result; make one change; compare the new result against the previous one; keep the change or undo it.
explanations: There is nothing to compare until a change has been made, so this ordering evaluates a result that the round has not yet produced.
Changing something before naming the defect means the change is aimed at nothing in particular, and the diagnosis arrives after it has been made.
Deciding whether to keep a change before making it inverts the round entirely, and the comparison happens with nothing new to compare.

Correct. Naming the defect gives the round a target, one change isolates the cause, the comparison shows whether it moved in the right direction, and the keep-or-undo decision makes the improvement deliberate rather than accidental.

question: A support lead wants to paste a year of customer complaint emails, which contain names and postal addresses, into Claude so it can find common themes. Her company's AI policy sets rules for handling customer personal data. What should she do first?
options: A) Use an incognito chat for the work, so the conversation cannot be used to improve Claude.
B) Take the names and addresses out of the emails herself, and paste what remains of the text.
C) Find out how the policy classifies this data and what it requires, before any of it is pasted.
D) Do the work inside the company's managed workspace, since company data is approved for use there.
correct_answers: C) Find out how the policy classifies this data and what it requires, before any of it is pasted.
explanations: Incognito chats are not used to improve Claude, but that addresses only training. The policy's rules on where and how customer personal data may be processed still apply in full.
Removing identifiers by hand may be exactly what the policy asks for, or may fall short of it. Deciding the treatment herself before reading the rules is what the policy exists to prevent.

Correct. The data is customer personal data and the company has rules for it, so the first step is to establish which category it falls into and what that category requires. That determines whether pasting is permitted at all, and under what conditions.

The managed workspace is very likely part of the answer, but a general approval for company data does not settle what is allowed for personal data specifically. That is what the policy has to be checked for.

question: A team applies the same single sign-off step to every Claude-assisted output, from internal meeting notes to a statement that will be filed with a regulator. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Irreversible, externally visible work gets no more scrutiny than notes nobody will ever act on.
B) Reviewers will refuse the extra workload, so the sign-off step will be abandoned within weeks.
C) Reviewers will start to rely on Claude's wording, and their comments will grow shorter over time.
D) Every output will take equally long to clear, which slows the team's routine work considerably.
correct_answers: A) Irreversible, externally visible work gets no more scrutiny than notes nobody will ever act on.
explanations: Correct. Review effort should scale with consequence and reversibility. A uniform step spends the same attention everywhere, which leaves the rare high-blast-radius output under-examined.
Incorrect. Workload may become a problem, but the immediate exposure is that the process cannot tell important work from routine work.
Incorrect. Review fatigue is real, but it is a consequence of the flat process rather than the central danger it creates.
Incorrect. Slower routine work is an efficiency cost. The serious risk sits at the other end of the range, on the filings.

question: A project coordinator has listed eight tasks for a product launch and wants to work through them with Claude in a sensible order. What should she do first?
options: A) Work out which tasks need another task's output before they can start, since that constrains the possible orders.
B) Start with the two tasks she finds hardest, so the difficult work is finished while there is still time to spare.
C) Put the eight tasks in the order they appear on the launch plan she was given, and work down the list from the top.
D) Group the eight tasks by which colleague owns them, and work through one colleague's tasks before the next.
correct_answers: A) Work out which tasks need another task's output before they can start, since that constrains the possible orders.
explanations: Correct. Dependencies are the only hard constraint on ordering: everything else is preference. Identifying which tasks consume another's output shows what must be sequenced and what can be done in any order.
Tackling the hardest work early is sound scheduling advice, but a hard task that depends on an unfinished one simply cannot be completed yet.
A plan's list order usually reflects how it was written rather than what depends on what, so following it can put a task before the input it needs.
Ownership is useful for assigning work, not for ordering it, and grouping this way routinely places a dependent task ahead of its input.

question: A user in Claude.ai asks Claude to write a 200-line Python script that parses log files and generates a summary report. The user says they plan to save the script and run it repeatedly. How should Claude present the script?
options: A) Split across several separate chat messages, because breaking long scripts into chunks makes each message easier to read and manage.
B) The script should be inline in the chat response, since code blocks provide helpful syntax highlighting and an easy copy mechanism.
C) Claude should present the script as an artifact, since it's a substantial, self-contained work for repeated reuse and iteration.
D) Claude should provide the script as a downloadable PDF, since the user's primary need is a formatted report, not the source code.
correct_answers: C) Claude should present the script as an artifact, since it's a substantial, self-contained work for repeated reuse and iteration.
explanations: Incorrect. Splitting the script across multiple messages may make individual chunks easier to read, but it fragments the code and complicates copying, editing, and reusing it as a single functional unit.

Incorrect. While inline code blocks offer syntax highlighting and a convenient copy mechanism, a script of this length and purpose is better suited as an artifact, which allows the user to save, edit, and run it as a standalone file without cluttering the conversation.

Correct. An artifact is designed for substantial, self-contained content that the user can edit, save, and reuse independently of the chat, making it ideal for a 200-line script intended for repeated iteration.

Incorrect. The user's primary need is the runnable Python script itself, not a formatted report; providing a downloadable PDF would prevent the script from being executed or modified, failing to meet the explicit request for a reusable code file.

question: A hospital deploys a Claude-powered chatbot on its patient portal to answer questions about medication side effects. According to Anthropic's Usage Policy for high-risk, consumer-facing use cases, what must the hospital do before patients rely on the chatbot's answers?

correct_answers: D) The hospital must clearly disclose to patients that they are interacting with an AI system before they receive medical guidance from the chatbot.
explanations: Incorrect. Redirecting every question avoids the disclosure obligation rather than fulfilling it, and is not what the policy requires.
Incorrect. Restricting content sourcing does not address the requirement to disclose that the interaction is AI-driven.
Incorrect. A liability waiver does not satisfy the Usage Policy's transparency requirement, which is about disclosing AI involvement, not shifting legal liability.
Correct. Consumer-facing chatbots in high-risk domains like healthcare must transparently disclose that the user is interacting with an AI system before providing guidance.

question: A service manager wants to use Claude to improve a customer refund process that everyone agrees is too slow. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Map how the process actually runs today; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
B) Map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records.
C) Test those proposals against real cycle-time records; have Claude propose where time is being lost; map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
D) Have Claude propose where time is being lost; map how the process actually runs today; agree the changes with the people who run the steps; test those proposals against real cycle-time records.
correct_answers: A) Map how the process actually runs today; have Claude propose where time is being lost; test those proposals against real cycle-time records; agree the changes with the people who run the steps.
explanations: Correct. The map grounds the analysis in the real process, Claude then does the pattern work of pointing at likely losses, the cycle-time records separate genuine bottlenecks from plausible-sounding ones, and the people who run the steps agree changes that have already been evidenced.
Agreeing changes immediately after mapping commits the team before Claude has identified anything, and the evidence check lands at the very end when the changes are already settled.
There are no proposals to test at the start, so the first step has nothing to act on, and mapping the process arrives after the analysis that depended on it.

Asking for proposals before the process is mapped means Claude reasons from an assumed refund process rather than this one, and the changes are agreed with the team before anyone has tested whether they hold.

question: A policy team keeps a handbook in a Drive folder that changes weekly, and also has one annual report that never changes. Which two set-ups fit best? Select two.
options: A) Connect the annual report and delete it from Drive, so that only one copy ever exists.
B) Upload the fixed annual report into Project knowledge, since its content will not change.
C) Paste the whole handbook into every new chat, so the newest version is always present.
D) Connect the Drive folder, so the weekly handbook changes are picked up from the source.
E) Upload a copy of the handbook just once and then rely on that copy for the rest of this year.
correct_answers: B) Upload the fixed annual report into Project knowledge, since its content will not change.
D) Connect the Drive folder, so the weekly handbook changes are picked up from the source.
explanations: Incorrect. Deleting the original to leave a single copy destroys the source of truth for no benefit.
Correct. A stable document is well suited to a one-time upload into Project knowledge, where it stays available to every chat.
Incorrect. Re-pasting a whole handbook per chat is the manual work Project knowledge and connectors exist to remove.
Correct. A connector reaches the live source, which is what a document that changes every week needs.
Incorrect. A one-time copy of a weekly-changing handbook goes stale fast and produces confidently outdated answers.

question: A marketer asks Claude to add citations to a draft that Claude had already written from general knowledge. What is the main concern?
options: A) Claude is unable to add citations to text it has already produced earlier in a conversation.
B) Citations added afterwards cannot be formatted in the style that the publication requires.
C) Adding citations later makes the draft longer, which the publication's word limit forbids.
D) Sources found to fit finished text may not actually support the claims attached to them.
correct_answers: D) Sources found to fit finished text may not actually support the claims attached to them.
explanations: Incorrect. It will readily do so, which is precisely what makes the practice risky rather than impossible.
Incorrect. Formatting is adjustable and is not what makes retrofitted citations unreliable.
Incorrect. Length is a practical constraint and is unrelated to whether the citations support the text.
Correct. When the text comes first, the sources are selected to match wording that was never derived from them, so the citation can look right while supporting nothing.

question: A team is deciding between Claude Haiku and Claude Opus for a new internal tool and wants a simple rule of thumb for when accuracy should be prioritized over cost and speed. According to Anthropic's guidance, which situation should push the team toward starting with Opus instead of Haiku?
options: A) When rapid iteration is needed for prototyping new features without real user testing, start with Opus to ensure high accuracy from the start.
B) For high-volume repetitive tasks with tight budgets, Opus is preferred over Haiku for its lower cost per task and faster speed.
C) Complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost, such as scientific or advanced coding, calls for Opus.
D) To ensure fast response times for low-latency chatbots during peak traffic, choose Opus over Haiku due to its optimized inference.
correct_answers: C) Complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost, such as scientific or advanced coding, calls for Opus.
explanations: Anthropic actually recommends Haiku over Opus for rapid prototyping. Haiku's faster speed and lower cost allow teams to iterate quickly and test ideas without incurring high expenses or latency, making Opus an unnecessarily costly and slow choice at this stage.

This statement inaccurately describes Opus. Anthropic guidance states that Haiku is the fastest and most cost-effective model, ideal for high-volume, budget-sensitive tasks. Opus, while more capable, is significantly more expensive and slower, making it unsuitable for such use cases.

According to Anthropic's official guidance, Opus models are the most capable and are recommended when accuracy and advanced reasoning are top priorities, even at higher cost. Use cases include complex scientific research, advanced coding, and high-stakes enterprise tasks where output must be reliable on the first pass. This rule of thumb directly aligns with documentation emphasizing Opus for 'complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost.'

Anthropic recommends Haiku for low-latency applications like peak-traffic chatbots because Haiku provides the fastest response times and lowest cost per request. Opus is designed for depth rather than speed, so using it here would lead to higher latency and cost without proportional benefit.

question: A nonprofit needs a grant report for both a technical evaluator and a general public donor newsletter, but the first draft uses terms like 'confidence interval' and 'effect size' throughout. What is the best way to adapt the newsletter version?
options: A) Remove all numbers from the newsletter so no explanation of findings is needed
B) Restate the statistical findings in plain language describing what the results mean practically
C) Keep the report identical for both audiences since the underlying data does not change
D) Keep the statistical terms but define each one in a footnote at the end of the newsletter
correct_answers: B) Restate the statistical findings in plain language describing what the results mean practically
explanations: Incorrect. Removing all numbers strips out meaningful impact information donors would want, rather than simply making it understandable.
Correct. Translating statistical jargon into plain, practical statements is exactly what adapting content for a general donor audience requires while preserving the actual findings.
Incorrect. Using the identical technical report for donors ignores that the intended audience has a different background and needs different phrasing.
Incorrect. Footnoted definitions still leave jargon embedded in the main text, requiring donors to cross-reference terms instead of reading naturally.

question: After one complaint about a single report, a team changes the shared instruction, re-runs that same report, is satisfied with the result, and rolls the change out to everyone. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The changed instruction cannot be reversed once other people begin using it
B) The person who complained will not be told the change was made for them
C) The change may fix that one report and quietly damage every other kind
D) Re-running one report will consume more of the team's allowance than usual
correct_answers: C) The change may fix that one report and quietly damage every other kind
explanations: Instructions can be changed back at any time, so reversibility is not the exposure here.
Failing to close the loop with the complainant is a courtesy issue, not the reason the rollout is unsafe.

Correct. Testing a fix only on the case that failed shows that the case now passes; it says nothing about the reports that were already fine. Trying it on a few different real cases is what would reveal the damage.
The cost of re-running one report is trivial and unrelated to whether the change was sound.

question: A small law firm uses Claude to draft first-pass responses to routine client contract questions. B) No, because the Usage Policy prohibits legal-advice use cases entirely regardless of professional review
C) Yes, but only if the firm also purchases a separate high-risk-use license directly from Anthropic
D) Yes, because a qualified professional reviews the output and the AI's involvement is disclosed to clients
correct_answers: D) Yes, because a qualified professional reviews the output and the AI's involvement is disclosed to clients
explanations: Incorrect. This statement is about legal liability, not about compliance with the Usage Policy's stated safeguards, which the firm has already met.
Incorrect. Legal advice is a high-risk use case that is permitted with safeguards, not a universally prohibited category like weapons development or CSAM.
Incorrect. The Usage Policy does not require a separate high-risk-use license; it requires professional review and disclosure, both of which are already present.
Correct. High-risk domains like legal advice require both qualified professional review of the content and disclosure that AI was used, and this scenario satisfies both safeguards.

question: An HR stakeholder proposes letting Claude autonomously make final hiring decisions from resumes with no human involvement, to speed up recruiting. What limitation should be raised, and what should be recommended instead?
options: A) Raise that Claude cannot read resume text at all, so the proposal is technically impossible to build.
B) Raise that hiring speed is the only relevant factor, so fairness and bias considerations can be dropped entirely.
C) Raise that model outputs can reflect biases in input data, and recommend keeping a human reviewer in the final decision.
D) Raise no concerns, since removing human involvement from hiring eliminates all risk of biased outcomes.
correct_answers: C) Raise that model outputs can reflect biases in input data, and recommend keeping a human reviewer in the final decision.
explanations: Incorrect. Claude can process and reason about resume text, so this claim is factually wrong and not the relevant concern here.
Incorrect. Fairness and legal compliance are material concerns in hiring and should not be deprioritized in favor of speed alone.

Correct. Like any model trained on real-world data, Claude's outputs can reflect biases present in that data, so high-stakes decisions like hiring should keep a human reviewer involved rather than being fully automated.
Incorrect. Removing human oversight does not eliminate bias risk; unsupervised automation can actually amplify it if left unchecked.

question: A policy officer must produce a short evidence review for a decision meeting later in the week. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Point Claude at the sources that count as evidence here; check the load-bearing claims before it is circulated; state the question and what a usable answer must cover; have Claude draft the review with references to passages.

B) Check the load-bearing claims before it is circulated; have Claude draft the review with references to passages; state the question and what a usable answer must cover; point Claude at the sources that count as evidence here.

C) State the question and what a usable answer must cover; point Claude at the sources that count as evidence here; have Claude draft the review with references to passages; check the load-bearing claims before it is circulated.

D) Have Claude draft the review with references to passages; state the question and what a usable answer must cover; point Claude at the sources that count as evidence here; check the load-bearing claims before it is circulated.
correct_answers: C) State the question and what a usable answer must cover; point Claude at the sources that count as evidence here; have Claude draft the review with references to passages; check the load-bearing claims before it is circulated.
explanations: Checking claims before anything has been drafted leaves nothing to check, and stating the question only after that verification means the sources were chosen without knowing what was being asked.
This inverts the whole order: verification comes first with nothing to verify, and the question that should have framed the work is settled after the review has already been written.

Correct. The question defines what the review must cover, the agreed sources bound what counts as evidence, the referenced draft makes each claim traceable, and verifying the claims the decision turns on happens while there is still time to correct them.
Drafting before the question is stated produces a review aimed at no particular decision, and the sources arrive after the draft that was supposed to rest on them.

question: A finance team wants Claude to take actions in a connected system, such as updating records, rather than only reading from it. Under a typical organisational AI policy, what matters most before this is enabled?

correct_answers: B) Approval for write access, with a human checkpoint before any change is committed to the system.
explanations: Data volume is a workload question and says nothing about the risk of unreviewed changes.

Limiting who may use it reduces exposure slightly but still leaves unreviewed writes possible.
A description in the chat is a weak record and does not prevent an incorrect change from being made.

question: A knowledge-management lead has asked Claude three times for a "brief, on-brand" summary of the weekly internal newsletter, and each attempt comes back at a different length and in a different register. Which two revisions to her prompt are most likely to fix this? Select two.
options: A) Replace "brief" with a checkable limit: no more than 150 words in three bullets.
B) Paste one past summary the team accepted and one it rejected, with a note on why.
C) Ask for a more formal register, since inconsistency usually reads as informality.
D) Resend the identical request with a line saying the earlier attempts fell short.
E) Restate the same two adjectives across a longer sentence to give them more weight.
correct_answers: A) Replace "brief" with a checkable limit: no more than 150 words in three bullets.
B) Paste one past summary the team accepted and one it rejected, with a note on why.
explanations: Correct. "Brief" is interpreted afresh each time, which is exactly why the length keeps moving. A word count and a bullet count are constraints Claude can meet and she can verify at a glance.

Correct, and independently of the word limit: it fixes register rather than length. "On-brand" is undefined in the abstract, and a worked accepted-versus-rejected pair shows the voice she means far better than any adjective.
Formality is one register among several, not a cure for varying between registers. She would be swapping an undefined target for a slightly narrower undefined target, and length would still drift.

Resending the same wording with a complaint attached communicates nothing new about what the summary should look like. Repeating a prompt with added emphasis is the classic non-fix for a vague specification.
Expanding "brief" and "on-brand" into more words leaves both terms exactly as unmeasurable as before. Length of instruction is not the same thing as precision of instruction.

question: A team lead has adopted a habit of splitting every request into stages. Today he needs a three-sentence note telling the team that a meeting has moved. How should he handle it?
options: A) Ask for the note in a single request, since the task is small enough that splitting it adds steps without adding value.
B) Ask for several versions of the note in separate stages, then run one more stage to choose between the versions.
C) Ask for an outline of the note first, approve that outline, and only then request the three sentences themselves.
D) Split it into drafting, then tone review and a final polish, so the habit is applied consistently to all writing tasks.
correct_answers: A) Ask for the note in a single request, since the task is small enough that splitting it adds steps without adding value.
explanations: Correct. Decomposition earns its keep when a task is large, has dependent stages, or needs checking before the next step. A short factual note has none of those properties, so one request is the right shape.
Generating and comparing variants is worth the effort when wording carries real weight, which a routine scheduling note does not.
An outline of a three-sentence note is longer than the note. The checkpoint exists to catch direction errors that are expensive later, and here there is nothing expensive to catch.
Applying the habit uniformly ignores what breaking work up is for. Three sentences can be read and judged at a glance, so the extra stages cost time and return nothing.

question: A team wants its fact-checking of Claude outputs to be reviewable by someone else months later. Which practice best achieves that?
options: A) Keep the full chat transcript, since it shows every single question the team put to Claude.
B) Record which claims were checked and against what, and keep that alongside the document.

correct_answers: B) Record which claims were checked and against what, and keep that alongside the document.
explanations: Incorrect. A transcript shows how the draft was produced but not which claims were subsequently checked or against which sources.
Correct. A record of coverage lets a later reviewer see what was verified and what was not, instead of having to redo the work or assume it was done.
Incorrect. A readability pass does not establish that any statement was traced to a source.

question: An operations manager on a Pro plan is working within a single Project whose uploaded reference files are approaching the context limit. The manager wants Claude to keep giving high-quality answers grounded in that large body of documents without manually trimming the file set. What underlying capability does the Project rely on to handle this?
options: A) Research mode replaces the uploaded files with live web search results, automatically expanding project context without manual trimming.
B) An artifact compresses all uploaded files into a summarized attachment, expanding project capacity while preserving response quality.
C) Retrieval Augmented Generation automatically expands project capacity by retrieving relevant chunks, preserving quality.
D) A downgrade to a smaller model uses a reduced context window per document, allowing more reference files within the same overall limit.
correct_answers: C) Retrieval Augmented Generation automatically expands project capacity by retrieving relevant chunks, preserving quality.
explanations: Incorrect. Research mode is a separate web-search capability; it does not tap into the project's uploaded document base or automatically replace files to expand context.

Incorrect. Artifacts are for displaying generated content like code or documents; there is no artifact-based compression or summarization mechanism for uploaded reference files. Capacity expansion is handled by RAG.

Correct. Projects use Retrieval Augmented Generation to automatically retrieve relevant chunks from uploaded files, expanding effective context capacity while maintaining answer quality without manual trimming.

Incorrect. Downgrading to a smaller model changes generation cost and speed, not the way a project handles its uploaded knowledge base; it does not reduce per-document context usage to fit more files.

question: An analyst breaks a market review into six stages and feeds each result straight into the next, reviewing nothing until the final report is written. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) A mistake in an early stage is carried into every later stage, and the final report is built on top of it.
B) Later stages will repeat wording from earlier ones, so the finished report reads as somewhat repetitive.
C) The six stages will take longer in total than simply asking for the whole market review in one single request.
D) The final report will be longer than the audience wants, because every stage adds material of its own.
correct_answers: A) A mistake in an early stage is carried into every later stage, and the final report is built on top of it.
explanations: Correct. In a chained breakdown each stage treats the previous output as settled fact. A misread figure or a wrong assumption at stage two is not questioned again, and by stage six it is woven through the analysis and expensive to unpick.
Repetition across stages is a tidying problem that a final editing pass resolves, and it does not affect whether the conclusions hold.
Staged work does take more elapsed time, but that cost is the point of the approach and is small next to acting on a flawed report.
Length is easily controlled by stating limits, and an overlong report is a presentation issue rather than a correctness one.

question: A finance analyst has broken a budget review into stages. The next stage compares actual spend against forecast, but she has not yet received the final month's figures from two departments. What should she do first?
options: A) Run the comparison on the figures she has now, and then repeat the whole stage once the outstanding numbers arrive.
B) Chase the two departments for the missing figures, because this stage cannot produce a usable answer without them.
C) Skip the comparison stage entirely and move to the commentary, returning to the numbers if time allows later.
D) Ask Claude to estimate the two missing departments from their spending pattern over the preceding months.
correct_answers: B) Chase the two departments for the missing figures, because this stage cannot produce a usable answer without them.
explanations: Running twice doubles the work and, worse, produces an interim comparison that circulates and gets quoted before the real figures arrive.
Correct. A stage that depends on an input it does not have cannot be rescued by restructuring the request. Securing the missing figures is the step that unblocks the sequence.
Commentary written without the comparison has no basis, and deferring the numbers means the conclusions are formed before the evidence exists.
Estimated departmental spend inserted into a budget review looks exactly like reported spend, and a variance driven by an estimate is indistinguishable from a real one.

question: After several rounds of instruction changes, a Claude-assisted complaints-response arrangement still gets the tone wrong on the cases that involve bereavement. What is the most appropriate change to the design?
options: A) Route bereavement cases to a person to write, and keep the arrangement for the routine ones.
B) Ask Claude to flag bereavement cases so that reviewers know to read those responses carefully.
C) Add more instruction detail about tone until the sensitive cases are handled acceptably as well.
D) Accept the current quality and ask reviewers to correct the tone on those cases before sending.
correct_answers: A) Route bereavement cases to a person to write, and keep the arrangement for the routine ones.
explanations: Correct. Iterating a design includes changing the division of labour, not only the instructions. Bereavement responses need judgment and care that the team must own, so returning that slice to a person while keeping the routine volume delegated is the sound redesign.
Flagging improves the odds that a reviewer pays attention, but Claude still writes the response and a person still has to rescue it. The step with the real consequence remains delegated.

Several rounds of instruction changes have already failed, which is evidence that the problem is the nature of the task rather than the wording. Continuing to add detail spends effort on the least promising fix.
Relying on reviewers to repair tone in the most sensitive cases puts the heaviest correction burden exactly where mistakes are least forgivable. One missed review reaches a bereaved complainant.

question: A marketing lead is writing the Project instructions for a Project her team will use every day. Which two choices make those instructions effective? Select two.
options: A) Listing an answer to each specific question the team happened to ask Claude during the last month.
B) Stating the audience and the tone that every response inside that Project should be written for.
C) Keeping the instructions vague, so that they never conflict with any individual chat request.
D) Repeating one rule several times in capital letters so it carries more weight than the others.
E) Giving the reason behind a house rule, so that Claude can apply it to unforeseen situations.
correct_answers: B) Stating the audience and the tone that every response inside that Project should be written for.
E) Giving the reason behind a house rule, so that Claude can apply it to unforeseen situations.
explanations: Incorrect. A list of past answers is a transcript, not direction, and it dates quickly as the team's questions change.
Correct. Audience and tone are exactly the durable direction Project instructions exist to hold, rather than being restated per chat.
Incorrect. Vague instructions give no usable direction, so responses drift back to whatever each individual chat happens to say.
Incorrect. Emphasis and repetition are not what makes an instruction effective; clarity and stated intent are.
Correct. Giving the reason behind a rule lets Claude generalise it to cases the instructions never anticipated.

question: A project lead needs Claude to work across a very large set of meeting notes inside one conversation on her paid plan. Which choice best supports that?

Correct. The newest flagship models provide a one-million-token window when chatting on any paid plan, which is the most room available for a single conversation.

question: An analyst has a Research-mode output on competitor pricing, with citations against most claims, that will inform a pricing decision. Which two validation steps are most useful? Select two.
options: A) Confirm the headline figure against the company's own records rather than one source.
B) Run the same research request again and accept the result if the two broadly agree.
C) Open a sample of cited pages and confirm each says what the summary claims.
D) Use the number of citations shown as a rough measure of how reliable the output is.
E) Accept anything carrying a citation and spend the time only on uncited statements.
correct_answers: A) Confirm the headline figure against the company's own records rather than one source.
C) Open a sample of cited pages and confirm each says what the summary claims.
explanations: Correct. Bringing in an independent record is a different technique from checking sources: it avoids treating Claude as a singular source of truth on a decision that matters.
Two runs can be wrong in the same way, so agreement between them is a consistency signal rather than any evidence about accuracy.
Correct. A citation shows where a claim came from, not that it was read correctly. Opening the page is what catches a figure taken out of context or from the wrong year.
Citation count measures volume, not quality. A heavily cited output can rest on weak sources, and a lightly cited one can be entirely sound.
A citation is not a guarantee, and cited claims are precisely the ones that feel safe to skip, which is what lets a misread source pass through unchallenged.
