question: Two tasks draw almost identically on a team's allowance: notes from an internal brainstorm that nobody will act on directly, and a figure that will appear in a published statement. A colleague argues the two should therefore be treated the same way. How should the team decide?
options: A) Treat them the same, since equal allowance draw means equal cost to the team and there is no clear financial reason to separate them.
B) Let what an error would cost drive the decision, so the published figure earns more depth and checking than the internal notes do.
C) Treat them the same, since a single rule applied to both tasks is easier for colleagues to remember and to follow consistently.
D) Let the person who happens to run each task decide, since they know their own deadline and how much allowance they have left.
correct_answers: B) Let what an error would cost drive the decision, so the published figure earns more depth and checking than the internal notes do.
explanations: Equal allowance draw only tells the team what each request costs to run. It says nothing about what a mistake costs, which is where the two tasks differ enormously.

Correct. Consequence, not price, should drive the choice: a wrong figure in a published statement is hard to retract, while a weak brainstorm note is discarded, so the published work justifies more depth and scrutiny.
A single rule is simpler to follow but forces one of two errors: over-spending on throwaway notes, or under-serving a published figure. Simplicity is not worth either outcome.
Leaving it to whoever runs the task makes an important external output depend on one person's remaining allowance and time pressure, which is exactly when the published figure would be short-changed.

question: A strategy lead is drafting a board paper and Claude supplies a precise market-size figure for a sector she does not follow. The figure would strengthen her case considerably. What should she do first?
options: A) Compare it against the market sizes of neighbouring sectors to see whether its scale looks about right.
B) Establish where the figure comes from and check that published source before the figure goes anywhere.
C) Include it while describing it as an estimate, which signals to the board that the precise value may move.
D) Ask for the figure again in a new conversation, and use it if the second answer gives the same value.
correct_answers: B) Establish where the figure comes from and check that published source before the figure goes anywhere.
explanations: A plausibility check may catch a figure that is wildly wrong, but it comfortably passes a number that is merely incorrect.
Correct. A precise figure for an unfamiliar sector is exactly the kind of claim that has to be traced to a published source before it is used. Provenance comes before presentation.
Calling a figure an estimate lowers its apparent precision but still places an unsourced number in front of the board as evidence.
A repeated answer shows only that the same figure is produced twice, which is consistency rather than any external support.

question: A university course administrator must confirm that a Claude-drafted section of the student handbook matches the university's published regulations. In which order should these steps be taken?
options: A) Find each of those statements in the published regulations; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.

B) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.

C) Correct any statement the regulations do not support; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.

D) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.
correct_answers: B) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.
explanations: She would be looking statements up before deciding which statements matter, so the search has no defined scope and ordinary descriptive sentences get treated as regulatory claims.

Correct. Singling out the sentences that make a regulatory claim scopes the work; each of those is then traced to the published regulations, which is the authoritative source rather than the draft itself; corrections follow from what that comparison found; and recording the version used makes the check repeatable when the regulations change.
Editing comes first of all, before either the claims have been identified or the regulations opened, so the handbook is changed on no evidence at all.
Corrections are made before the regulations have been consulted, which means they rest on what she assumes the rules say. The lookup that should have driven the edits arrives after them.

question: A project lead pastes the same 40-page requirements document into every new chat instead of storing it anywhere. What is the greatest concern with this approach?
options: A) Each re-paste spends both window space and usage allowance that storing the document once would save.
B) The document will be copied into other people's projects across her organisation without her consent.
C) Claude will answer only from the closing pages of the document and silently ignore everything before.
D) Claude will refuse to accept a document of that size and will ask her to shorten it before continuing.
correct_answers: A) Each re-paste spends both window space and usage allowance that storing the document once would save.
explanations: Correct. The document consumes a large share of the conversation's working memory every time, and the repeated processing draws on her usage budget for no added benefit.
Incorrect. Pasting into her own chat does not propagate the document to colleagues' workspaces.
Incorrect. Claude does not restrict itself to the final pages; the real exposure is cost and space, not truncation by position.
Incorrect. A document of that size is readable; the cost is in the space and allowance it consumes, not a refusal.

question: A programme sponsor asks who is accountable for the requirements catalogue now that most of it is drafted with Claude. Which answer best reflects sound practice?
options: A) The named business owner still signs it off; Claude speeds the drafting but cannot carry accountability.
B) The analyst who wrote the prompts signs it off, since they know best how the catalogue was put together.
C) Claude signs the catalogue off, and the business owner reviews only the items Claude marks as uncertain.
D) Sign-off can wait while the catalogue is a draft, because every item will be reviewed again in delivery.
correct_answers: A) The named business owner still signs it off; Claude speeds the drafting but cannot carry accountability.
explanations: Correct. Delegating the drafting does not move the accountability. The business owner remains the person who can commit to the requirements being right, and keeping sign-off there is what makes the faster drafting safe to rely on.

Knowing how the catalogue was produced is not the same as being able to commit the business to it. Prompt authorship is a process detail; sign-off is a statement that these are the needs the organisation will fund.
A tool cannot be accountable for a commitment the organisation makes, and reviewing only self-flagged items means the errors Claude is confident about, which are the dangerous ones, go unexamined.

Deferring sign-off pushes accountability into a phase where changing a requirement is far more expensive. Delivery review checks whether the build matches the catalogue, not whether the catalogue was ever right.

question: A manager has fifteen minutes to check a six-page recommendation before a decision meeting. She cannot verify everything in it. What should she concentrate on?
options: A) The passages that are written most confidently, because strongly worded claims carry the most weight in a meeting.
B) An even sample drawn from each of the six pages, so that no part of the document goes entirely unexamined.
C) The opening and closing sections, since these are what most attendees will actually read before the meeting.
D) The few facts the recommendation depends on, since the decision changes if any one of them turns out to be wrong.
correct_answers: D) The few facts the recommendation depends on, since the decision changes if any one of them turns out to be wrong.
explanations: Confidence of expression is unrelated to whether a claim is load-bearing, and a quietly stated figure can be the one the recommendation turns on.
Even sampling spreads scarce attention across material of very unequal importance, so a decisive figure gets the same scrutiny as background.
Checking what will be read protects the meeting's impression of the document but leaves the reasoning behind the recommendation unexamined.

Correct. With limited time, verification should follow consequence. Identifying the handful of facts that would reverse the recommendation concentrates the check where an error would actually change the outcome.

question: A team's prompt says "Do not use markdown in your response," but Claude's output still includes headings and bullet lists inconsistently. What rewording is more effective at controlling the format?

question: A communications officer needs a one-page summary to hand out at an event, with the supporting detail available for anyone who asks afterwards. How should she organise the material?
options: A) Produce one long document containing both the summary and every piece of supporting detail.
B) Produce the handout only, and answer any requests for supporting detail verbally on the day.
C) Produce a short handout as the deliverable and keep the detail as a separate reference document.
D) Produce the supporting detail only, since anyone wanting a summary can read its opening section.
correct_answers: C) Produce a short handout as the deliverable and keep the detail as a separate reference document.
explanations: Incorrect. A single document that tries to do both is too long to hand out and too summary-led to serve as a reference.
Incorrect. Relying on recall leaves the detail unavailable afterwards and inconsistent between conversations.
Correct. Two audiences with different needs are served by two artefacts, so neither the handout nor the reference is compromised to accommodate the other.
Incorrect. An opening section written for a detailed document is not a handout, and event audiences will not read the rest.

question: A financial services firm asks Claude to generate personalized investment recommendations for retail clients based on their stated goals. Before any recommendation is sent to a client, what should happen?
options: A) A licensed financial advisor reviews the recommendation for suitability and regulatory compliance
B) The recommendation is sent as-is since it was generated from the client's own stated goals
C) Claude is asked to double-check its own math and confirm the recommendation is internally consistent
D) A marketing team member reviews the wording only for tone and readability before sending
correct_answers: A) A licensed financial advisor reviews the recommendation for suitability and regulatory compliance
explanations: Correct. Investment advice is a regulated, high-stakes domain, so a licensed advisor must confirm suitability and compliance before a recommendation reaches a client.
Incorrect. Basing the recommendation on client-stated goals does not eliminate the risk of an unsuitable or non-compliant suggestion reaching the client unreviewed.
Incorrect. Self-checking arithmetic does not address whether a recommendation is suitable for the client or compliant with financial regulations.
Incorrect. Reviewing only tone and readability ignores the substantive suitability and compliance risks that matter most for financial advice.

question: A stakeholder asks why a complex multi-step reasoning task takes longer and costs more than a simple lookup task run on the same model. What tradeoff should be explained?
options: A) Explain that all tasks cost the same regardless of complexity, so the difference must come from a network outage.
B) Explain that deeper reasoning consumes more tokens and time, so settings that improve quality on hard tasks add cost.
C) Explain that complex reasoning tasks are always cheaper, since they need fewer output tokens than simple lookups.
D) Explain that latency differences are random and unrelated to how much reasoning a given request requires.
correct_answers: B) Explain that deeper reasoning consumes more tokens and time, so settings that improve quality on hard tasks add cost.
explanations: Incorrect. Cost and latency do scale with task complexity and token usage; attributing the difference to an outage misrepresents normal behavior.

Correct. Increasing reasoning depth (for example through higher effort or thinking settings) generally uses more tokens and processing time, which is the direct tradeoff between response quality and cost/latency.
Incorrect. Complex reasoning tasks typically use more output tokens, not fewer, making them more expensive rather than cheaper.
Incorrect. Latency is meaningfully related to reasoning depth and token volume, not simply random variation.

question: A strategy analyst is told, "Research our competitors and come back with something useful." She has two days and intends to use Claude for most of the work. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to produce a broad overview of every competitor in the sector and narrow the list afterwards.
B) Collect the competitors' public material into one place so Claude has something concrete to work from.
C) Agree with the requester which decision the research supports and which competitors and factors matter.
D) Ask Claude which competitor comparison factors are most commonly used in this kind of market study.
correct_answers: C) Agree with the requester which decision the research supports and which competitors and factors matter.
explanations: A broad sweep first spends most of the two days on competitors that will turn out to be irrelevant. Narrowing afterwards requires the very criteria the analyst has not yet agreed, so the effort has to be repeated.

Gathering source material is a sensible early move, but doing it before the question is fixed means gathering the wrong material. Which brochures, filings and reviews matter depends entirely on what the requester needs to decide.

Correct. "Something useful" is not a research question, and no amount of good prompting rescues an undefined one. Fixing the decision the work feeds and the comparison factors that bear on it determines what to gather, what to ignore, and when the analyst can stop.

Common comparison factors describe what other studies did, not what this requester needs. Adopting them substitutes a generic frame for the specific business question and leaves the analyst no closer to knowing what useful means here.

question: A user needs to generate a report and then make direct edits to its content. Which Claude feature is most appropriate?
options: A) Enable Research mode to refine the report with external sources.
B) Generate the report as an Artifact, then edit it in the artifact editor.
C) Use Chat to output the report and then edit the raw text inline.
D) Use Projects to store the report and make edits in a separate file.
correct_answers: B) Generate the report as an Artifact, then edit it in the artifact editor.
explanations: Incorrect. Research mode is designed to gather and incorporate external sources, not to directly edit or refine report text. It does not include a built-in editor for modifying the report's content.

Correct. Artifacts provide a dedicated editing workspace for longer-form content like reports. Generating the report as an Artifact allows direct, structured modifications in the artifact editor, aligning perfectly with the user's need.

Incorrect. Chat can generate the report, but editing raw text inline in the chat interface is inefficient and lacks dedicated editing tools. This method is not suited for making structured, direct edits to a report.

Incorrect. Projects are intended for organizing conversations and files, not for direct editing of reports. Storing a report and then editing it in a separate file is a manual workaround that lacks the integrated editing experience needed here.

question: A workforce planning lead uses Claude to condense several years of performance notes into short profiles, then ranks the profiles to build a promotion shortlist. Reviewing them, she sees that people from one team are consistently described in warmer language than people from another. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The profiles will read inconsistently to the panel, which may find the varying tone across the shortlist distracting during the meeting.
B) The condensing step will have shortened some profiles more than others, so the panel spends unequal reading time on each individual.
C) A skew in the language becomes a skew in the ranking, so a decision about people's careers is shaped by a pattern nobody examined.
D) The notes may be old enough that some achievements described in the profiles have since been superseded by more recent work.
correct_answers: C) A skew in the language becomes a skew in the ranking, so a decision about people's careers is shaped by a pattern nobody examined.
explanations: Inconsistent tone is a real presentational flaw, but it is a cosmetic one. It understates what is happening: the tone difference is tracking group membership, and that is what makes it serious rather than untidy.

Uneven length affects how much attention each profile receives, which is a genuine fairness concern, but it is a second-order effect next to systematically warmer wording being applied to one group of people.

Correct. Bias in a summary becomes bias in the outcome once the summaries are ranked, and converting it into a shortlist hides the original wording, so an unexamined pattern silently drives a high-stakes decision about people.

Stale source notes would undermine accuracy and are worth checking separately, but they do not explain a pattern that follows team membership, and they are not the greatest risk in a promotion decision.

question: A European team wants to use Claude to analyse a customer database that includes personal data about EU residents. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A) Involve the people responsible for data protection to confirm the lawful basis and required safeguards.
B) Proceed, because analysing data the company already holds does not raise any new privacy questions.
C) Move the analysis onto a personal account so that it falls outside the organisation's compliance scope.
D) Ask Claude to summarise the relevant regulation and treat that summary as the compliance decision.
correct_answers: A) Involve the people responsible for data protection to confirm the lawful basis and required safeguards.
explanations: Correct. Regulated personal data requires a decision from the accountable data-protection function, not an individual.
Introducing a new processing tool is itself a change that has to be assessed.
Using a personal account does not remove the obligation and removes the oversight as well.
A summary of a regulation is not a compliance decision and carries no accountability.

question: A team wants to decide whether a lighter tier is good enough for its weekly summary work. What is the most reliable way to make that call?
options: A) Run real examples of their own summaries on both tiers and judge them against an agreed standard.
B) Read published comparisons of the tiers and adopt whichever one they describe as sufficient.
C) Adopt the lighter tier and revisit that decision if the team's allowance stops running out so early.
D) Ask Claude to compare its own output on both tiers and report which version is the stronger.
correct_answers: A) Run real examples of their own summaries on both tiers and judge them against an agreed standard.
explanations: Correct. Adequacy is specific to the task and the bar, so only their own work compared against a stated standard answers the question.
Incorrect. General descriptions cannot tell the team whether a lighter tier meets their particular standard on their own material.
Incorrect. Allowance consumption measures cost, not whether the summaries still meet the required standard.
Incorrect. A self-assessment is not independent evidence, and it has not been told what this team's summary must achieve.

question: A department wants Claude to take over a large slice of its quarterly reporting work. Which two steps belong before any full rollout? Select two.
options: A) Start with the reports carrying the highest legal exposure, since they save the most time.
B) Pilot the change on one report, so the result can be compared with the current output.
C) Agree what counts as an acceptable result before any of the work is handed over at all.
D) Announce the change as settled, so that the department commits to the new way of working.
E) Remove the existing review step first, so the pilot measures the fully automated version.
correct_answers: B) Pilot the change on one report, so the result can be compared with the current output.
C) Agree what counts as an acceptable result before any of the work is handed over at all.
explanations: Incorrect. Starting where legal exposure is greatest maximises the blast radius of a mistake in an untested process.
Correct. Piloting on a small scope gives a comparison against today's output before anything is committed department-wide.
Correct. Defining what good looks like before delegating is what makes the pilot's result interpretable at all.
Incorrect. Announcing the change as finished commits the department before there is any evidence the new way works.
Incorrect. Stripping review out of a pilot removes the safeguard exactly when the risk of an unnoticed error is highest.

question: Explanation
options: A) Put the request and the relevant material in the opening message; work through follow-ups that refer back to it; open a new chat for the next unrelated task; decide what she needs before starting.
B) Open a new chat for the next unrelated task; decide what she needs before starting; work through follow-ups that refer back to it; put the request and the relevant material in the opening message.
C) Decide what she needs before starting; put the request and the relevant material in the opening message; work through follow-ups that refer back to it; open a new chat for the next unrelated task.
D) Work through follow-ups that refer back to it; open a new chat for the next unrelated task; decide what she needs before starting; put the request and the relevant material in the opening message.
correct_answers: C) Decide what she needs before starting; put the request and the relevant material in the opening message; work through follow-ups that refer back to it; open a new chat for the next unrelated task.
explanations: Everything here is done before she has decided what she needs, so the opening message is assembled blind.
Opening a chat for the next task before the current one has been started puts the last step first.

Correct. Planning before starting, front-loading the material in one well-specified message, then building on it, is what keeps the exchange short; unrelated work starts fresh rather than dragging old context along.
Following up before the request has even been made, and deciding what is needed last, inverts the whole habit.

question: A team is about to change a shift handover process on Claude's suggestion, and wants to be able to tell in a month whether the change actually helped. What most makes that judgement possible?
options: A) A baseline of the old process's timings and error rates, captured before the change is made.
B) A note of how confident Claude was that its suggested change would improve the handover process.
C) A list of the other changes that Claude suggested and the team decided not to make at this time.
D) A record of the prompts used when Claude was asked to analyse the handover process originally.
correct_answers: A) A baseline of the old process's timings and error rates, captured before the change is made.
explanations: Correct. Improvement is a comparison, and the comparison is impossible once the old process has gone. Capturing timings and error rates beforehand is the only step that must happen now, and it turns a month of impressions into evidence.
Claude's stated confidence is a prediction, not a measurement, and it was formed before the change met real shifts. Treating it as evidence of improvement substitutes expectation for observation.
A record of rejected suggestions is useful for the next round of improvement work. It tells the team what they chose not to try, not whether what they did try worked.
Keeping the prompts helps the team repeat or explain the analysis, which is good practice. It says nothing about whether the process is faster or more accurate than it used to be.

question: An employee's organisation has no written policy on AI tools, and they want to use Claude with supplier contracts. What should they do first?
options: A) Write their own policy for the team and begin using the tool under the rules that they drafted.
B) Assume it is permitted, since the absence of a written policy means that nothing has been prohibited yet.
C) Ask their manager or legal contact for a decision before putting any supplier material into the tool.
D) Use the tool but avoid saving anything, so that no record of the contracts is kept anywhere at all.
correct_answers: C) Ask their manager or legal contact for a decision before putting any supplier material into the tool.
explanations: An individual cannot grant the organisation's permission to themselves.
Silence in a policy is not permission for third-party contractual material.
Correct. Where no policy exists, the accountable route is to obtain a decision rather than to assume one.
Not saving output does not change whether the contracts could be entered in the first place.

question: A consultant works in a free Claude account and keeps a separate project for each client. She already has five projects and has just signed a sixth client whose material she wants to keep separate too. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask an administrator to raise the project allowance on her account before she starts the work.
B) Review her five projects and retire or repurpose one, since a free account is capped at five projects.
C) Create the sixth project as normal, since the cap on the number of projects applies only to shared ones.
D) Keep this client in ordinary chats instead, since projects are only offered on the paid plans.
correct_answers: B) Review her five projects and retire or repurpose one, since a free account is capped at five projects.
explanations: A personal free account has no administrator who can lift the cap; the plan defines the limit.
Correct. Projects are available to everyone, but a free account is limited to five of them, so she has to free one up before a sixth client workspace can exist.
The five-project cap on free accounts is not limited to shared projects; it covers her projects.
Projects are available to all users, including free accounts, so this misreads the constraint.

question: A team lead is about to hand a multi-step campaign preparation task to Claude in Cowork, where it will work across her files and connected tools. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Describe the outcome wanted and the constraints; decide which actions need approval before they happen; let Claude work through the task; review what was actually done before anything is final.
B) Decide which actions need approval before they happen; review what was actually done before anything is final; describe the outcome wanted and the constraints; let Claude work through the task.
C) Let Claude work through the task; describe the outcome wanted and the constraints; decide which actions need approval before they happen; review what was actually done before anything is final.
D) Review what was actually done before anything is final; let Claude work through the task; describe the outcome wanted and the constraints; decide which actions need approval before they happen.
correct_answers: A) Describe the outcome wanted and the constraints; decide which actions need approval before they happen; let Claude work through the task; review what was actually done before anything is final.
explanations: Correct. Describing the outcome and constraints gives the task a target, deciding in advance which actions need approval keeps the consequential steps under human control, and reviewing what was done before anything is finalised keeps the team lead accountable for the result.

Reviewing before the task has run leaves nothing to review, and the outcome is described only after the approval points have been fixed, so those points were chosen without knowing what the task involves.

Starting the work before the outcome and the approval points are set means Claude acts on files and tools under no agreed constraint, which is exactly the situation the approval decision exists to prevent.
This puts the review first and the description of the goal third, so the work runs with no stated outcome and the approval decision is made after everything has already happened.

question: A team is adding a new Claude-assisted output into an existing process and has to work out how much checking it will get. In which order should these steps be taken?
options: A) Set the level of review that degree of risk requires; judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience.

B) Release the output to its audience; judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; set the level of review that degree of risk requires; have the named reviewer carry out that review.

C) Judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; set the level of review that degree of risk requires; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience.

D) Judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience; set the level of review that degree of risk requires.
correct_answers: C) Judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; set the level of review that degree of risk requires; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience.
explanations: The review level is being fixed before anyone has worked out the risk, so the assessment that should have driven the decision arrives too late to inform it.
Releasing first defeats the whole exercise. Any risk assessment and review that follow publication cannot prevent the harm they were meant to catch.

Correct. Visibility and reversibility determine how much scrutiny an output deserves, so they are assessed first; that assessment sets the required level of review, the named reviewer then performs it, and only then does the output reach its audience.
The review happens with no agreed standard behind it, and the level of review is only settled after the output has already gone out, which is the wrong way round.

question: A team drafts a long monthly report in Claude and keeps exhausting its usage allowance before the month ends. Some sections are routine - recurring summaries and figures pulled from the same sources each time - while other sections carry the analysis the report is read for. The team already signs the report off against an agreed quality checklist, and it wants to cut usage by moving some of the drafting to a lighter Claude model tier without weakening the sections that matter. Which sequence of steps should the team follow?
options: A) Run the routine sections on a lighter tier; decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
B) Decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
C) Decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short; run the routine sections on a lighter tier.
D) Check the drafts against the agreed checklist; decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
correct_answers: B) Decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
explanations: Incorrect. The routine sections are moved to the lighter tier before anyone has worked out which sections carry the judgment, so the split is guesswork about the content rather than a decision based on it, and the checklist pass that follows can only repair a division that was arbitrary to start with.

Correct. Deciding which sections need human judgment comes first because it is the only step that reasons about the content rather than the tooling; the lighter tier is then applied only where quality is not at stake; and the checklist the team already signs the report off against is what tells them which moves to keep and which to send back to the deeper tier. Claude Academy's model-selection tutorial applies the same test - run the work on the lighter model, then judge whether the output met your bar.

Incorrect. The drafts are checked and sections are sent back to the deeper tier before the lighter tier has been used at all, so the move to the lighter tier is the last thing done and nothing verifies its output - the one step the team cannot afford to leave unchecked given that quality is the stated constraint.

Incorrect. The checklist pass happens before anything has been moved, so it measures the drafts the team already produces and says nothing about how the lighter tier performs; the final step then sends back sections that were never re-checked after the change.

question: A writer drafting a long-form article wants Claude to avoid starting the response with phrases like 'Here is the article you requested' and instead jump straight into the content. What is the recommended way to achieve this with current models?
options: A) Add an instruction telling Claude to respond without preamble or opening phrases
B) Ask the writer to manually delete the opening sentence from every single response
C) Provide a prefilled assistant message that begins the article for Claude to continue from
D) Leave the request as-is, since preamble phrasing cannot be steered at all in prompts
correct_answers: A) Add an instruction telling Claude to respond without preamble or opening phrases
explanations: Correct. Current models support direct instructions in the system prompt telling Claude to respond without preamble and avoid phrases like 'Here is...', which is the recommended replacement for older prefill-based techniques.
Incorrect. Manually trimming every response after the fact is unnecessary post-processing when a direct instruction can prevent the preamble in the first place.
Incorrect. Prefilled assistant messages on the last turn are no longer supported on current models, so this is not a viable way to eliminate preambles.
Incorrect. Preamble phrasing can be steered directly through prompt instructions, so this is not the recommended path.

question: A startup needs to brainstorm low-cost marketing tactics under a tight $500 budget. Which prompt will generate the most actionable ideas?
options: A) Ask Claude to brainstorm a list of innovative and unusual marketing ideas, emphasizing wild creativity and viral potential, while deliberately ignoring budget limits or resource constraints to encourage unfiltered ideas.

B) Instruct Claude to generate a wide range of creative marketing tactics, covering everything from social media campaigns to guerrilla marketing stunts, while encouraging unconventional approaches without filtering by cost or practicality.

C) Prompt Claude to devise a list of practical, low-cost marketing ideas with a strict $500 budget, emphasizing tactics that utilize social media, local partnerships, and guerrilla marketing techniques.

D) Direct Claude to find and compile a list of real-world examples of successful low-budget marketing campaigns, detailing the specific strategies, outcomes, and budget constraints, to derive actionable insights.
correct_answers: C) Prompt Claude to devise a list of practical, low-cost marketing ideas with a strict $500 budget, emphasizing tactics that utilize social media, local partnerships, and guerrilla marketing techniques.
explanations: Incorrect. Asking for innovative and unusual ideas while ignoring budget limits encourages unfiltered creativity. However, many suggestions may be too costly or resource-intensive, making them impractical for the startup's $500 constraint.

Incorrect. This prompt instructs Claude to generate ideas without filtering by cost or practicality. The resulting wide range of creative tactics may include expensive or unrealistic ideas that cannot be executed within the tight $500 budget.

Correct. By specifying a strict $500 budget and requesting practical, low-cost marketing ideas, this prompt directly constrains Claude to generate feasible tactics. Emphasizing social media, local partnerships, and guerrilla marketing techniques further focuses the output on actionable, budget-friendly channels.

Incorrect. Directing Claude to compile real-world examples focuses on summarization of past campaigns rather than generating new, actionable ideas. The startup needs tailored, low-cost tactics, not just case studies that may not fit their specific budget and context.

question: A team summarises each of twenty customer interviews, then works only from those summaries to decide which product problems to fix. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The summaries will use the team's own vocabulary rather than the words the interviewed customers actually used.
B) Summarising twenty interviews separately takes longer than reading through all twenty of the transcripts once.
C) The twenty summaries will vary in length, so some interviews will appear to carry more weight than the others do.
D) Details that would identify the real problem are dropped at the summary stage and cannot be recovered later.
correct_answers: D) Details that would identify the real problem are dropped at the summary stage and cannot be recovered later.
explanations: Vocabulary drift is a genuine annoyance and one reason to keep quotes, but it is a milder form of the detail loss described above.
Time spent is a cost of the approach, not a threat to the decision the team is about to make.
Uneven summary lengths are worth normalising, but they signal how much was said rather than distorting what the problems are.

Correct. A summary keeps what seemed important without knowing which decision it will serve. The concrete detail that distinguishes a pricing objection from a trust objection is exactly what gets compressed away, and once the team works only from summaries the loss is invisible.

question: A finance team wants Claude's help making its slow month-end reporting process faster. Which two opening moves make sense? Select two.
options: A) Describe the current process step by step so Claude can point at the slowest handoffs in it.
B) Ask Claude to approve the final numbers so that the human reviewer step can be removed.
C) Ask Claude which of the team members is the real cause of the delay in the closing cycle.
D) Ask Claude to rewrite the entire process, then adopt the result at the very next month-end close.
E) Ask Claude for options with their trade-offs, which the team then tests on a single cycle.
correct_answers: A) Describe the current process step by step so Claude can point at the slowest handoffs in it.
E) Ask Claude for options with their trade-offs, which the team then tests on a single cycle.
explanations: Correct. Optimisation starts from the actual process, and pasting the real steps is what lets Claude find where time is lost.
Incorrect. Sign-off on financial figures is accountable human work, and removing the reviewer is exactly the wrong optimisation.
Incorrect. Claude cannot judge individual performance from a process description, and framing delay as blame is the wrong question.
Incorrect. Adopting a wholesale rewrite untested at the next close bets the month-end on a change nobody has validated.
Correct. Options with trade-offs, piloted on one cycle, is how a process change is tested before it is trusted at scale.

question: A manager asks to see the intermediate steps when working out which cost lines drove a budget overspend, but not when generating names for a new staff award. Why is that difference reasonable?
options: A) Because a numerical answer is more likely to be wrong than a creative answer produced for the same team.
B) Because working through a naming task takes longer than working through a numerical one of the same size.
C) Because the overspend answer can be wrong in ways only the steps reveal, while a name is judged as it stands.
D) Because name suggestions are shorter, so the reasoning behind each of them is easier to reconstruct afterwards.
correct_answers: C) Because the overspend answer can be wrong in ways only the steps reveal, while a name is judged as it stands.
explanations: This compares how error-prone the two tasks are, when the real difference is whether an answer can be wrong in a way that inspection would expose.
Relative effort is not what decides this. Steps are asked for because they can be checked, not because the task is slow.

Correct. Analysis produces a conclusion that depends on how it was reached, so the steps are what make it checkable. A proposed name either works or does not, and there is no chain of reasoning behind it to verify.
Length is incidental. Even if reconstructing the thinking behind a name were easy, doing so would not tell the manager whether the name is any good.

question: A team lead wants a reusable onboarding checklist that colleagues will revise over time. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Share it with the team; agree the steps it must cover; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place.
B) Ask Claude for the checklist as a document; agree the steps it must cover; revise it in place; share it with the team.

D) Agree the steps it must cover; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place; share it with the team.
correct_answers: D) Agree the steps it must cover; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place; share it with the team.
explanations: Incorrect. Nothing exists to share at the first step, which makes the whole ordering unworkable.
Incorrect. The checklist is drafted before anyone has agreed what belongs in it, so the revision step is doing work the first step should have done.
Incorrect. The checklist is shared before it has been written, and the revision happens after colleagues have already received it.
Correct. Content is settled first, a self-contained editable document is the right home for something reused and revised, and it is shared once it is ready.

question: An HR team has a Claude-drafted consultation letter that will be sent to forty staff whose roles are at risk, and the wording is governed by employment law. Which sequence is correct?
options: A) Judge the stakes of the letter, then name the reviewer it requires, then have that reviewer check it against the consultation policy, then send it once approval is recorded.
B) Record who approved the wording, then send the letter to the forty staff, then check it against the consultation policy, then have the HR lead read it.
C) Send the letter to the forty staff, then have the HR lead read it, then check it against the consultation policy, then record who approved the wording.
D) Check the letter against the consultation policy, then send it to the forty staff, then judge the stakes of what was sent, then name a reviewer to look over it carefully afterwards.
correct_answers: A) Judge the stakes of the letter, then name the reviewer it requires, then have that reviewer check it against the consultation policy, then send it once approval is recorded.
explanations: Correct. The stakes are high, regulated and irreversible, so the level of scrutiny is decided first, a named person is made accountable for the review, the check is made against the governing policy, and despatch happens only after recorded approval.
Recording an approval before anyone has reviewed the letter documents a sign-off that never happened, and the substantive checks still fall after the letter has already gone out.

Sending first makes every later step a post-mortem. A consultation letter cannot be recalled from forty recipients, so review carried out after despatch cannot prevent the harm it is meant to prevent.

Checking against the policy first is sensible, but sending before any named person has reviewed the letter or the stakes have been weighed removes the human review gate exactly where irreversibility demands it.

question: An operations lead must give all staff a one-page summary of a new expense policy. The full twenty-page policy document is open on her screen. What should she do first?

correct_answers: B) Paste the policy text itself into the request, so the summary is built from the wording staff will be held to.
explanations: She has no way to tell whether the first result is wrong without the policy in front of Claude, because a fluent summary of the wrong content still reads well.

question: A team lead is writing a short local practice note to sit underneath the company-wide AI standard. Which two items genuinely belong in it? Select two.
options: A) Who to contact when a situation arises that the company-wide AI standard does not clearly cover.
B) Which categories of team data must never be pasted into Claude under any circumstances at all.
C) The exact number of days for which the vendor keeps stored conversations before removal.
D) A ranked list telling each team member which model tier they should prefer for all of their own work.
E) A target for the number of working hours that every team member should save each week using Claude.
correct_answers: A) Who to contact when a situation arises that the company-wide AI standard does not clearly cover.
B) Which categories of team data must never be pasted into Claude under any circumstances at all.
explanations: Correct for a different reason: a named escalation contact is what stops people improvising when the standard runs out.
Correct. A local note is where the general standard becomes concrete about the specific data this team actually handles.
Retention periods are vendor facts that change and are documented by the vendor; copying a number into a team note invites it to go stale.
Model choice is a task-fit judgment made per piece of work, not a governance rule to assign per person.
A savings target pressures people towards using Claude and belongs to performance management, not to a governance note.

question: An engineer asks Claude to analyze why a distributed system intermittently drops requests, a problem that requires working through several interacting causes before reaching a conclusion. Which approach best fits this analytical task?
options: A) Let Claude reason through the multi-step causal analysis before its final answer
B) Ask Claude to list every possible cause without linking it to the symptom
C) Ask Claude to guess the most likely cause without examining interactions
D) Ask Claude to answer in just one sentence without reasoning through any of the causes
correct_answers: A) Let Claude reason through the multi-step causal analysis before its final answer
explanations: Correct. Reasoning capabilities are especially helpful for tasks involving complex multi-step reasoning, such as working through several interacting causes of an intermittent distributed systems issue before concluding.
Incorrect. An unconnected list of possible causes does not perform the causal analysis needed to explain how the causes interact to produce the intermittent symptom.
Incorrect. Guessing a single cause immediately bypasses the careful analysis of interacting causes that this kind of problem requires.
Incorrect. A single-sentence answer skips the multi-step reasoning needed to work through interacting causes of an intermittent, hard-to-diagnose issue.

question: A project lead is demonstrating a new Claude-assisted reporting workflow to executives who could fund its wider use. What should the demonstration make clear alongside the benefits?
options: A) The wording of the instructions used, so that executives can see how the workflow was actually built.
B) Where the workflow still needs a person to check the output, and the kinds of error it can produce.
C) The number of hours the project lead spent designing and refining the workflow before the demonstration.
D) The other tools the team considered and the reasons each of them was set aside before Claude was chosen.
correct_answers: B) Where the workflow still needs a person to check the output, and the kinds of error it can produce.
explanations: Showing the instructions is transparent about the mechanics but not about the risk. Executives are not well placed to infer failure modes from wording, and detail here can create false reassurance.

Correct. Honest communication of capability and limitation is what makes the funding decision sound: executives need to know which checks remain human and what kinds of error to expect, or they will plan for a level of automation the workflow does not deliver.
Design effort is a cost already incurred and tells executives nothing about whether the workflow is dependable. It answers a question about the team rather than about the decision being funded.
A tool comparison explains how the team arrived here, which may be of passing interest. It does not tell executives what they will be relying on or where it can go wrong.

question: A business analyst needs to use Claude to analyze a dataset containing customer satisfaction scores, demographic information, and purchase history. The analyst wants to identify key drivers of customer dissatisfaction. Which prompting approach would most effectively guide Claude to produce accurate, step-by-step analysis?
options: A) Instruct Claude to generate a comprehensive statistical report: perform regression analysis, hypothesis testing, and create visualizations to determine causation, and then draft a formal business report with recommendations using the provided data.

B) Guide Claude to first examine the distribution of satisfaction scores, then explore simple correlations with demographic variables, and summarize the most likely drivers based on observed patterns, without performing deep statistical tests.

C) Ask Claude to brainstorm a list of possible key reasons for dissatisfaction based on the data provided, relying only on qualitative judgment, then select the most plausible ones, and very briefly explain why they might be relevant to the business context.

D) Prompt Claude to conduct a step-by-step analysis: first, analyze satisfaction score distributions; next, correlate dissatisfaction with demographics and purchase history; then identify the top predictive factors, citing specific data points and patterns.
correct_answers: D) Prompt Claude to conduct a step-by-step analysis: first, analyze satisfaction score distributions; next, correlate dissatisfaction with demographics and purchase history; then identify the top predictive factors, citing specific data points and patterns.
explanations: Incorrect. This prompt asks Claude to perform regression analysis, hypothesis testing, and create visualizations, tasks it cannot reliably execute without external tools. Additionally, it incorrectly assumes causation can be determined from observational data, which is methodologically unsound.

Incorrect. This approach avoids deep statistical tests and does not require citing specific data points, which may lead to a superficial summary that misses the true drivers. It also omits exploration of purchase history, limiting the analysis.

Incorrect. This approach is suited for idea generation rather than rigorous data analysis, as it relies on qualitative judgment without a structured, quantitative methodology. The subjective selection process weakens its ability to accurately identify key drivers of dissatisfaction.

Correct. This prompt guides Claude through a logical, step-by-step process, including examining distributions, correlating dissatisfaction with both demographics and purchase history, and identifying top predictive factors. Requiring citation of specific data points and patterns ensures analytical rigor and accuracy.

options: A) Grouping a year of tenant survey comments into recurring themes for the quarterly service report.

C) Rewriting the published tenancy policy into plain language for the department's public web pages.
D) Issuing the final written refusal to tenants whose appeal against rehousing has failed.
E) Deciding which households are removed from the housing waiting list for failing to respond in time.
correct_answers: A) Grouping a year of tenant survey comments into recurring themes for the quarterly service report.
C) Rewriting the published tenancy policy into plain language for the department's public web pages.
explanations: Correct. Theme-finding across free-text feedback informs a report rather than determining anything about an individual, and the themes can be checked against the source comments.
A priority score decides who is housed first; that is a rights-affecting judgment Claude may inform but must not make.
Correct. Rewriting already-published policy is drafting work that a person reviews before it goes live, so any error is caught and reversible.
A final refusal of an appeal is an authoritative outcome for a named person and must be owned and issued by a human decision-maker.
Removing a household from a waiting list affects a person's access to housing and needs a named person answerable for the decision.

question: A city government wants to use Claude to build a system that cross-references live facial-recognition camera feeds with social media posts to covertly track individual protest attendees, without a warrant or their consent. Is this an appropriate use of Claude?
options: A) No, because the Usage Policy bans covert individual tracking through facial recognition without consent
B) Yes, because public safety agencies are exempt from the Usage Policy's surveillance provisions here
C) Yes, because these cameras are located in public spaces where there is no expectation of privacy
D) No, but only because the city lacks a proper data-retention policy for the collected camera footage
correct_answers: A) No, because the Usage Policy bans covert individual tracking through facial recognition without consent
explanations: Correct. The Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to build systems that covertly track or identify specific individuals through facial recognition without their consent, which matches this scenario.
Incorrect. Government or public-safety status does not exempt an organization from the Usage Policy's restrictions on non-consensual individual tracking via facial recognition.
Incorrect. Being in a public space does not authorize covert identification and tracking of specific individuals using facial recognition; the policy restriction still applies.
Incorrect. A missing retention policy is not the core problem; the covert, non-consensual tracking of individuals is itself the prohibited activity.

question: A knowledge base tool asks Claude to answer users' questions using only information retrieved from company documents, and the team wants every claim traceable to the exact retrieved passage it came from. Which technique best supports this analysis and answering task?
options: A) Have Claude answer directly from memory instead of using the retrieved documents at all
B) Have Claude answer first and only fetch supporting documents afterward instead
C) Have Claude paraphrase only the general topic of the documents, not any passage
D) Have Claude quote the specific passages from the retrieved documents before answering
correct_answers: D) Have Claude quote the specific passages from the retrieved documents before answering
explanations: Incorrect. Answering from memory instead of the retrieved documents does not produce claims traceable to specific retrieved passages.
Incorrect. Answering before retrieving documents reverses the order needed to ground the answer in the actual retrieved passages.
Incorrect. A general paraphrase without quoting specific passages does not give the traceability to exact source text that the team needs.

Correct. Grounding responses in quotes, having Claude quote relevant passages before answering, helps produce traceable, source-grounded answers, which fits the requirement that every claim be traceable to a passage.

question: Explanation
options: A) The prompt lacks clarity and specificity, because a reader with minimal context could not follow it and Claude likely cannot either.

D) The exercise is inconclusive, because whether a person can follow a prompt says nothing about how Claude will interpret the same text.
correct_answers: A) The prompt lacks clarity and specificity, because a reader with minimal context could not follow it and Claude likely cannot either.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's golden rule of clear prompting is to show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it; if they would be confused, Claude will be too, so the fix is a clearer and more specific prompt.
Incorrect. The diagnostic deliberately uses a reader with minimal context on the task, so training that reader up would remove the very gap the exercise is designed to expose.

Incorrect. A confused human reader points at an under-specified prompt, and the documented response is to add the missing clarity and specificity. Moving to a stronger model tier does not supply context that the prompt never contained.
Incorrect. Anthropic's prompting guidance uses human comprehension as the signal precisely because it predicts model confusion, so the exercise is informative rather than inconclusive.

question: A programme office is setting a policy for how much scrutiny Claude-generated work should receive. Which two factors raise the level of human review required? Select two.
options: A) The prompt that produced the output was long and included pasted background.
B) A large number of people would be affected if the output turned out to be wrong.
C) The action that follows from the output would be hard to undo once taken.
D) The output arrived in a document format the team has not used very often before.
E) The output was produced faster than the same work would have taken by hand.
correct_answers: B) A large number of people would be affected if the output turned out to be wrong.
C) The action that follows from the output would be hard to undo once taken.
explanations: Prompt length says nothing about consequence. A well-supplied prompt may even reduce risk, and it certainly does not raise the review bar by itself.
Correct. Blast radius is independent of reversibility: a mistake that is easy to correct can still reach many people before anyone notices it.
Correct. Low reversibility means an error cannot be quietly fixed later, so the check has to happen before the action rather than after it.
An unfamiliar file format is a practical inconvenience for the team, not a reason to apply more scrutiny to the content inside it.
Speed of production is not a risk factor. How long the work took has no bearing on what happens if the content is wrong.

question: A Team account with fifteen members has just had the Gmail connector enabled by the Primary Owner. How does each member gain access through the connector?
options: A) One member authenticates once, granting Gmail access to the whole team.
B) The Primary Owner authenticates for everyone through a single shared service account.
C) Members share one OAuth token that IT distributes to the whole team.
D) Each member individually authenticates via OAuth with their own Google credentials.
correct_answers: D) Each member individually authenticates via OAuth with their own Google credentials.
explanations: Incorrect. Authentication is per-user; one member's OAuth grant does not extend to teammates' inboxes.
Incorrect. There is no shared service account model; each user connects their own Google account individually.
Incorrect. Shared or distributed tokens are not how the connector works; per-user authentication keeps data separate.
Correct. Even after org-level enablement, each user authenticates through standard OAuth with their own credentials, keeping access per-person.

question: A marketing lead asks Claude for a competitor briefing, and the draft states that the competitor won a named industry award last year. She can find no record of that award anywhere. What should she do first?
options: A) Establish whether the award claim came from material she supplied or from Claude's general knowledge.
B) Ask Claude whether it is confident about the award before she spends any more time on it.
C) Ask Claude to restate the award claim with more supporting detail so that it becomes easier to check.
D) Delete the sentence about the award and circulate the remainder of the draft to her wider team.
correct_answers: A) Establish whether the award claim came from material she supplied or from Claude's general knowledge.
explanations: Correct. Knowing where a claim originated is what separates a fabrication from a real detail she simply has not located, and it determines every step that follows.
Incorrect. A statement of confidence is generated the same way the claim was, so it adds no independent information about whether the award exists.
Incorrect. Asking for more detail around an unsupported claim usually produces more unsupported detail, which makes the claim harder to dismiss rather than easier to check.
Incorrect. Removing one sentence treats the symptom. If the claim was invented, other statements in the same draft may be too, and she has not yet found out.

question: A sponsor wants to skip evaluation and move straight to full production rollout of a new Claude-powered feature to save time. How should the solutions architect explain the risk of this plan?
options: A) Explain that skipping evaluation is safe as long as the feature is reviewed by the engineering team after launch instead of before.
B) Explain that benchmark testing against real prompts and data is needed first to catch accuracy issues before they reach every user.
C) Explain that evaluation can be skipped since production issues can always be reversed instantly with no impact to users.
D) Explain that evaluation is optional because Claude's output quality is guaranteed to be identical across every possible use case.
correct_answers: B) Explain that benchmark testing against real prompts and data is needed first to catch accuracy issues before they reach every user.
explanations: Incorrect. Reviewing after full launch means issues are discovered only once they have already reached all users, defeating the purpose of pre-launch evaluation.
Correct. Building benchmark tests and evaluating against representative prompts and data before rollout is the standard way to catch quality or accuracy issues before they affect the full user base.
Incorrect. Production issues involving inaccurate or inappropriate outputs are not instantly reversible in terms of user trust or downstream impact.
Incorrect. Output quality varies by task and data, so there is no guarantee of uniform performance across different use cases without evaluation.

question: A project manager asks Claude to map out a five-stage approval workflow with branching decision points so the team can reference it during a planning meeting. What is the best way for Claude to present this?

C) An artifact containing a Mermaid flowchart, since diagrams are a supported artifact type well suited to visualizing branching workflows

correct_answers: C) An artifact containing a Mermaid flowchart, since diagrams are a supported artifact type well suited to visualizing branching workflows
explanations: Incorrect. Structured JSON is intended for programmatic data consumption, not for a human-facing reference the team will look at during a meeting.
Incorrect. A text list cannot easily convey branching decision points the way a flowchart can, so it is not the best fit here even though it could work for a simple linear list.
Correct. Diagrams and flowcharts are a supported artifact content type, and a branching workflow with decision points is naturally suited to visual representation the team can reference later.
Incorrect. Strict tool use validates parameters sent to an application tool; it is not a presentation format for sharing a workflow with a team.

question: A grants officer wants to use a Claude feature that her university's written AI standard does not mention at all, on funding applications containing unpublished research plans. Which two actions follow good governance? Select two.
options: A) Ask Claude to read the standard and confirm whether or not the university permits this particular feature.
B) Raise it with whoever owns the AI standard and get a decision before using it on the applications.
C) Try the capability first on material that is public, so nothing confidential is involved in the trial.
D) Treat the standard's silence as permission, on the basis that nothing in it forbids using the capability.
E) Go ahead now and record the use in the project file so that it can be reviewed by someone else afterwards.
correct_answers: B) Raise it with whoever owns the AI standard and get a decision before using it on the applications.
C) Try the capability first on material that is public, so nothing confidential is involved in the trial.
explanations: Claude can summarise a document but cannot grant an approval, and its reading of the standard carries no authority.
Correct. A gap in the standard is a question for the policy owner, and the escalation happens before the confidential work begins, not after.
Correct for an independent reason: trying it on non-confidential material lets the officer learn what it does without putting the research plans at risk.
Silence is not approval; policies cannot enumerate every capability, which is exactly why an escalation route exists.
Recording the use afterwards does not undo the disclosure of applicant data under an unapproved feature.

question: A newly designed way of working has Claude approve expense claims under a set threshold outright, with no person seeing the ones it approves. What is the greatest concern with this design?
options: A) Approved payments leave the organisation with no one accountable for the decision to pay.
B) The threshold may need adjusting as expense patterns change over the course of the year.
C) Employees may submit more claims once they learn that approvals are handled automatically.
D) Claims written in unusual formats may take the arrangement longer to work through fully.
correct_answers: A) Approved payments leave the organisation with no one accountable for the decision to pay.
explanations: Correct. Once money has left the organisation the action is not reversible, and because nobody reviews the approved claims there is no person who can answer for the decision. Payment approval is the kind of accountable, irreversible step that should keep a human in it.
Threshold maintenance is routine tuning of a control that already exists. It is a reason to review the design periodically rather than a reason the design is unsound.
A rise in claim volume is a behavioural effect worth monitoring, and it can be managed by sampling or by adjusting the threshold. It does not describe what happens when an approval is wrong.
Unusual formats slow processing and may produce the occasional query. That is a throughput problem, not a governance one, and it is visible enough to be corrected.

question: A marketing team wants Claude to draft product descriptions in a specific brand voice and needs the tone and structure to stay consistent across many descriptions. What is the most reliable way to steer this drafting task?
options: A) Describe the brand voice in one adjective and let Claude infer the rest
B) Give no examples and repeat the word 'consistent' several times instead
C) Provide three to five diverse examples wrapped in tags that mirror the brand voice
D) Provide a single long example and ask Claude to make all future ones roughly similar
correct_answers: C) Provide three to five diverse examples wrapped in tags that mirror the brand voice
explanations: Incorrect. A one-word tone descriptor without examples leaves too much of the format and structure to be inferred rather than steered.
Incorrect. Repeating a vague adjective like 'consistent' does not give Claude concrete examples of the actual tone, format, or structure desired.
Correct. Using three to five relevant, diverse examples wrapped in example tags, few-shot prompting, is one of the most reliable ways to steer output format, tone, and structure.
Incorrect. A single example risks Claude picking up unintended, overly narrow patterns instead of generalizing the brand voice across varied product types.

question: A marketer's long-running chat has begun producing copy that ignores the campaign brief agreed weeks earlier. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Open a fresh chat; check whether the old chat had grown too long; paste the brief in; capture the decisions afterwards.
B) Capture the decisions; open a fresh chat; check whether the old chat had grown too long; paste the brief in afterwards.
C) Check whether the chat has simply grown too long; capture the brief and decisions; open a fresh chat; paste them in there.
D) Paste the brief in again; capture the decisions; check whether the chat has grown too long; open a fresh chat right at the end.
correct_answers: C) Check whether the chat has simply grown too long; capture the brief and decisions; open a fresh chat; paste them in there.
explanations: Incorrect. Restarting before capturing the decisions risks losing them, and diagnosing after the fact wastes the step.
Incorrect. Working in the new chat before the brief is in place produces exactly the drift she is trying to fix.
Correct. Diagnosing the cause comes before acting, capturing the durable material protects it, and only then is restarting safe rather than destructive.
Incorrect. Re-pasting into an already overloaded conversation adds pressure to the window before anything has been diagnosed.

question: A communications officer pastes a ten-page partner agreement into the chat and types her instructions directly underneath it, with nothing marking where the pasted document ends and her request begins. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The conversation will become too long to continue, so she will have to start the whole exchange again shortly.
B) The signed agreement will be reformatted as it is pasted, so its clauses arrive in a different order from the original.
C) Claude will answer only from the closing paragraphs, because material earlier in a long message is set aside.
D) Claude may read wording inside the agreement as directions to follow, and act on it instead of her actual request.
correct_answers: D) Claude may read wording inside the agreement as directions to follow, and act on it instead of her actual request.
explanations: A ten-page agreement is well within what a single chat handles, and length is a separate concern from failing to separate instructions from source material.
Some layout is lost when text is pasted, but clause order is preserved, and reordering is not what makes an unlabelled paste risky.
Claude works from the whole message rather than only its final paragraphs, so this misstates how a long pasted document is handled.

Correct. Contracts contain imperative language such as 'the supplier shall notify' or 'provide a summary within ten days'. With no boundary between the pasted material and her instructions, that wording can be taken as part of the task, and the output drifts away from what she asked for.

question: A grants officer reads a Claude-written explainer of a funding scheme and notices that it gives one closing date in the opening paragraph and a different closing date three paragraphs later. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude which of the two dates it meant, and use whichever one it settles on when it is asked to resolve the conflict.
B) Delete the earlier paragraph so the explainer no longer contradicts itself, and circulate the corrected version today.
C) Go back to the funder's own published scheme rules and establish which closing date, if either of them, is the real one.
D) Keep the later of the two dates on the basis that it was written after Claude had processed more of the scheme material.
correct_answers: C) Go back to the funder's own published scheme rules and establish which closing date, if either of them, is the real one.

options: A) No, because the Usage Policy bans fake grassroots campaigns that misrepresent the scale of public support

explanations: Correct. The Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to generate fake grassroots or astroturf campaigns that misrepresent how widespread or organic public support actually is.

Incorrect. Disclosing AI involvement to the platform does not fix the deception, since the posts are still designed to misrepresent that many distinct residents independently hold the same view.
Incorrect. The prohibition on astroturfing and fabricated grassroots support applies to both ballot measures and candidate campaigns.

question: During a troubleshooting chat, a user asks Claude, "Is port 443 the default HTTPS port?" Claude's answer is a single confirming sentence. What is the appropriate output treatment for this response?
options: A) Ask a strict tool to validate the port number against a schema before responding, since numeric facts require schema validation
B) Create a Markdown document artifact titled "HTTPS Port Reference," since any factual networking answer should be saved for later use
C) Package the answer as a JSON object with a "confirmed" boolean field, since factual yes/no answers should always use structured data
D) Answer inline within the conversation, since a single confirming sentence has no reuse value that would justify an artifact
correct_answers: D) Answer inline within the conversation, since a single confirming sentence has no reuse value that would justify an artifact
explanations: Incorrect. Claude can directly answer common factual questions like default port numbers from its training data without needing external tool validation. Using a tool for such a basic fact would introduce unnecessary overhead and complexity.

Incorrect. Not every factual answer demands an artifact. Artifacts are intended for content that is substantial and reusable, such as comprehensive guides or documents. A single port confirmation is too trivial to warrant an artifact.

Incorrect. While structured data can be useful for programmatic interactions, a casual chat does not require packaging every fact into a JSON object. Anthropic’s documentation does not mandate that all yes/no answers be structured; inline natural language is perfectly acceptable.

Correct. Inline answers are appropriate for short, simple responses that do not constitute a substantial, reusable piece of content. Artifacts are reserved for content that is more complex and self-contained, such as code, documents, or long-form text. This aligns with Anthropic’s guidance on using artifacts for significant content.

question: A marketing team has always written its weekly client status note by hand. They now plan to switch to a new arrangement in which Claude drafts the note each week and an account manager edits it before sending. Before the first Claude-drafted note under the new arrangement reaches a client, what should the team do first?
options: A) Agree in advance exactly how many minutes of editing per note the account manager should expect to spend on this every week.
B) Send the first Claude-drafted note straight to the client, along with a short note explaining that Claude helped produce it.
C) Run Claude on a past month's inputs and compare its drafts with the hand-written notes actually sent to clients that month.
D) Ask Claude to check its own draft against the account manager's usual style before it goes out to the client.
correct_answers: C) Run Claude on a past month's inputs and compare its drafts with the hand-written notes actually sent to clients that month.
explanations: An editing-time budget measures effort, which only means something once the drafts are known to be usable. Agreeing on one before that check risks pressuring the account manager to spend less time editing than the drafts actually need.

Disclosure is good practice, but it does not test anything the team needs to know yet. The client would still receive the first output of an arrangement nobody has tried, and explaining that Claude helped does not make an inaccurate status note acceptable.

Correct. Feeding Claude the same weekly inputs the account manager already used, for a month that has already happened, produces drafts the team can check against a known right answer: the hand-written note the client actually received that week, before Claude was involved. That lets the team see where Claude's drafts fall short before any client sees output from the new arrangement.

Self-review can catch obvious slips, but Claude judging its own draft uses the same understanding that produced the draft in the first place. That is no substitute for comparing drafts against notes the team already knows were accurate.
