question: A charity plans to have Claude pre-screen grant applications and produce a shortlist that trustees then review. Which two safeguards matter most before the charity starts? Select two.
options: A) Applications are gathered into a single file so that the whole set fits inside one continuous conversation.
B) The criteria Claude applies are written down and match the criteria the charity published to applicants.
C) Trustees read the applications Claude ranked lowest before any of them are set aside without funding.
D) The charity times each shortlisting round so it can report how many staff hours the new approach has saved.
E) The shortlist is produced on the most capable model available, so the ranking is more accurate.
correct_answers: B) The criteria Claude applies are written down and match the criteria the charity published to applicants.
C) Trustees read the applications Claude ranked lowest before any of them are set aside without funding.
explanations: How the files are packaged is a convenience question and has no bearing on whether the screening is fair or reviewable.
Correct. Applicants were judged against published criteria, so the screening must apply those same criteria and they must be inspectable.
Correct. For a different reason: it keeps the harmful outcome recoverable, because a wrongly down-ranked application can still be rescued by a person.
Measuring time saved is useful for the business case but does nothing to protect applicants from an unfair screen.
A stronger model does not make a rights-affecting screen safe, and model choice is not the governance safeguard here.

question: An analyst has forty Claude-drafted product descriptions. About half will be posted on the public website and half will sit in an internal catalogue, and she has time to check roughly twenty of them properly before the deadline. What should she do first?
options: A) Check the longest descriptions first, because a longer description contains more claims to get wrong.
B) Check the descriptions in the order they were generated, until the time she has set aside runs out.
C) Sort the batch by where each description will end up and how hard an error there would be to undo.
D) Ask Claude to mark the descriptions it is least sure of, and check only the ones that it flags.
correct_answers: C) Sort the batch by where each description will end up and how hard an error there would be to undo.
explanations: Length is not a proxy for stakes. A short line of public-facing copy can be far more damaging than a long internal entry, so sorting by length would leave the riskiest items unchecked.

Working in generation order spends her limited review time at random. The website copy and the internal catalogue do not carry the same consequences, so order of arrival is the wrong basis for choosing.

Correct. With review capacity smaller than the batch, the first step is to triage by exposure and reversibility. Externally published copy that is hard to retract earns the scarce review time; an internal entry anyone can correct does not.
A model's own stated uncertainty is a weak and unvalidated signal, and it says nothing about consequences. It can be a useful supplement, but it cannot decide which outputs need human eyes.

question: A learning and development specialist has a Claude-drafted explanation of a new expenses process written for finance staff. She now needs a version for field engineers who never open the finance system. What should she do first?
options: A) Cut the draft down to roughly half its present length so that the field engineers will read it.
B) Ask Claude to simplify the wording of the existing text until it reads a good deal more easily.
C) Ask Claude to add a glossary explaining the finance terms that the draft already uses.
D) Work out what the field engineers actually have to do differently, and write to that.
correct_answers: D) Work out what the field engineers actually have to do differently, and write to that.
explanations: Halving the length is an arbitrary cut with no principle behind it, and it is as likely to remove the steps the engineers need as the ones they do not.

Simplifying the wording keeps the finance staff's version of the process and only changes its surface. The engineers would get an easier read of material that is still organised around someone else's job.
A glossary makes unfamiliar terminology survivable but leaves the engineers reading a finance-system walkthrough that mostly does not apply to them.

Correct. Adapting for an audience starts from what that audience needs to do, not from the existing text. Once she knows which parts of the process the engineers actually touch, the register, the length and the level of detail all follow from it.

question: A product team wants to brainstorm features for a new fitness app. They want a wide range of creative ideas without early criticism. Which prompting strategy fosters the most innovative brainstorming session with Claude?
options: A) Guide Claude to compile a list of the 10 most prevalent features in top-rated fitness apps by referencing common market knowledge, then use that list as a foundation to brainstorm derivative features, ensuring the team has a concrete starting point for ideation.

B) Ask Claude to develop a user survey to gather preferences for fitness app features, including crafting open-ended and multiple-choice questions, and use the responses to spark creative feature ideas during a team brainstorming session focused on novelty.

C) Instruct Claude to conduct a competitive analysis: identify major fitness apps, catalog their features, and present findings in a structured matrix comparing feature sets, noting which are standard versus differentiators, and use the matrix to spark ideas for novel features.

D) Prompt Claude to brainstorm 20 innovative and unconventional feature ideas for the fitness app, explicitly encouraging far-fetched concepts and deferring feasibility analysis; emphasize that quantity and creativity are the primary goals of this exercise.
correct_answers: D) Prompt Claude to brainstorm 20 innovative and unconventional feature ideas for the fitness app, explicitly encouraging far-fetched concepts and deferring feasibility analysis; emphasize that quantity and creativity are the primary goals of this exercise.
explanations: Incorrect. This approach starts by compiling existing prevalent features, which anchors the session in conventional ideas rather than pushing beyond them. Brainstorming derivative features from a known list limits true innovation and lacks the explicit deferral of judgment essential for creative brainstorming.

Incorrect. Developing a user survey is a data-gathering method that collects preferences rather than generating novel concepts. Even if responses later inspire ideas, the process shifts focus to validation and user input, which stifles the spontaneous, judgment-free atmosphere required for truly innovative brainstorming.

Incorrect. Competitive analysis is an analytical, research-oriented task that catalogs existing features and competitor differentiators. Although it may inspire ideas, the structured, comparative focus constrains open-ended creative generation and does not embody the unfettered ideation needed for innovation.

Correct. This prompt explicitly requests a large quantity of unconventional, far-fetched ideas and defers feasibility analysis, directly encouraging divergent thinking. By prioritizing creativity and volume over early criticism, it aligns perfectly with proven brainstorming principles that foster innovation.

question: A marketing analyst wants Claude to summarise campaign results that live in the company's Google Drive, so she plans to link Drive to her Claude account. Her company's AI policy states that any new data source must be approved by the data owner before it is connected. What should she do first?
options: A) Request the data owner's approval through the process the AI policy defines, before connecting anything at all.
B) Link Drive to one test folder first, then request approval once she can show the results it produces for her.
C) Link Drive and rely on the fact that Claude works only with files her own account already has permission to open.
D) Ask Claude to list the Drive files it is able to read, and use that answer to judge whether approval is needed.
correct_answers: A) Request the data owner's approval through the process the AI policy defines, before connecting anything at all.
explanations: Correct. The policy makes approval a precondition for connecting a data source, so the approval request is the first action, not something obtained after the fact.
Connecting even a single folder is still connecting a data source, which is exactly what the policy says requires approval first.
Inheriting her own permissions limits exposure but does not replace the organisational approval the policy requires.
Asking Claude what it can see does not change the fact that the connection itself needed approval before it was made.

question: A grants officer facing a deadline has used Claude to draft eligibility determinations for ninety applicants, and each determination will be sent directly to the applicant. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, which two things must happen before the determinations are issued? Select two.
options: A) Claude is asked to review its own determinations and flag any it is unsure about.
B) A qualified officer checks each determination against the published eligibility rules.
C) Each determination that goes out tells the applicant that Claude helped produce it.
D) Only the determinations that look borderline are pulled out for a person to read.
E) Claude is recorded as the decision-maker, so responsibility for each one rests with the tool.
correct_answers: B) A qualified officer checks each determination against the published eligibility rules.
C) Each determination that goes out tells the applicant that Claude helped produce it.
explanations: Self-review is not verification. A determination that misread a rule will often be reported as confident, so the cases most in need of attention stay hidden.

Correct. The Usage Policy requires that a qualified professional review a decision directly affecting individuals before it is finalized. Eligibility for funding is such a decision, so each one needs checking against the actual rules rather than sampling or spot checks.

Correct. When model outputs are presented directly to individuals, the Usage Policy requires disclosing to them that AI helped produce the decision, so each determination sent to an applicant must say that Claude helped produce it. An internal file note alone would not tell the applicant.
Borderline cases are identified by the same process being verified, so anything wrongly classed as clear-cut is exactly what this approach fails to catch.

Responsibility cannot be handed to the tool. The Usage Policy states that the user or their organization is responsible for the accuracy and appropriateness of the information, so recording Claude as the decision-maker leaves no accountable person and does nothing to make the determinations correct.

question: A corporate trainer uses a personal Max plan for her own course-design work. Her manager asks her whether her Claude conversations are being used to improve Anthropic's models. What should be her first step?
options: A) Assume that they are, because conversations on personal plans always feed model improvement work.
B) Ask her manager to raise it with Anthropic, as only the vendor can answer that question.
C) Check her own model improvement privacy setting, since on a personal plan the choice is hers.
D) Assume that they are not, because Anthropic never trains on customer data on any plan at all.
correct_answers: C) Check her own model improvement privacy setting, since on a personal plan the choice is hers.
explanations: Consumer plans are not automatically in scope for model improvement. It is a user-controlled setting, so assuming the worst gives her manager an answer that may simply be wrong.
Escalating to the vendor is unnecessary for something visible in her own account settings, and it leaves the manager waiting for an answer she could give today.

Correct. On Free, Pro and Max the user chooses whether their conversations may be used to improve Claude, so the honest answer depends on how her own setting is configured. Checking it is a step she can take herself and it produces a factual answer rather than an assumption.

This states the commercial position, where inputs and outputs are not used for training by default, and applies it to a personal plan. The consumer and commercial rules are different and must not be conflated.

question: A team is considering using Claude to triage inbound complaints, some of which allege safety issues. What should they do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to judge which complaints are serious enough to need a person, and follow that judgement.
B) Decide which complaint categories must always reach a person, and route those out of the automation.
C) Delay the project until every complaint category has been rewritten into a standard template form.
D) Automate the whole queue and review the outcomes at the end of the first quarter of operation.
correct_answers: B) Decide which complaint categories must always reach a person, and route those out of the automation.
explanations: Delegating the escalation boundary itself removes the safeguard the team is trying to build.
Correct. Defining the cases that require human handling has to happen before any triage is automated.
Standardising the intake forms does not address which complaints need a human at all.
A quarter of unreviewed safety complaints is exactly the harm this design needs to prevent.

question: A sales operations lead asked Claude to summarise two quarters of win-loss notes. Early in the summary it states that deals are lost mainly on price, and two paragraphs later it attributes most losses to slow implementation timelines. What should she do first?
options: A) Go back to the win-loss notes themselves and see what they actually say about the losses.
B) Keep the price explanation, since it appears first and is the more familiar of the two.
C) Ask Claude to produce the summary again and go with whichever explanation comes back next.
D) Ask Claude which of the two explanations it considers the more likely to be correct.
correct_answers: A) Go back to the win-loss notes themselves and see what they actually say about the losses.
explanations: Correct. An internal contradiction means at least one of the two statements is unsupported, and the notes she uploaded are the ground truth. Reading what the losses were actually recorded as resolves the inconsistency and shows which half of the summary can be trusted.

Position in the text is not evidence, and preferring the more familiar explanation is exactly the bias the review is supposed to catch. It could entrench a wrong conclusion about why the company is losing deals.
Regenerating gives a fresh answer, not a checked one, and picking whichever version arrives next chooses between two unverified claims at random.

Asking the same conversation to arbitrate between its own two claims produces another confident statement with nothing new behind it. The contradiction is evidence that the summary has drifted from the source, and only the source settles it.

question: A department has used Claude to redraft a board paper over six rounds. Each round was reviewed by whoever was free that week, and each reviewer applied their own idea of what a good board paper looks like. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) No shared standard of quality, so the team cannot tell whether the paper improved
B) The reviewers may use up their monthly usage allowance before the sixth round ends
C) Claude may carry wording the reviewers rejected in earlier rounds into later drafts
D) The paper may end up shorter than the format the board has asked for in the past
correct_answers: A) No shared standard of quality, so the team cannot tell whether the paper improved
explanations: Correct. Six reviewers applying six private ideas of quality means each round pulls the draft in a different direction, so the department has no agreed measure against which to judge round six versus round one. Anthropic's AI Fluency material defines Product Discernment as evaluating the quality of what the model produces for accuracy, appropriateness, coherence and relevance, and describes Discernment as working hand-in-hand with Description in a continuous feedback loop; that loop only converges when the criteria being applied stay the same from round to round.

Usage allowance caps how much work can be sent to Claude in a period, and reviewers would notice they were running low well before it halted the cycle. It says nothing about whether the drafting process is producing a better board paper.

Wording from an earlier round can resurface when every round shares the same conversation, but a reviewer reading the draft will see it and ask for it to go. It does not explain why the department cannot tell whether the paper is getting better.

A draft drifting away from the length the board is used to is visible on the page and corrected with one more instruction. It is a symptom of an unmanaged review cycle rather than the thing that makes six rounds of work impossible to evaluate.

C) Select Claude Haiku because code generation and analysis tasks should default to the cheapest model tier available.
D) Opt for Claude Opus because content platforms need peak reasoning and visual analysis, requiring the top tier.
correct_answers: B) Choose Claude Sonnet, as it offers frontier intelligence for coding, analysis, and visual understanding at scale.
explanations: Incorrect. Claude models, especially Sonnet, include robust data analysis and visual understanding features, so the described product's needs are well covered without resorting to external models.

Correct. Claude Sonnet offers frontier intelligence for coding, analysis, and visual understanding at scale, making it the right tier for a product that needs strong, general capabilities without the highest cost.

Incorrect. Defaulting to the cheapest tier ignores that this product requires robust performance across demanding tasks; Haiku is optimized for cost-efficient, simpler workloads, not the breadth of capabilities needed here.

Incorrect. Opus is designed for the most complex, high-autonomy, or accuracy-critical tasks; a scaling content and analysis product fits Sonnet's balanced profile better than the top, most expensive tier.

question: A finance team wants to use Claude to calculate and report final loan interest figures directly to customers with no further checks. What risk should be communicated about this workflow?
options: A) Communicate that Claude's arithmetic has been certified as error-free for all financial and regulatory calculations, making separate validation unnecessary.
B) Communicate that manual validation is unnecessary because customers are legally obligated to review all figures and will identify any calculation errors on their own.
C) Communicate that Claude is not designed for precise financial calculations, so loan interest determinations must be delegated to a dedicated accounting system.
D) Communicate that outputs involving precise financial calculations should be validated against a deterministic calculation system before use.
correct_answers: D) Communicate that outputs involving precise financial calculations should be validated against a deterministic calculation system before use.
explanations: Incorrect. Claude's arithmetic is not certified as error-free for financial and regulatory calculations. Claiming such certification overstates its reliability and could lead to unvalidated outputs being used in high-stakes contexts.

Incorrect. Relying on customers to catch errors is not a responsible validation approach; financial outputs should be verified internally before they reach customers. Legal obligations on customers do not absolve the provider from ensuring accuracy.
Incorrect. While Claude is not a dedicated financial engine, it can assist with such workflows when outputs are validated. The risk is not total incapability but the need for verification before use.

Correct. Precise financial calculations demand high accuracy, and language model outputs are not inherently deterministic or error-free. Therefore, any output involving such calculations should be validated against a deterministic calculation system before being used.

question: A customer support chatbot built on Claude detects that a customer's message expresses distress and references potential legal action. What should the system do with this conversation?

explanations: Incorrect. Adding more apologies does not address the substantive risk of mishandling a distressed customer or a legal threat.
Incorrect. Closing the ticket automatically ignores the escalation risk and could leave a serious concern unresolved.
Correct. Messages signaling distress or potential legal action are high-risk situations where a trained human agent should take over rather than continuing fully automated handling.
Incorrect. A longer automated response does not provide the human judgment needed for a sensitive, potentially legal situation.

question: A market research team on the company's Claude for Work plan wants Claude to analyse interview transcripts containing participants' names, employers and health conditions. Which two steps should they take before uploading? Select two.
options: A) Confirm the consent participants gave covers having their transcripts processed in an external tool.
B) Open an incognito chat for the upload so that these health details cannot be retained anywhere at all.
C) Strip out the direct identifiers that the thematic analysis does not actually need in order to work.
D) Divide the transcripts across several separate chats so that no single conversation ever holds them all.
E) Turn off the model improvement setting on the account so the transcripts cannot be used for training.
correct_answers: A) Confirm the consent participants gave covers having their transcripts processed in an external tool.
C) Strip out the direct identifiers that the thematic analysis does not actually need in order to work.
explanations: Correct. Independently of minimisation, health data about identifiable people carries a consent and lawful-basis question that must be settled before processing.
Incognito chats are not used to improve Claude, but they are not a lawful basis for processing sensitive personal data and do not address consent.
Correct. Data minimisation comes first: if the themes can be found without names and employers, that sensitive detail should never be pasted in.
Splitting the same sensitive content across chats does not reduce what was disclosed; it only makes the work harder to manage.
Commercial plans such as Claude for Work do not use inputs or outputs to train models by default, so this changes nothing about the real risk.

question: A programme officer needs to answer the question 'what are our reporting obligations for this funding stream'. What should she settle first?
options: A) How much reasoning to ask for, since obligations of this kind are usually explained across several steps.
B) Whether the answer must come from her own funding documents or from material published outside them.
C) Whether to ask the question in one go or split it across several smaller and more specific questions.
D) How long the answer should be and which colleagues it will need to be circulated to once it is finished.
correct_answers: B) Whether the answer must come from her own funding documents or from material published outside them.
explanations: Asking for more explanation makes the answer easier to follow without making it any more grounded in the right source.

Correct. The two cases call for different approaches. If her grant agreement governs, the documents should be supplied and the answer confined to them; if the obligation is set publicly, the task becomes a research one where cited sources matter. Everything else follows from that choice.
Splitting the question is a useful technique for large tasks, but it does not determine what the answer will be based on.
Length and audience shape how the answer is presented, and they can be decided once she knows where the answer is coming from.

question: A team building an insurance claims triage tool on Claude wants to minimize the risk that the model's outputs unfairly disadvantage claimants from a particular demographic group, even though no single field in the input data directly names race or ethnicity. What is the most ethically sound step for the team to take?
options: A) Add a single disclaimer stating outputs may be biased, in place of testing for disparate outcomes
B) Test outputs for disparate impact across groups, since proxies like zip code can encode bias
C) Conclude that bias is not possible, since the input data excludes explicitly protected fields
D) Restrict testing to overall accuracy metrics, since subgroup fairness is outside model evaluation
correct_answers: B) Test outputs for disparate impact across groups, since proxies like zip code can encode bias
explanations: Incorrect. A disclaimer does not substitute for actually evaluating and mitigating disparate outcomes in a high-risk application like insurance claims.

Correct. Even without explicit protected fields, proxy variables can encode demographic information, so responsible practice requires testing for disparate impact across groups using representative scenarios before deployment.
Incorrect. Excluding explicit protected fields does not prevent bias, since correlated proxy variables can still produce disparate outcomes.
Incorrect. Overall accuracy can mask unequal error rates across subgroups, so subgroup-level fairness evaluation is necessary in high-risk contexts.

question: A prompt engineering team wants a quick sanity check to decide whether a draft prompt is clear enough before sending it to Claude in production. What check reflects the recommended "golden rule" for prompt clarity?
options: A) Show it to a colleague with minimal context and see if they could follow it correctly
B) Ask Claude itself to guess what the prompt author must have originally intended
C) Send the same prompt to several people and average their reactions numerically
D) Translate the prompt into another language and back to test for consistency
correct_answers: A) Show it to a colleague with minimal context and see if they could follow it correctly
explanations: Correct. The golden rule for prompt clarity is to show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it; if they'd be confused, Claude will be too.
Having Claude guess the original intent does not test whether the instructions themselves are clear and specific enough for a new reader to follow.
Averaging numerical reactions from multiple people is not the documented golden rule and adds unnecessary process without checking for actual confusion or ambiguity.
Round-trip translation tests linguistic stability, not whether the instructions are explicit and unambiguous to someone unfamiliar with the task.

question: A team is evaluating a customer support assistant and only measures whether responses are factually correct, ignoring tone, relevance, and consistency. Following recommended evaluation practice, what is the main risk of this approach?
options: A) Adding more evaluation dimensions reduces overall assessment reliability, so the team should keep the evaluation limited to factual correctness.
B) Single-dimension evaluation misses important quality issues, so complex tasks should be scored across multiple criteria.
C) Multidimensional evaluation is only needed for safety-critical systems, so factual correctness alone is appropriate for customer support.
D) Factual correctness is the single most important factor for customer support, making this evaluation approach fully adequate.
correct_answers: B) Single-dimension evaluation misses important quality issues, so complex tasks should be scored across multiple criteria.
explanations: Incorrect. Adding more evaluation dimensions does not reduce reliability; rather, it provides a more comprehensive and accurate assessment. Multidimensional evaluation is encouraged for complex tasks to capture quality aspects beyond factual accuracy.

Correct. Single-dimension evaluation misses important quality issues like tone, relevance, and consistency. Recommended practice calls for multidimensional scoring to ensure comprehensive assessment of complex tasks.

Incorrect. Multidimensional evaluation is recommended broadly for complex tasks, not only safety-critical systems. A customer support assistant benefits from evaluating tone and relevance, as these influence user satisfaction.

Incorrect. Factual correctness alone is insufficient for complex tasks like customer support; ignoring tone, relevance, and consistency can lead to poor user experiences. Recommended practice emphasizes multidimensional evaluation to fully assess quality.

question: A small charity has no legal adviser. Its manager asks Claude what the new reporting rules require, receives a clear and specific answer, and files the return on that basis alone. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The explanation may be pitched at a level of detail that the charity's own trustees find difficult to follow later.
B) A single unverified answer is being treated as authoritative on a filing with real consequences for the charity.
C) The explanation may cover the reporting rules while leaving out related rules the charity has not asked about.
D) The explanation may use technical vocabulary the manager has to look up before he can act on any of it.
correct_answers: B) A single unverified answer is being treated as authoritative on a filing with real consequences for the charity.
explanations: Detail pitched wrongly for trustees is a communication issue that a rewrite fixes, and it does not affect whether the filing is correct.

Correct. Regulatory filings carry consequences that are hard to reverse, and a confident answer is not a verified one. High-stakes guidance should be confirmed against the regulator's own material or a professional adviser.
Adjacent obligations being missed is a genuine gap, but it is one instance of the broader problem of relying on a single unchecked answer.
Unfamiliar vocabulary slows the manager down and is easily resolved by asking for a plainer explanation.

question: A compliance lead is writing an internal FAQ explaining how staff may use Claude. Which statement about model training is accurate to include?
options: A) Inputs and outputs from commercial products are used for training unless an organisation owner opts the account out.
B) Training behaviour is the same on personal and commercial plans, so a single sentence can cover every account type.
C) Inputs and outputs from commercial products such as Claude for Work are not used to train models by default.
D) Personal Free, Pro and Max accounts never contribute any conversation content to model training under any circumstance.
correct_answers: C) Inputs and outputs from commercial products such as Claude for Work are not used to train models by default.

question: An events manager is preparing an attendee FAQ. She has last year's FAQ, the signed contract for this year's venue, and an email thread with the caterer. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to draft the FAQ from last year's version, then check it against the contract and the caterer emails.
B) Paste all three documents together and ask Claude to work out which of the details in them are the most current ones.
C) Summarise each of the three documents on her own, and paste only those summaries so the request stays compact.
D) Decide which document is authoritative this year, and label each as she pastes it so Claude knows which one wins.
correct_answers: D) Decide which document is authoritative this year, and label each as she pastes it so Claude knows which one wins.
explanations: Drafting from the superseded document first anchors the FAQ on last year's arrangements, and checking afterwards catches only the differences she happens to look for.
Nothing in the documents states which is newest or which governs, so this hands a decision she alone can make to a source that cannot see the contractual hierarchy.
Her own summaries drop the specifics attendees ask about, such as exact times and access rules, and the precedence problem is still unresolved.

Correct. The three sources disagree by design: the contract supersedes last year's FAQ, and the email thread may supersede both on catering. Establishing precedence and labelling each source is what stops last year's details being presented as this year's.

question: A team wants Claude to research an open-ended market question, tracking multiple competing explanations and its confidence in each as it gathers evidence over many searches. What approach best supports this research task?
options: A) Run one broad search and answer directly from that result with no further checks
B) Avoid recording any intermediate findings so the final answer reflects only the very last search
C) Develop competing hypotheses, track confidence in notes, and self-critique while searching
D) Commit to a single explanation immediately so later searches confirm that theory
correct_answers: C) Develop competing hypotheses, track confidence in notes, and self-critique while searching
explanations: Incorrect. A single unverified search skips the source verification that complex research questions need before drawing conclusions.
Incorrect. Discarding intermediate findings loses the calibration and transparency that a persisted research notes file is meant to provide across a long research task.
Correct. For complex, open-ended research, Claude should develop competing hypotheses, track confidence in progress notes, and self-critique regularly to work through evidence methodically.
Incorrect. Committing to one explanation immediately biases the research toward confirming a single theory instead of weighing competing hypotheses against gathered evidence.

question: A finance director asks why the team is proposing a smaller, faster Claude model for a high-volume invoice classification workflow instead of the most capable model available. What is the best way to justify this choice?
options: A) Explain that the most capable model cannot process invoices at all, so a smaller model is the only technically possible option.
B) Explain that classification is a straightforward task, so a faster and cheaper model can meet accuracy needs at lower cost and latency.
C) Explain that model choice has no effect on cost, so picking the smaller model is purely a matter of team preference.
D) Explain that smaller models are always more accurate than larger models for every business task the company might have.
correct_answers: B) Explain that classification is a straightforward task, so a faster and cheaper model can meet accuracy needs at lower cost and latency.
explanations: Incorrect. The most capable model can process invoices; it is simply not the most cost- or latency-efficient choice for this task.

Correct. For high-volume, relatively simple tasks like classification, a faster and cheaper model often delivers sufficient accuracy while reducing cost and latency, which is the standard model-selection tradeoff to communicate.
Incorrect. Model choice directly affects per-token cost and response speed, so it is not merely a matter of preference.
Incorrect. Smaller models are not universally more accurate; capability, task complexity, and cost must be weighed case by case.

question: A hospital foundation's fundraising officer wants to upload a donor list containing home addresses and giving histories so Claude can segment it for a campaign. The foundation is on a Claude for Work plan. What should she do first?
options: A) Confirm that the Claude for Work plan does not use the foundation's data to train models.
B) Run the segmentation in an incognito chat so that none of the donor details are retained at all.
C) Remove the home addresses but keep the giving history, which she considers less sensitive.
D) Check what the foundation's own policy and its donor commitments allow her to do with the list.
correct_answers: D) Check what the foundation's own policy and its donor commitments allow her to do with the list.
explanations: It is true that commercial plans do not use inputs and outputs for model training by default, but that is already settled and it is not the constraint here. Training is only one of the questions a donor list raises.
Incognito chats are not used to improve Claude, but they are not a substitute for permission to process donor data in the first place, and they do not address what the foundation promised its donors.

Stripping one field is a reasonable minimisation step, but choosing which fields to remove on her own judgement pre-empts the policy and consent questions that should decide it. Giving history is itself sensitive personal data.

Correct. The plan already settles the training question; what is unresolved is whether the foundation's own rules and the privacy commitments made to donors permit this data to be put into the tool at all. That governs everything else she does with the list.

question: A facilities manager wants Claude to turn her site-visit notes into short summaries that engineers read on their phones between jobs, so each summary must stay under 150 words. She will make this same request many times with different notes. How should she express the length limit?
options: A) Ask for the shortest summary she can get, and then cut anything back that still runs over the word limit.
B) State the 150-word limit and the reason for it: engineers read the summaries on a phone between jobs.
C) State the 150-word limit on its own, as any explanation around it only lengthens her request.
D) Repeat the 150-word limit in capital letters at the start and again at the end of the request.
correct_answers: B) State the 150-word limit and the reason for it: engineers read the summaries on a phone between jobs.
explanations: An unspecified target produces inconsistent lengths and moves the work back onto the manager.
Correct. Giving the reason behind a constraint lets Claude apply the underlying intent sensibly to new notes, rather than treating 150 words as an arbitrary rule to satisfy.
The limit alone works, but without the reason Claude cannot judge what to keep when notes vary.
Emphasis and repetition do not add information; the constraint was already clear the first time.

question: An operations lead has two hundred short, standard customer replies to prepare today and is worried about her weekly allowance. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to estimate how much of her allowance the batch is likely to consume in total.
B) Run the whole batch on the deepest-reasoning model, so no reply needs to be redone afterwards.
C) Separate the replies that genuinely need judgment from the routine bulk of the batch.
D) Split the batch across several days, so that no single day uses too much of her allowance.
correct_answers: C) Separate the replies that genuinely need judgment from the routine bulk of the batch.
explanations: Incorrect. An estimate of consumption does not change what the batch costs or tell her which parts need care.
Incorrect. Applying the most expensive tier to two hundred routine items is the fastest way to exhaust the allowance she is worried about.
Correct. Once the small number of awkward cases is identified, the routine bulk can go to the fastest and cheapest tier and the allowance is reserved for the cases that need it.
Incorrect. Spreading the work delays the replies without reducing the total allowance the batch consumes.

question: A trainer keeps asking Claude to make a technical explanation simpler, and after four rounds it reads very easily. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The explanation will become too short for the length the training materials require overall.
B) Each round can quietly drop a qualifier, leaving a version that reads well but is no longer true.
C) Repeated rounds of rewriting will make the tone of the explanation gradually more informal.
D) The final version will use vocabulary that differs from the earlier training material on the topic.
correct_answers: B) Each round can quietly drop a qualifier, leaving a version that reads well but is no longer true.
explanations: Incorrect. Length is easy to see and easy to fix, and a shorter explanation is often the point of the exercise.
Correct. Simplification removes conditions and caveats, and the wording that goes first is often what made the statement accurate rather than merely clear.
Incorrect. Drifting tone is noticeable on a read-through and does not by itself make the content wrong.
Incorrect. Inconsistent vocabulary is a presentation issue and is easily reconciled across materials.

question: An Enterprise organisation wants its members to use the Google Drive connector, but with read access only. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Members authenticate individually; the owner enables the connector; the team confirms the limits; the owner restricts it to read actions.
B) The owner enables the connector; the owner restricts it to read actions; members authenticate individually; the team confirms the limits.
C) The owner restricts it to read actions; the team confirms the limits; members authenticate individually; the owner enables the connector.
D) The team confirms the limits; members authenticate individually; the owner restricts it to read actions; the owner enables the connector.
correct_answers: B) The owner enables the connector; the owner restricts it to read actions; members authenticate individually; the team confirms the limits.
explanations: Members cannot authenticate before the owner has enabled the connector.
Correct. Enablement and action restrictions are owner-level and come before individuals connect their own accounts.
Restrictions are configured for a connector that has not been enabled yet.
The limits are confirmed first and the connector is enabled last, which reverses the setup.

question: After rewriting an instruction to say "write in flowing prose, avoid bullet points," a team still finds Claude's responses returning to bulleted lists in some outputs. They notice their own prompt itself is written using bullet points and headers throughout. Which additional iteration is most likely to help?
options: A) Increase the temperature parameter so Claude's output becomes more random, discouraging the rigid structure that leads to bullet points.
B) Add even more bullet points to the prompt, perhaps using numbered lists, to make the instruction to avoid bullets impossible for Claude to overlook.
C) Move the anti-bullet-point instruction into a separate, later user turn right before the final request, so it is more recent in the conversation.
D) Remove the bullet points and headers from the prompt itself so the prompt's own style matches the desired flowing-prose output.
correct_answers: D) Remove the bullet points and headers from the prompt itself so the prompt's own style matches the desired flowing-prose output.
explanations: Incorrect. Increasing temperature affects randomness in word choice and phrasing, but it does not discourage structural elements like lists or bullet points, which are determined more by the prompt's formatting.
Incorrect. Adding more bullet points would reinforce, not reduce, the bullet-point pattern the team is trying to eliminate, making it even harder for Claude to avoid that structure.

Incorrect. The core issue is not instruction recency but the prompt's own style. Moving the anti-bullet instruction to a later turn does not address the underlying influence of the prompt's bulleted formatting.

Correct. Anthropic notes that the formatting style used in the prompt influences Claude's response style, so removing bullet points and headers from the prompt can help the model adopt the desired flowing-prose style.

question: A chatbot answers a user's question about a niche historical event with a detailed, confident, but entirely fabricated account, since no similar event exists in its training data. The team wants to reduce this kind of failure through prompt design alone, without adding any tools. Which instruction is most effective for reducing this type of fabrication?
options: A) Instruct Claude to always answer within a strict two-sentence limit regardless of how complex the topic is
B) Instruct Claude to answer every question using only information gathered during its most recent training run
C) Tell Claude it is acceptable, and preferred, to say it cannot verify an answer rather than guessing when unsure
D) Instruct Claude to always adopt a highly confident, authoritative tone in every reply so users trust the response
correct_answers: C) Tell Claude it is acceptable, and preferred, to say it cannot verify an answer rather than guessing when unsure
explanations: Limiting response length does not address the underlying cause of fabrication and may even worsen it by forcing an answer without room for caveats.
Claude cannot selectively restrict itself to only the most recent training run, and this instruction does nothing to prevent fabrication on topics with sparse training data.

Correct. Explicitly permitting Claude to express uncertainty or decline to answer when it lacks grounded information is a well-established prompting technique for reducing confident fabrication, since models often default to producing a plausible-sounding answer when not told otherwise.
Encouraging a confident tone works against fact-checking goals, since it makes fabricated answers sound more credible rather than flagging uncertainty.

question: A user asks Claude to build an interactive to-do list where items can be checked off and reordered directly in the browser. Which artifact type fits this request?

B) An inline chat message with each item as a separate bullet, since inline lists let the user check items off directly in the conversation
C) A plain Markdown document artifact, since Markdown documents support checkboxes and are the standard format for to-do lists
D) An interactive React component artifact, since it supports the stateful, clickable interactions the to-do list requires
correct_answers: D) An interactive React component artifact, since it supports the stateful, clickable interactions the to-do list requires
explanations: Incorrect. CSV is a flat data format meant for tabular data exchange, not for delivering an interactive, clickable interface.
Incorrect. Inline chat text is static; a user cannot click to check off or reorder items directly within the conversation text.
Incorrect. A static Markdown document can show checkbox syntax but cannot support live reordering or interactive click behavior the way a component can.
Correct. React components are a supported artifact type built for interactive, stateful UI such as checking off and reordering items in the browser.

question: An executive asks a planner to use Claude to help answer whether the company should enter a new market over the next five years. Which use of Claude is most appropriate?
options: A) Ask Claude for a single clear recommendation so the executive receives an unambiguous answer to act on.
B) Ask Claude to draft the market entry announcement so the timeline can then be worked backwards from it.
C) Ask Claude to predict the market's size in five years so the decision can rest on one concrete figure.
D) Ask Claude to set out the realistic options with the trade-offs and evidence behind each one.
correct_answers: D) Ask Claude to set out the realistic options with the trade-offs and evidence behind each one.
explanations: A single recommendation hides the reasoning the executive most needs to test. Market entry turns on the company's risk appetite and capacity, which the executive holds and Claude does not, so a clean answer here is false confidence.

Drafting the announcement assumes the decision has been made and then reverse-engineers a plan to fit it. That is a good technique for communicating a chosen course, not for deciding whether to take it.

A five-year market size figure is a projection presented as a fact. Resting the decision on one number invites precision that the underlying uncertainty cannot support and crowds out the trade-offs that actually matter.

Correct. Claude is strongest here as an analyst that widens and structures the option space, surfacing trade-offs and the evidence behind each path. The executive keeps the strategic choice, which is where the accountability sits.

question: A consultant is briefing colleagues on the guidance that Claude should not be relied on as a singular source of truth. What does that principle mean in day-to-day practice for a claim she intends to act on?
options: A) That she should avoid Claude for factual work altogether and confine her use of it to drafting, wording and brainstorming.
B) That she should raise the same question in several fresh conversations and treat consistent answers as adequate confirmation.
C) That she should keep her questions narrow, because short and tightly scoped requests are inherently less prone to inaccuracy.
D) That a claim she is going to act on needs corroboration from an independent source before she treats it as established.
correct_answers: D) That a claim she is going to act on needs corroboration from an independent source before she treats it as established.
explanations: Abandoning factual work overstates the guidance, which is about verifying rather than avoiding. It also gives up genuinely useful help with research and synthesis that a person can then check.

Repeated conversations are still the same source, so agreement between them is not independent corroboration. A confidently wrong claim can be reproduced consistently across as many chats as she cares to open.

Narrower questions can improve focus, but scope is not a guarantee of accuracy and a short answer can be just as wrong. This substitutes a prompting habit for the verification the principle actually calls for.

Correct. The principle is about where confirmation comes from: anything consequential should be corroborated outside the conversation, so Claude informs the decision rather than being the only thing standing behind it.

question: A teacher wants Claude to answer student questions from a large and steadily growing set of course materials, across many separate chats. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Add the course materials to each chat; create a Project; ask questions in that project; keep the instructions brief.
B) Ask questions in a plain chat; keep the instructions brief; create a Project; add the course materials as project knowledge.
C) Keep the instructions brief; create a Project; ask questions in that project; add the course materials as project knowledge.
D) Create a Project; add the course materials as project knowledge; keep the instructions brief; ask questions in that project.
correct_answers: D) Create a Project; add the course materials as project knowledge; keep the instructions brief; ask questions in that project.
explanations: Incorrect. Pasting the materials into individual chats is the very repetition a project is meant to remove.
Incorrect. The questions are asked before any of the course materials exist as project knowledge, so those first answers have nothing to draw on.
Incorrect. Asking before the materials are uploaded means the early answers have nothing to draw on.
Correct. The project has to exist before materials can be attached, brief instructions leave more room for the materials themselves, and only chats started inside the project can draw on them.

question: While researching a niche technical topic, an analyst receives a confident, well-written answer from Claude that includes a specific statistic with no source cited and no search tool used. What should the analyst do before citing this statistic in a report?

Incorrect. Detailed, confident writing is not evidence that a specific unsourced statistic is factually accurate.
Correct. An uncited, ungrounded statistic may be a hallucination, so the analyst should confirm it against an independent authoritative source before citing it.

question: A facilitator wants Claude to produce short prompts and summaries live during workshops, with participants waiting in the room. She standardises on the deepest-reasoning tier so that the material is always as good as it can be. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The facilitator becomes reliant on having Claude available, so a session held somewhere without connectivity is harder to run.
B) The material becomes more detailed than a live workshop can absorb, so participants receive more text than they can read aloud.
C) The workshop material varies in tone between sessions, so participants attending more than one workshop notice the difference.
D) The answers take longer to come back than a room of waiting participants can tolerate, so the help is unusable in the moment.
correct_answers: D) The answers take longer to come back than a room of waiting participants can tolerate, so the help is unusable in the moment.
explanations: Dependence on connectivity is a sensible contingency to plan for, but it applies equally whichever tier she picks, so it is not the risk created by standardising on the deepest one.
Over-long output is a genuine annoyance, but it is fixed by asking for something shorter. It is not caused by the tier choice, and the facilitator can control length in the request itself.
Some variation between sessions is expected with any tier and matters little for workshop prompts. It is a consistency preference rather than something that stops the session working.

Correct. Depth is bought with time, and in a live setting responsiveness is the binding constraint. Choosing the deepest tier here sacrifices the very quality, immediacy, that made Claude useful in the room.

question: A developer asks Claude to build a small interactive React component that visualizes sales data with adjustable filters, and expects to iterate on the code across several follow-up messages. explanations: Project knowledge is meant for background reference documents the user uploads, not for displaying and iteratively editing generated code with version tracking.
Research mode is for gathering external information through web searches, not for rendering or iterating on generated code.
Printing code inline in the main transcript does not provide the dedicated side-panel view or version history that iterative component development benefits from.

Correct. Artifacts open substantial, self-contained content like a React component in a dedicated side panel and provide a version selector, letting the developer iterate and switch between revisions.

question: A legal assistant needs to summarize a 50-page contract, highlighting obligations, risks, and key dates. Which prompting strategy yields the most precise and actionable summary?
options: A) Instruct Claude to review the contract and draft a summary focusing on what it determines to be the central points, including obligations and dates it selects based on its own analysis, organizing the output with headings it deems appropriate.

B) Ask Claude to read the contract and produce an abstract that emphasizes the overall intent and identifies the key parties, describing the general nature of the agreement without going into specific obligations, risk allocations, or dates.

C) Guide Claude to methodically parse the contract: first list party obligations, then identify risk allocation clauses (e.g., indemnities, limitations), then extract key dates into a timeline, and organize under these headings.

D) Prompt Claude to generate a high-level overview that broadly covers the contract's purpose, parties, and general terms, while explicitly avoiding detailed extractions such as specific obligations, risk allocation clauses, and key dates.
correct_answers: C) Guide Claude to methodically parse the contract: first list party obligations, then identify risk allocation clauses (e.g., indemnities, limitations), then extract key dates into a timeline, and organize under these headings.
explanations: Incorrect. This strategy leaves too much to Claude's discretion, which may result in missing key obligations, risks, or dates, or organizing them in an unstructured way. Without explicit guidance, the summary may not be sufficiently precise or actionable for legal purposes.

Incorrect. Like option B, this produces a general abstract that omits the critical specifics. It does not extract the actionable details (obligations, risks, dates) necessary for the assistant's task.

Correct. This prompt provides a structured, methodical approach that ensures all required elements (obligations, risks, dates) are systematically extracted and organized. It directly addresses the need for precision and actionability by breaking down the task into clear steps and explicit headings.

Incorrect. This approach explicitly avoids the detailed extractions required, making it unsuitable for a precise and actionable summary. It will not provide the specific obligations, risks, or dates needed for legal analysis.

B) Compare the fact sheet against a second Claude draft written from the same brief and topic.

correct_answers: D) Re-establish which sources the fact sheet rests on, since checking needs something to check against.
explanations: Incorrect. A disclaimer does not make unverified statements safe to publish; it just moves the risk onto the reader.
Incorrect. Agreement between two generated drafts is not evidence, since both can be wrong in the same way.
Incorrect. Claude cannot inspect how an earlier response was produced, and it has no access to the sources that were or were not used.
Correct. Verification is a comparison, and without an agreed set of authoritative sources there is nothing to compare the statements with.

question: A developer wants to grade thousands of Claude outputs for quality and plans to have the same model that generated the outputs also score them. A colleague flags this as a risky design. What is the main concern with using the same model to both generate and grade its own outputs?
options: A) The model cannot process its own prior outputs as input, so grading requests will fail
B) The model will exceed its context window whenever it grades more than a few responses
C) The model's pricing doubles whenever it is reused for both generation and grading tasks
D) The model may favor its own outputs, so a separate model or human should grade instead
correct_answers: D) The model may favor its own outputs, so a separate model or human should grade instead
explanations: Incorrect. A model can process its own prior text as input to a new request; there is no technical restriction preventing this.
Incorrect. Context window limits depend on total input size, not on whether the grading model is the same one that generated the text.
Incorrect. Pricing is based on token usage per request, not on whether the same model is reused across generation and grading steps.
Correct. A recommended best practice is to use a separate model or human reviewers for grading, since a model grading its own generations can be biased toward judging them favorably.

question: A legal operations stakeholder plans to send Claude-generated contract redlines directly to clients without any attorney review, to reduce turnaround time. What should the solutions architect recommend?

B) Recommend sending Claude's redlines directly to clients, since its legal reasoning always equals an attorney's judgment.
C) Recommend removing Claude from the workflow entirely, since it cannot generate any useful redline suggestions.

correct_answers: A) Recommend keeping attorney review before delivery, since Claude can miss jurisdiction-specific or contextual nuances.
explanations: Correct. Claude can accelerate redlining, but it may miss jurisdiction-specific nuances or context only a qualified attorney would catch, so attorney review before external delivery reduces legal risk.
Incorrect. Claude's outputs are not guaranteed to be equivalent to attorney-level legal judgment, so skipping review is risky.
Incorrect. Claude can meaningfully assist with drafting and redlining; the concern is about unsupervised external delivery, not usefulness.
Incorrect. Shifting verification onto clients does not address the firm's own responsibility for quality and risk in what it sends out.

question: A newsletter editor needs a Claude-drafted piece to quote the organisation's own published figures accurately. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Ask Claude to draft the piece; gather the published figures; check the draft's numbers against them; send the piece out to readers.
B) Gather the published figures; check the draft's numbers against them; give them to Claude as the material; send the piece out to readers.
C) Gather the published figures; give them to Claude as the material; check the draft's numbers against them; send the piece out to readers.
D) Give them to Claude as the material; send the piece out to readers; gather the published figures; check the draft's numbers against them.
correct_answers: C) Gather the published figures; give them to Claude as the material; check the draft's numbers against them; send the piece out to readers.
explanations: Incorrect. Drafting before the figures are supplied invites Claude to fill the gaps, which creates the errors the later check then has to catch.
Incorrect. The numbers are checked before a draft exists, and the source material reaches Claude only after the piece has been written.
Correct. Supplying the authoritative figures first keeps the draft grounded, and the check afterwards confirms nothing drifted during writing.
Incorrect. The piece goes to readers before the figures have been gathered or any check has taken place.

question: A marketer runs a new campaign chat each week and re-pastes the same brand guidelines and tone-of-voice document into every one. She wants to stop repeating herself. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Add project instructions; run each campaign chat inside it; create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge.
B) Upload the guidelines as project knowledge; run each campaign chat inside it; create a Project; add project instructions.
C) Create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge; add project instructions; run each campaign chat inside it.
D) Run each campaign chat first; add project instructions; create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge.
correct_answers: C) Create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge; add project instructions; run each campaign chat inside it.
explanations: Incorrect. Instructions and chats are both scoped to a project, so neither can come before the project is created.

question: An HR team is using Claude to rework the onboarding checklist for four departments at once. Which two practices will make the staged approach hold together? Select two.
options: A) Begin from the final recommendation and ask Claude to justify it across the four teams.
B) Put a human check after the stage where an unnoticed error would carry into later work.
C) Keep all four departments inside one prompt so that the wording stays perfectly aligned.
D) State the concrete output each stage must hand to the next, such as a named gap list.
E) Ask Claude to pick the stages itself and work straight through them without showing them.
correct_answers: B) Put a human check after the stage where an unnoticed error would carry into later work.
D) State the concrete output each stage must hand to the next, such as a named gap list.
explanations: Starting from a conclusion invites the evidence to be arranged to fit it, which is the reverse of the order a decomposed analysis should follow.
Correct. This addresses a different risk from the hand-off format: checkpoints stop a wrong fact being built upon, which is the main cost of chaining steps.
One prompt covering four departments is what caused the shallow result in the first place. Consistency is better handled by reusing a stated format across stages.
Correct. Naming the artefact each stage produces gives the next stage something concrete to consume, instead of a vague hand-off the team has to interpret.
Hidden stages remove the team's ability to catch a wrong plan early, and produce a long output whose reasoning cannot be inspected or corrected.

question: A marketing operations lead is deciding which steps of the campaign brief intake process to hand to Claude. Which characteristic most reliably marks a step as a good candidate for delegation?
options: A) The step is repetitive and text-heavy, and the team can describe clearly what a good result looks like.
B) The step depends on one manager's undocumented sense of which stakeholders need careful handling.
C) The step commits agency spend externally as soon as it completes, so speed matters more than review.
D) The step is the one that team members complain about most often during retrospectives and planning days.
correct_answers: A) The step is repetitive and text-heavy, and the team can describe clearly what a good result looks like.
explanations: Correct. Repetitive, text-heavy work with a describable standard of success is the classic strong delegation candidate: there is volume to save, the material suits language work, and the team can tell whether the result is acceptable because they agreed in advance what acceptable means.

Work that rests on one person's undocumented judgment cannot be specified well enough to delegate, and there is no written standard against which the output could be checked. Sole-source judgment is a reason to keep a step human.

A step that spends money externally the moment it finishes is irreversible, so an error cannot be caught and corrected. Irreversibility is one of the standard markers of a step that should stay with a person, not move to Claude.

How much a step is disliked says nothing about whether it can be delegated well. Unpopular steps are often unpopular precisely because they demand awkward judgment calls, which is the profile of a poor candidate rather than a good one.

question: After a cost review, a team switches every Claude task to the fastest and cheapest tier. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Every task will now be completed rather faster than the team is able to review the output properly.
B) Responses will be much shorter, so colleagues will have to ask more follow-up questions.
C) The small number of genuinely hard analyses will thin out with no agreed standard to catch it.

correct_answers: C) The small number of genuinely hard analyses will thin out with no agreed standard to catch it.

question: An HR team uses Claude to generate a shortlist recommendation from a stack of job applications. Before any candidate is rejected based on this shortlist, what should the team do?
options: A) Have a recruiter review the underlying applications to check for bias or overlooked qualified candidates
B) Shorten the job description so future applicant pools are easier for the model to rank consistently
C) Reject every applicant left off the shortlist since the model already considered all submitted application details
D) Ask Claude to regenerate the shortlist a second time and merge both lists into the final decision
correct_answers: A) Have a recruiter review the underlying applications to check for bias or overlooked qualified candidates
explanations: Correct. Employment decisions carry legal and fairness risk, so a recruiter should review the underlying applications to catch bias or qualified candidates the model may have overlooked.
Incorrect. Changing the job description does not address whether the current shortlist decision requires human review before candidates are rejected.
Incorrect. Rejecting candidates purely based on an unreviewed AI shortlist risks embedding bias or errors into a consequential employment decision.
Incorrect. Merging two outputs from the same model does not introduce the independent human judgment needed to catch bias in a hiring decision.

question: A Claude-assisted tender-response arrangement runs well, but it depends on adjustments that the one person who built it makes by hand each time and has never written down. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The manual adjustments may take that person longer as tender volumes continue to increase.
B) Other teams may build slightly different versions of the same arrangement for their own use.
C) The person may find it hard to explain the arrangement's benefits when funding is next reviewed.
D) The arrangement stops working the moment that person is unavailable, and nobody can rebuild it.
correct_answers: D) The arrangement stops working the moment that person is unavailable, and nobody can rebuild it.
explanations: Growing effort as volumes rise is a scaling concern that would show up gradually and can be planned for. It is a reason to invest further, not the thing that could remove the capability overnight.
Divergent local versions cause inconsistency across teams and are worth avoiding. That is an organisational tidiness problem rather than a threat to this team's ability to respond to tenders.
Difficulty explaining the benefits could cost future funding, which matters. It is a communication weakness rather than the structural fragility of a process nobody else can run.

Correct. The working design lives in one person's head, so leave, illness or a change of role removes the capability entirely and leaves no way to reconstruct it. An arrangement that cannot be handed over has not really been designed, only performed.

B) A context limitation, since the source document was too long for Claude to fully process
C) A bias, since Claude systematically favored one publication over equally valid alternatives

correct_answers: A) A hallucination, since Claude fabricated a citation with no basis in any verifiable source
explanations: Correct. A hallucination is content presented as fact that is not grounded in the source material or any verifiable reference; an invented citation is a classic example.
Incorrect. Nothing in the scenario indicates the document exceeded the context window; the issue is a fabricated reference, not truncation.
Incorrect. Bias involves skewed treatment of topics, groups, or viewpoints, not the invention of a nonexistent source.
Incorrect. Inconsistency refers to conflicting statements within or across responses, not a fabricated fact that never existed.

question: In an earlier stage a bid team agreed three criteria for evaluating partner organisations. They now start the scoring stage in a fresh conversation. What should they include in the scoring request?
options: A) A note that criteria were agreed earlier, and a request that Claude apply the same ones it used in that stage.
B) The name of the earlier conversation, so that the reasoning from that stage is picked up and continued here.
C) A request to propose fresh criteria for scoring partners, which they will then compare against the three they agreed.
D) The three agreed criteria written out in full, together with the partner information the scoring is to be based on.
correct_answers: D) The three agreed criteria written out in full, together with the partner information the scoring is to be based on.
explanations: A reference to work done elsewhere cannot be relied on to carry the agreed criteria into this stage, so the scoring may proceed against criteria that were never the ones the team settled.
Naming a previous conversation is not a dependable way to bring its contents forward, so the stage can run without the criteria it is meant to apply.
Regenerating criteria reopens a decision the team already made, and comparing two sets adds work without improving the scores.

Correct. A new conversation starts with nothing from the previous stage, so anything the next step depends on has to be carried across explicitly. Restating the criteria and supplying the partner information makes the scoring reproducible and traceable.

question: A prompt asks Claude to solve multi-step word problems, but final answers are frequently arithmetically wrong even though the described approach sounds reasonable. Which change is most likely to reduce these errors?
options: A) Shorten the word problem's wording considerably so there is simply much less text overall for Claude to process carefully before it answers.
B) Repeat the exact same word problem twice within the prompt so Claude effectively gets two separate chances to parse it correctly.
C) Have Claude work through the problem step by step before the final answer, separating its reasoning from the answer using structured tags.
D) Ask Claude to skip any intermediate explanation entirely and output only the final numeric answer so there is less room for error.
correct_answers: C) Have Claude work through the problem step by step before the final answer, separating its reasoning from the answer using structured tags.
explanations: Incorrect. Shortening the wording doesn't address the missing step-by-step reasoning that catches arithmetic mistakes, and could remove necessary problem details.
Incorrect. Duplicating the problem statement does not add a reasoning process and is not a documented technique for reducing calculation errors.

Correct. Encouraging step-by-step reasoning (chain-of-thought), with structured tags to separate reasoning from the final answer, is Anthropic's documented technique for catching errors reliably, especially in coding and math tasks.
Incorrect. Removing the reasoning step is the opposite of the documented fix; skipping intermediate steps tends to increase arithmetic errors on multi-step problems.

question: A researcher wants to use Claude to synthesize findings from multiple academic papers. Which workflow is most effective for leveraging Claude's capabilities?
options: A) Ask Claude to rank all papers by citation count, then perform a thorough analysis and synthesis of only the top three, ignoring the rest.
B) Manually summarize each paper first, then ask Claude to paraphrase those summaries into a single narrative without further analysis.
C) Feed all papers to Claude at once and request a bullet list of interesting quotes without any thematic grouping or structure.
D) Extract key findings from each paper individually, then synthesize them via comparison and contrast, and finally request a gap analysis.
correct_answers: D) Extract key findings from each paper individually, then synthesize them via comparison and contrast, and finally request a gap analysis.
explanations: Incorrect. Ranking papers by citation count may overlook highly relevant but less-cited studies, such as recent or niche works. Limiting analysis to only the top three papers discards potentially important insights, resulting in a skewed or incomplete synthesis.

Incorrect. Manual summarization adds unnecessary effort and prevents Claude from working with original content directly. Having Claude only paraphrase those summaries into a single narrative forgoes deeper comparison and analysis, reducing the depth of the synthesis.

Incorrect. Asking for a bullet list of interesting quotes without thematic grouping or structure limits Claude's ability to provide a coherent synthesis. This approach may produce a superficial and disorganized collection of excerpts rather than meaningful insights.

Correct. Extracting key findings from each paper individually ensures reliable source-level capture before synthesis. Comparing and contrasting those findings, then requesting a gap analysis, yields a structured, comprehensive synthesis that leverages Claude's analytical strengths.

question: A team has revised its Claude-assisted reporting arrangement four times in two months. The latest version is worse for certain reports, and nobody can work out which change caused it. What practice would have helped most?
options: A) Testing each revision on a larger sample of reports before it replaced the earlier version.
B) Having a single person own all revisions so the changes are made consistently over time.
C) Limiting revisions to one per month so that each change has time to settle before the next.
D) Recording what changed at each revision and why, so a step backwards can be traced.
correct_answers: D) Recording what changed at each revision and why, so a step backwards can be traced.
explanations: Wider testing would have caught the regression sooner, which is valuable. It still would not tell the team which change was responsible, so they could not undo the right one.
A single owner makes changes more consistent and is good practice. It does not help anyone reconstruct which of four revisions introduced the regression once the memory of them has faded.

Slowing the pace of change reduces how often revisions collide, but four undocumented changes over eight months would leave the team in the same position. The problem is that nothing was recorded, not that it happened quickly.

Correct. Iteration only compounds if each change is traceable. A short record of what was altered and why lets the team match the regression to the revision that caused it and roll back precisely instead of guessing.

question: A benefits team proposes letting Claude decide which employee insurance claims are denied, with staff spot-checking only a sample each month. What is the greatest concern?

correct_answers: C) A decision affecting people's benefits would be made with nobody accountable for each individual outcome.
explanations: Repetitive, well-specified work is well suited to assistance; the problem is who owns the decision.
Keeping guidance current is routine maintenance, not the greatest risk in this proposal.
Correct. Decisions about entitlements need a person answerable for every case, not a sampled review afterwards.
Sampling is cheaper than full review; the concern is accountability, not cost.
