question: A client asks a project lead to confirm in writing that material shared during the engagement will not be used to train Anthropic's models. What is the appropriate first step before he answers?
options: A) Confirm which Claude plan the engagement's work is actually being carried out on.
B) Tell the client the team will use incognito chats throughout the whole engagement.
C) Assure the client that no Anthropic product ever trains on any customer material.
D) Send the client the instructions for changing model improvement privacy settings.
correct_answers: A) Confirm which Claude plan the engagement's work is actually being carried out on.
explanations: Correct. The answer depends entirely on which plan the work sits on: commercial products such as Claude for Work do not use inputs and outputs for model training by default, whereas on personal Free, Pro and Max accounts it turns on a user-controlled setting. He cannot answer honestly until he knows which applies.

Incognito chats are never used to improve Claude, but reaching for that before knowing how the team actually works substitutes a workaround for an accurate answer, and would not suit an engagement's ongoing work.
This is too broad to be true. It ignores the difference between commercial and consumer plans, and would be an inaccurate written assurance if any of the work is happening on personal accounts.
Those instructions cover personal accounts only. Sending them implies the engagement runs on consumer plans, which he has not established and which may misrepresent the arrangement.

question: A school office wants to bring Claude into its existing parental-enquiry workflow. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Map the workflow as it runs now; run it alongside the old way; choose one step to hand over; compare the two and then decide
B) Choose one step to hand over; map the workflow as it runs now; compare the two and then decide; run it alongside the old way
C) Run it alongside the old way; compare the two and then decide; map the workflow as it runs now; choose one step to hand over
D) Map the workflow as it runs now; choose one step to hand over; run it alongside the old way; compare the two and then decide
correct_answers: D) Map the workflow as it runs now; choose one step to hand over; run it alongside the old way; compare the two and then decide
explanations: Running the new way before deciding which step it replaces leaves the parallel run undirected, and the choice is then made after the evidence.
Choosing a step before the workflow is mapped means the choice is guesswork, and comparing before running has nothing to compare.
Running and comparing before the workflow is understood produces a result nobody can interpret, and the mapping arrives too late to matter.
Correct. Map what exists, choose one step, run the new way in parallel so nothing is lost, then compare before committing. Parallel running is what makes the comparison safe.

question: An operations team must summarise several thousand short product blurbs every night, and the summaries get only a light human check. Which two factors should drive the tier choice? Select two.
options: A) How long each finished summary turns out to be, because length is what separates the tiers.
B) The reasoning depth the hardest problem anywhere in the company would need, as a safety margin.
C) The allowance the run consumes, because this same job repeats every single night of the week.
D) Whether the deepest tier appears on their plan at all, since availability settles the whole matter.
E) The throughput needed each night, because the volume makes speed per item a real constraint.
correct_answers: C) The allowance the run consumes, because this same job repeats every single night of the week.
E) The throughput needed each night, because the volume makes speed per item a real constraint.
explanations: Incorrect. Output length is set by the request, not by the tier, so it tells you nothing about which tier to pick.
Incorrect. Sizing for an unrelated hardest-case task overspends depth and quota on work that is simple and lightly reviewed.
Correct. A nightly repeat multiplies the allowance the job consumes, so recurring cost is a legitimate driver of the decision.
Incorrect. Availability is not the question; suitability for the task on cost, speed and quality is.
Correct. Thousands of items a night makes speed per item a genuine constraint, which is a core input to tier choice.

question: An analyst must deliver a carefully reasoned briefing by the end of the day and has limited allowance left. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Check it against the brief; cut the scope to what the briefing needs; run that scope on the deepest tier; expand it if time allows.
B) Cut the scope to what the briefing actually needs; run that scope on the deepest tier; check it against the brief; expand it if time allows.
C) Run the full scope on the deepest tier; cut the scope to what the briefing needs; check it against the brief; expand it if time allows.
D) Cut the scope to what the briefing actually needs; expand it if time allows; run that scope on the deepest tier; check it against the brief.
correct_answers: B) Cut the scope to what the briefing actually needs; run that scope on the deepest tier; check it against the brief; expand it if time allows.
explanations: Incorrect. Checking comes before anything has been produced, which makes the first step impossible.
Correct. Narrowing scope is what makes the deeper tier affordable within the remaining allowance, and the check confirms the reduced briefing still meets the requirement.
Incorrect. Running the full scope on the most expensive tier first spends the constrained allowance before any trimming happens.
Incorrect. Expanding the scope before it has been produced undoes the trimming that made the deeper tier affordable.

question: A brand team is running a brainstorming session for a new ad campaign and wants Claude to keep generating fresh concepts rather than settling on the first workable idea. Which instruction best supports this goal?

correct_answers: A) Ask Claude to keep generating distinct concepts after producing a workable one
explanations: Correct. Explicitly asking for continued generation of distinct concepts keeps a brainstorming session open rather than converging on the first workable answer.
Incorrect. Pre-rating the first concept highly biases the comparison against later ideas rather than encouraging open generation of fresh concepts.
Incorrect. Stopping at the first workable concept defeats the purpose of a brainstorming session meant to surface a range of fresh ideas.
Incorrect. Elaborating only on the first concept narrows the session into refining one idea instead of generating a variety of new ones.

question: Which task is most aligned with analyzing requirements and use cases for a time management application?
options: A) Ask Claude to start developing the software code for the time management application.
B) Ask Claude to generate user personas and high-level use cases for a time management app.
C) Ask Claude to provide a formal definition and explanation of the key time management concepts.
D) Ask Claude to create a marketing plan with user personas for the time management app.
correct_answers: B) Ask Claude to generate user personas and high-level use cases for a time management app.
explanations: Incorrect. Starting to develop software code is a later implementation step, not part of analyzing requirements and use cases. Analysis should always precede coding to ensure the solution is grounded in user needs, and skipping this step risks building features without a clear problem understanding.

Correct. Generating user personas and high-level use cases directly supports the analysis of requirements and use cases by clarifying who the app serves, what problems it solves, and which capabilities are most valuable. This foundational understanding is essential for designing an effective time management solution.

Incorrect. Providing a formal definition and explanation of key concepts offers background knowledge, but it does not directly address the practical analysis of user requirements and use cases. This task is too abstract and academic, lacking the user-centered insights needed to design the application's features and workflows.

Incorrect. Creating a marketing plan with user personas is a marketing and go-to-market activity, not a step in analyzing requirements and use cases. While it may later inform promotion, it does not help define the core functionality or technical requirements of the application.

question: A hospital operations lead proposes letting Claude autonomously approve treatment plans without any clinician sign-off, citing faster patient throughput. What is the most appropriate response to this proposal?
options: A) Approve the proposal as written, since faster throughput cuts wait times and Claude's output is reliable enough for sign-off, based on internal testing.
B) Recommend disabling Claude for any healthcare task, since its training data excludes recent treatment guidelines, leading to outdated recommendations.
C) Recommend keeping a licensed clinician in the loop, since Claude can support analysis but should not make unsupervised medical decisions.
D) Recommend that clinicians only review treatment plans once per quarter, since periodic oversight ensures safety while minimizing clinician burden.
correct_answers: C) Recommend keeping a licensed clinician in the loop, since Claude can support analysis but should not make unsupervised medical decisions.
explanations: Incorrect. Removing clinician sign-off entirely introduces unacceptable patient-safety risks; no internal testing can fully guarantee Claude's reliability for unsupervised medical decisions.

Incorrect. Claude can still add significant value in clinical support roles, such as summarizing records or drafting plans for review; the concern here is unsupervised autonomy, not its usefulness in healthcare tasks.

Correct. High-stakes medical decisions require a human expert in the loop; Claude can assist with analysis and accelerate workflows but should not make autonomous treatment approvals without clinician oversight.

Incorrect. Reviewing treatment plans only once per quarter leaves the vast majority of decisions unsupervised for extended periods, failing to address the fundamental safety requirement of consistent clinician oversight.

question: A manager asks Claude to pull figures from several uploaded reports into one table and plans to paste it straight into a board deck. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) A tidy table hides which report each number came from and which ones were inferred rather than read.
B) The table will be formatted in a way the presentation software cannot display neatly on a slide.
C) The table will contain more rows than a board audience can reasonably absorb during a meeting.
D) Building the table will use up rather more of her allowance than reading the reports herself would have.
correct_answers: A) A tidy table hides which report each number came from and which ones were inferred rather than read.
explanations: Correct. Putting figures in a grid strips away their provenance and any caveats, so numbers of very different reliability end up looking equally authoritative to the board.
Incorrect. Layout problems are visible immediately and take minutes to correct, unlike a wrong figure nobody notices.
Incorrect. Too much detail is an editing problem, and it is easily fixed once someone reads the table.
Incorrect. The cost of producing the table is minor compared with a board decision resting on untraceable figures.

question: A user has iterated on a code artifact through four rounds of edits and now decides the second version was actually the best one. How can the user return to that earlier version?
options: A) Start an entirely new conversation, since artifact versions cannot be recovered once a newer version has been created
B) Use the artifact's version selector to switch back to the second version, since each iteration is preserved and can be revisited
C) Ask Claude to recall the exact wording of the second version from memory, since earlier artifact versions are not stored anywhere
D) Manually retype the second version from the chat history, since artifacts only ever display the most recent iteration
correct_answers: B) Use the artifact's version selector to switch back to the second version, since each iteration is preserved and can be revisited
explanations: Incorrect. Version history persists within the same conversation, so starting a new conversation is not required to view an earlier version.
Correct. The artifact interface includes a version selector that lets users switch between prior iterations of the same artifact without losing any of them.
Incorrect. Prior versions are stored and browsable through the version selector, not something Claude needs to reconstruct from memory.
Incorrect. Artifacts retain their edit history, so manually retyping an earlier version is unnecessary.

question: A customer-success manager writes one request asking Claude to summarise thirty support tickets, rank the underlying problems, draft an apology to the largest affected account, and outline a slide for the leadership review. Every part comes back thin. How should she restructure the request?
options: A) Keep the single request as it stands and attach the tickets as a file so that there is more to work from.
B) Send the same four-part request again, this time asking for much more detail in each part.
C) Keep the single request but split the tickets into three batches and send it once per batch.
D) Establish the summary and the ranking first, then ask for the apology and the slide as separate steps.
correct_answers: D) Establish the summary and the ranking first, then ask for the apology and the slide as separate steps.
explanations: The tickets were never the constraint here; the request is doing four different jobs at once.
The problem is that one request carries four jobs, so repeating it with more emphasis changes little.
This multiplies the overloaded request rather than separating the work it is trying to do at once.
Correct. The four parts are one analysis feeding three different deliverables; settling the analysis first gives each later step something solid and specific to work from.

question: A department is picking which parts of its work to hand to Claude first. Which two tasks are the stronger candidates for that first handover? Select two.
options: A) Approving contract terms for the company without any lawyer reviewing what was agreed.
B) Sending payments out to suppliers automatically once an invoice arrives in the inbox.
C) Drafting first-pass summaries of long vendor documents that a specialist then checks over.
D) Making the final call on which of the employees will be promoted in this year's review round.
E) Reformatting a high volume of well-specified status updates into one agreed house template.
correct_answers: C) Drafting first-pass summaries of long vendor documents that a specialist then checks over.
E) Reformatting a high volume of well-specified status updates into one agreed house template.
explanations: Incorrect. Binding the company to contract terms without legal review is both irreversible and outside what should be delegated.
Incorrect. Sending money is irreversible, which is the textbook sign that a step should not be handed over unattended.
Correct. Text-heavy first drafts with a specialist review afterwards are the classic good candidate: repetitive work, recoverable errors.
Incorrect. Promotion decisions affect people's livelihoods and need human accountability, so Claude may inform but not decide.
Correct. High-volume, well-specified reformatting is delegable precisely because the standard is clear and the output is checkable.

options: A) Route every ticket to a larger model on the assumption that added model capacity will infer the missing category definitions.

correct_answers: D) Rewrite the prompt to list the exact categories, the desired output format, and the criteria for choosing between them.

Incorrect. Manual relabeling is a workaround applied after generation, not a fix to the prompt causing the inconsistency.

Correct. Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions; a vague one-line prompt lacking the category list, output format, and selection criteria is the classic underperformance pattern, and the documented fix is to be specific about desired output and constraints.

question: An operations coordinator notices a teammate pasting spreadsheets of customer names and order histories into a personal Claude account, even though the company provides a managed Claude for Work workspace. What should the coordinator do first?
options: A) Ask the teammate to delete those conversations, and treat the matter as closed once deletion is confirmed.
B) Post a general reminder about approved tools in the team channel so everyone is aware of the expectation.
C) Wait and see whether the practice continues, raising it only if customer data later appears in a shared file.
D) Raise it through the escalation path the company's AI policy defines for suspected data-handling problems.
correct_answers: D) Raise it through the escalation path the company's AI policy defines for suspected data-handling problems.
explanations: Deletion may be part of the remedy, but an individual arrangement bypasses the assessment and record the policy requires.
A general reminder does not address a specific incident that has already put customer data outside the managed workspace.
Waiting leaves an active exposure unreported and makes the eventual review harder, since the extent will be larger.
Correct. Customer data has already left the approved environment, and the policy's escalation path exists precisely so this is assessed by the people accountable for it.

question: A team manager wants to change how his team uses Claude, in a way the team's current written standard does not allow. In which order should these steps be taken?
options: A) Write down the proposed change and the data it would involve; update the written standard to match the decision; brief the team on the updated standard; get the policy owner's decision on it.
B) Update the written standard to match the decision; write down the proposed change and the data it would involve; get the policy owner's decision on it; brief the team on the updated standard.
C) Write down the proposed change and the data it would involve; get the policy owner's decision on it; update the written standard to match the decision; brief the team on the updated standard.
D) Brief the team on the current standard; write down the proposed change and the data it would involve; get the policy owner's decision on it; update the written standard to match the decision.
correct_answers: C) Write down the proposed change and the data it would involve; get the policy owner's decision on it; update the written standard to match the decision; brief the team on the updated standard.
explanations: The standard is updated and the team briefed on the updated standard on the strength of an unapproved proposal, with the policy owner asked only at the end, once the change is already in effect.
The standard is amended to match a decision that has not been made yet. Rewriting governance ahead of approval is exactly the shortcut a policy exists to stop.

Correct. A written proposal naming the change and the data involved is what the policy owner needs in order to decide; the decision is what authorises the change; the written standard is then updated to match it; and the team is briefed on the updated standard, which is the one they will actually follow.

The team is briefed on the current standard before anything has changed, so the briefing is out of date as soon as the standard is rewritten, and the update only lands after they have already been informed.

question: A colleague proposes running every request on two different tiers and comparing the two answers each time. What is the most reasonable assessment?
options: A) It is wasteful, because the two tiers will always return answers that are effectively identical.
B) It is sensible, because using two tiers spreads consumption across two separate allowances.
C) It is wasteful, since it doubles the allowance spent on a comparison worth doing only once.
D) It is sensible, since comparing two answers each time is the surest way to catch any error.
correct_answers: C) It is wasteful, since it doubles the allowance spent on a comparison worth doing only once.
explanations: Incorrect. They genuinely differ on demanding work, so the objection is cost rather than a lack of difference.
Incorrect. Usage is measured across all of a person's activity, so nothing is spread by using two tiers.
Correct. Comparing tiers is worth doing on a representative sample to settle the choice; repeating it on every request pays twice for a decision already made.
Incorrect. Two answers that agree can both be wrong, so this buys far less assurance than it costs.

question: A marketing associate's project instructions say "keep it short", yet the drafts Claude produces are still far longer than the team wants. What should the associate do first?

correct_answers: A) Replace the vague rule with a specific limit, such as a stated word count and a section structure.
explanations: Correct. Vague direction is the root cause; the fix is to make the requirement concrete enough to follow.
A stronger model does not repair an under-specified instruction.
Emphasis does not add the missing information about how short is short enough.
Moving a behaviour rule into reference material makes it less likely to shape every answer, not more.

question: A consultant has an hour to review a long research brief before sending it to a client. Which sequence should she follow?
options: A) Read the conclusion; identify the claims the conclusion rests on; check those claims; verify the supporting detail.
B) Check those claims; verify the supporting detail; identify the claims the conclusion rests on; read the conclusion.
C) Identify the claims the conclusion rests on; verify the supporting detail; read the conclusion; check those claims.

correct_answers: A) Read the conclusion; identify the claims the conclusion rests on; check those claims; verify the supporting detail.
explanations: Correct. Reading the conclusion first reveals what the brief is asking the client to accept, which identifies the load-bearing claims. Those are checked while time remains, and remaining detail is verified with whatever is left.
Checking claims that have not yet been identified is not possible, and reading the conclusion last leaves the review with no organising purpose.
The claims a conclusion rests on cannot be identified before the conclusion has been read, so this ordering starts from an unknown.
Starting on supporting detail spends the scarce hour on material that may not matter, and the conclusion is read only after that time is gone.

question: A stakeholder asks the solutions architect to define, in plain terms for a non-technical audience, what it means when Claude "hallucinates" during a research summarization task. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: A) It means the input document was corrupted, containing garbled or missing sections, which is the only possible reason that factual errors could appear in a summary.
B) It means Claude can generate text that sounds plausible and confident but is factually incorrect or not supported by the source material.
C) It means Claude has detected a technical error in its own systems, such as a conflict in its training data, and automatically halted the response before completion.
D) It means Claude is intentionally inserting false information, such as a made-up date or name, into the summary to test whether the user is paying close attention.
correct_answers: B) It means Claude can generate text that sounds plausible and confident but is factually incorrect or not supported by the source material.
explanations: Incorrect. Hallucinations can happen even when the input document is perfectly clean and complete, so corruption is not the only or primary cause. The model may still generate plausible-sounding but incorrect information regardless of input quality.

Correct. Hallucination means the model generates text that sounds confident and plausible but is factually incorrect or not supported by the source material. This behavior underscores the importance of verifying Claude's outputs, especially in research summarization where accuracy is critical.

Incorrect. Claude does not detect hallucinations as technical errors and halt responses; it is unaware of its own inaccuracies. Hallucination refers to generating incorrect content, not to system-level error detection.

Incorrect. Claude does not intentionally insert false information as a test; hallucinations are unintended and arise from the model's generation process. The model has no awareness or intent behind its errors.

question: A finance manager is running a Cowork task that will reorganise files and send messages on her behalf. Which approach best matches sound practice for work that has real consequences?
options: A) Stay close and approve the actions that send or change things, reviewing what Claude does.
B) Let the task run without any pauses, then review the whole session once it has finished completely.
C) Approve every action once at the outset so the task is not interrupted while it is running.
D) Let the task run unattended overnight and check the results at the start of the next day.
correct_answers: A) Stay close and approve the actions that send or change things, reviewing what Claude does.
explanations: Correct. No approval setting replaces the person's judgment, and this task touches things with real consequences. Staying close and approving the sending and changing actions keeps her in control of exactly the steps that cannot be walked back.
Reviewing afterwards is fine for work that can be undone, but messages already sent in her name cannot be recalled. The review would document the damage rather than prevent it.
Blanket approval at the start grants permission for actions nobody has seen yet, which defeats the purpose of an approval step. Convenience is bought by removing the control the task most needs.
Running unattended overnight maximises the time between a mistake and its discovery. Recipients will have read the messages long before anyone looks at what happened.

question: A company's customer service chatbot tells a customer, 'Our support team works only from our London office.' Later in the same conversation, it tells the same customer, 'Our support team works only from our New York office.' Someone reviewing this transcript cannot check where the company's offices really are. Which issue does the transcript itself clearly show?
options: A) The chatbot gave two answers that contradict each other.
B) The chatbot favors customers in one city over another.
C) The chatbot's statements are confirmed to be factually wrong.
D) The chatbot made up a source for its claim.
correct_answers: A) The chatbot gave two answers that contradict each other.
explanations: Correct. The chatbot first says its support team works only from the London office and later says it works only from the New York office. Both statements cannot be true at once, so the transcript alone shows the chatbot contradicting itself within one conversation, and no outside fact-checking is needed to see it.
Incorrect. Both replies describe where the support team works and say nothing that treats one group of customers better than another, so the transcript shows no preferential or prejudiced treatment.

Incorrect. Without the company's real office details the reviewer cannot confirm that either statement is wrong, and nothing in the transcript settles it. What the transcript does establish is that at most one of the two statements can be true, which is a contradiction rather than a confirmed factual error.

Incorrect. Neither reply cites or quotes any source, so there is no invented citation anywhere in the transcript. What is visible is that the two replies disagree with each other, not that supporting evidence was fabricated.

question: A research team has delegated literature gathering and first-pass summarising to Claude. Which part of the work should most clearly stay with the researchers themselves?
options: A) Deciding the order in which the summarised sources appear in the final written research output.
B) Deciding which findings actually matter for this organisation's decision and what follows from them.
C) Deciding how many separate sources to gather before the first-pass summaries are considered complete.
D) Deciding which file format the collected material should be stored in for the rest of the project.
correct_answers: B) Deciding which findings actually matter for this organisation's decision and what follows from them.
explanations: Ordering the sources is a presentation decision that can be delegated and then reviewed. Getting it wrong makes the output slightly harder to read and is corrected in a moment.

Correct. Gathering and summarising are volume tasks that suit delegation, but working out which findings bear on this organisation's decision requires context Claude does not hold and carries consequences the researchers must answer for.
How many sources to gather is a scoping rule that can be agreed once and applied mechanically. It matters, but it is far less consequential than deciding what the evidence means for the organisation.
File format is an administrative convention with no bearing on the quality of the conclusions. It is exactly the kind of low-stakes, easily specified choice that does not need senior attention.

explanations: Structured outputs controls response formatting, not access to current external information.

question: While checking a twelve-page report, an analyst finds that one section has used last year's headcount figures. Which sequence should she follow next?
options: A) Correct that section; re-read the conclusions in light of the correction; look for the same error elsewhere; approve the report.
B) Look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it; approve the report.
C) Re-read the conclusions in light of it; correct that section; approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere.
D) Approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it.
correct_answers: B) Look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it; approve the report.
explanations: Fixing only the section where the error was noticed leaves identical errors elsewhere, and the conclusions are re-read before those are found.

Correct. One instance of stale data suggests a source problem rather than a typing slip, so the scope of the error is established first, every affected section is then corrected, and the conclusions are re-read against the corrected figures before approval.
Re-reading conclusions before the figures are corrected judges them against numbers already known to be wrong, and approval precedes the wider search.
Approval comes before any of the corrective work, so the report is signed off in the state that was already known to be wrong.

question: A research analyst uses Claude to summarize long industry reports and extract key data points into a spreadsheet for internal use, then verifies the figures against the source documents before including them in a client deliverable. Is this an appropriate use of Claude?
options: A) No, because summarizing third-party reports without direct publisher permission always violates policy
B) Yes, because summarizing reports and extracting data points are core supported use cases here
C) No, because spreadsheet data extraction falls outside Claude's supported text and code capabilities
D) Yes, but only if extracted data is used solely internally and never in any client-facing document
correct_answers: B) Yes, because summarizing reports and extracting data points are core supported use cases here
explanations: Incorrect. Summarizing publicly or lawfully accessed reports for internal analysis does not require separate written publisher permission under the Usage Policy.
Correct. Summarizing documents and extracting data points are core supported use cases, and verifying the output before it reaches a client reflects appropriate diligence.
Incorrect. Extracting structured data points from text, including into spreadsheet form, is well within Claude's supported text-processing capabilities.
Incorrect. Nothing in the Usage Policy bars verified, accurate extracted data from being used in a client deliverable; the analyst's verification step supports appropriate use.

question: A project lead has a single sentence from a director: "We need faster case handling." She wants to use Claude to turn this into a requirement set that goes to stakeholders for sign-off with no open questions left once it is drafted. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) List the open gaps; draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected; take the gaps to stakeholders.
B) State the outcome and who is affected; list the open gaps; take the gaps to stakeholders; draft the requirement set.
C) Take the gaps to stakeholders; list the open gaps; draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected.
D) Draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected; list the open gaps; take the gaps to stakeholders.
correct_answers: B) State the outcome and who is affected; list the open gaps; take the gaps to stakeholders; draft the requirement set.
explanations: Incorrect. This option drafts the requirement set in step two, before the outcome is even stated in step three and before the gaps are ever taken to stakeholders in step four -- the draft goes out carrying the same open questions the project lead wanted resolved first, and the closing stakeholder step happens too late to change a draft that already exists.

Correct. Naming the outcome and who is affected turns the director's one sentence into a target the gaps can be measured against; listing what is still unknown surfaces the open questions; taking those to stakeholders closes them before anything is written down; only then does the draft go out with no open questions left, which is exactly what the project lead needs.

Incorrect. This option takes gaps to stakeholders in step one, before any gap has been listed in step two, so there is nothing yet to ask stakeholders about; it also drafts the requirement set before the outcome and audience are named, so the draft is written without knowing what it is meant to achieve or for whom.

Incorrect. The project lead wants a requirement set with no open questions left once it is drafted, so drafting cannot be the first step: nothing is known yet about the outcome, who is affected, or what is missing when this option's draft is written, and that draft is never revisited after the outcome is stated or the gaps are surfaced.

question: A nonprofit organization wants to use AI-generated content to create emotional appeals for fundraising. Is this appropriate?
options: A) No, AI‑generated fundraising content is inherently deceptive because it fabricates beneficiary stories.
B) Yes, AI‑generated emotional appeals are always permissible, as the charitable purpose outweighs concerns.
C) No, because any emotional appeal in fundraising is manipulative, regardless of AI involvement.
D) Yes, but only if the beneficiary stories are truthful and accurately represent real events.
correct_answers: D) Yes, but only if the beneficiary stories are truthful and accurately represent real events.
explanations: Incorrect. AI-generated fundraising content is not inherently deceptive; its ethical status depends on how it is created and disclosed. It can be responsible when it faithfully represents real stories and avoids misleading the audience.

Incorrect. Charitable purpose does not automatically justify AI-generated emotional appeals, as they can still be misleading or untruthful. The key concern is whether the content is accurate and transparent, not the nobility of the cause.

Incorrect. Emotional appeals are not inherently manipulative; they are a common and ethical fundraising tool when based on true stories. The ethical issue is whether the content distorts facts or exploits, not whether it evokes emotion.

Correct. AI-generated fundraising content can be appropriate if the beneficiary stories are truthful and accurately represent real events. Ethical use demands that the content not mislead donors or fabricate details, ensuring authenticity and transparency.

question: A procurement lead has four supplier proposals and must recommend one to her director. Which sequence of stages should she work through with Claude?
options: A) Summarise each proposal against them; compare the summaries side by side; write the recommendation; agree the criteria that matter.
B) Compare the proposals side by side; agree the criteria that matter; write the recommendation; summarise each proposal against them.
C) Write the recommendation; agree the criteria that matter; summarise each proposal against them; compare the summaries side by side.
D) Agree the criteria that matter; summarise each proposal against them; compare the summaries side by side; write the recommendation.
correct_answers: D) Agree the criteria that matter; summarise each proposal against them; compare the summaries side by side; write the recommendation.
explanations: Summarising against criteria that have not been agreed is not possible, and settling them last leaves the completed comparison resting on nothing.
Comparing before criteria exist means each proposal is described on whatever terms it chose for itself, and the summaries arrive after the decision is already written.
Writing the recommendation first turns every later stage into a search for support, which is how a preferred supplier gets justified rather than chosen.
Correct. Criteria fix what counts as a good proposal, the per-proposal summaries then say the same things about each one, the comparison becomes like-for-like, and the recommendation follows from it.

question: Within a single Claude Project, what is the functional difference between project instructions and the project knowledge base?
options: A) Project instructions define behavioral guidance like tone or role, while the knowledge base supplies reference files
B) Project instructions and the knowledge base are simply two names for the same underlying feature
C) Project instructions apply to a single chat at a time, while the knowledge base applies to every project a user owns
D) Project instructions store uploaded files, while the knowledge base only accepts text typed into a settings field
correct_answers: A) Project instructions define behavioral guidance like tone or role, while the knowledge base supplies reference files
explanations: Correct. Project instructions establish behavioral guidelines such as tone or role applied to all chats, while the knowledge base holds uploaded documents, text, and code used as background context.
Incorrect. The two are distinct features serving different purposes: behavioral guidance versus reference content.
Incorrect. Project instructions apply to every chat within the project, not just one, and the knowledge base is scoped to that project, not to all of a user's projects.
Incorrect. This reverses the roles; file uploads belong to the knowledge base, not the instructions field.

question: A Team-plan owner shares a project organisation-wide so that more colleagues can benefit from the documents it contains. What is the greatest concern?
options: A) Everyone in the organisation gains access to knowledge that may include restricted or confidential material.
B) Organisation-wide sharing converts the project's documents into training data for future Claude models.
C) The original owner loses the ability to edit the project once it is visible to the whole organisation.

question: A manufacturing engineer has a detailed transcript of a production process and wants to convert it into a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) using Claude. Which approach best leverages Claude's capabilities to create an accurate, complete, and company-standard SOP?
options: A) Ask Claude to generate a generic manufacturing SOP, then insert specific details from the transcript into the template, relying on manual review to align steps with the process.
B) Provide the transcript to Claude and request a complete SOP without specifying details, letting the model infer all necessary steps and formatting.
C) Ask Claude to extract steps from the transcript, then iteratively add safety notes, tools, and quality checks, and format as a company SOP template.
D) Manually rewrite the transcript into bullet points, then structure them into an SOP draft, and use Claude only to check grammar and style, not to suggest or organize content.
correct_answers: C) Ask Claude to extract steps from the transcript, then iteratively add safety notes, tools, and quality checks, and format as a company SOP template.
explanations: Incorrect. Starting with a generic SOP template and inserting details from the transcript can lead to misalignment between the template's structure and the actual process, requiring extensive manual review to correct. This approach fails to capitalize on Claude's capacity to directly generate a tailored, accurate SOP from the source material.

Incorrect. Providing the transcript without specifying details relies entirely on Claude's inference, which may overlook critical safety notes, tools, or quality checks necessary for a complete SOP. This approach also lacks iterative refinement to ensure the output matches company-specific formatting and content requirements, increasing the risk of omissions or inaccuracies.

Correct. This method leverages Claude's capabilities by breaking the task into logical steps: extracting process steps, then iteratively adding safety notes, tools, and quality checks, and finally formatting into a company SOP template. This iterative process ensures the SOP is accurate, complete, and aligned with company standards.

Incorrect. Limiting Claude to only grammar and style checks underutilizes its ability to analyze the transcript, suggest organizational improvements, and ensure procedural completeness. Manual rewriting and structuring risk introducing errors or missing details that Claude could otherwise catch and enhance.

question: An analyst asks Claude, without web search enabled, to describe the outcome of an event that occurred last week. Claude responds with a confident, detailed description. What should the analyst do with this response?

B) Treat the description as unverified and confirm the details against a current, independent source

correct_answers: B) Treat the description as unverified and confirm the details against a current, independent source

Incorrect. Publishing unverified claims about a recent event risks spreading inaccurate information that an independent source check would have caught.
Incorrect. Repeating a question to the same model without new grounding data can simply reproduce the same unverified fabrication.

question: A procurement officer needs a supplier comparison that must fit on one page and must not name any supplier outside the approved shortlist. Where do these two limits belong?
options: A) After the first draft arrives, so the comparison is not narrowed before she has seen the full range of options.
B) In the original request, since both limits change what belongs in the comparison, not merely how it is presented.
C) In neither place, since limits of this kind are best handled by trimming and correcting the draft she gets back.
D) Only the page limit belongs in the request; the shortlist restriction is simpler to apply while editing the draft.
correct_answers: B) In the original request, since both limits change what belongs in the comparison, not merely how it is presented.
explanations: Seeing the wider market may be useful for her own understanding, but it is a separate task. Applied here it produces a draft that has to be rebuilt around a different set of suppliers.
Correct. Both constraints determine which suppliers are compared and how much can be said about each, so stating them up front shapes the analysis instead of leaving her to reconstruct it by hand.
Trimming to one page after the fact means deciding what to cut without the original weighting, and the shortlist rule is not a trimming problem at all.
Splitting the limits leaves the harder one to manual editing, and removing an off-shortlist supplier from a comparison changes the surrounding analysis rather than a single line.

question: A manager has two Claude outputs in front of her: notes from an internal brainstorm, and a statement that will be sent to a regulator. What should determine how much verification each one receives?
options: A) How long each took to produce, since a quickly generated output has had less care put into it.
B) The length and detail of each output, since a longer output contains more claims to get wrong.
C) What acting on each would cost, and how easily a mistake in it could afterwards be undone.
D) How confident each output sounds, since hedged writing signals that Claude was less sure of it.
correct_answers: C) What acting on each would cost, and how easily a mistake in it could afterwards be undone.
explanations: Incorrect. Generation time carries no information about correctness and none about what an error would cost.
Incorrect. Length correlates with the number of claims but not with the cost of an error, and a single wrong sentence in the filing outweighs pages of brainstorm notes.
Correct. Consequence and reversibility set the bar. Brainstorm notes are cheap to correct internally; a regulatory statement is externally visible and hard to retract.
Incorrect. Tone is not a reliable indicator of accuracy, and the regulator's statement would need checking however confidently it reads.

question: Explanation
options: A) Rephrase the request as a direct instruction to make the edit, such as telling Claude to change the function to improve its performance.
B) Move the question into the system prompt instead of the user message, while keeping the exact same original suggestive wording as before.
C) Send a follow-up message that just says "good suggestions" so that Claude infers approval to proceed with implementing them.
D) Increase the effort or thinking configuration considerably so Claude reasons for longer before answering the exact same phrasing.
correct_answers: A) Rephrase the request as a direct instruction to make the edit, such as telling Claude to change the function to improve its performance.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's guidance notes that phrasing like "can you suggest changes" leads Claude to provide suggestions rather than implement them; being explicit with a direct instruction, such as telling Claude to make the change, is the documented fix for getting Claude to take action.
Incorrect. Moving the same suggestive wording to the system prompt does not change its meaning; the ambiguity about suggesting versus acting remains.
Incorrect. A vague follow-up acknowledgment doesn't constitute an explicit instruction to implement changes and is not the documented technique for triggering action.
Incorrect. More reasoning effort affects how thoroughly Claude thinks through a response, not whether ambiguous suggestive phrasing gets interpreted as a request for action.

question: A team lead on a Team plan wants a shared project whose instructions the whole team relies on. Which sequence of steps is correct?

question: What is the best approach for using Claude to create a detailed timeline from a marketing campaign brief?
options: A) Provide the brief, specify the exact launch date, ask for a backward-scheduled timeline with dependencies and responsible teams, and request that Claude flag any unrealistic constraints.

B) Tell Claude to create a timeline based on typical marketing best practices, specify a generic campaign structure, ask for a forward-scheduled plan with standard phases, and ignore any specific dates from the brief.

C) Use Claude to rewrite the brief as a press release, specify the dateline and boilerplate, ask for a narrative flow, and then extract a timeline from the generated release for the campaign's key phases.

D) Instruct Claude to list all possible marketing activities, categorize them by phase, and output a sequential plan without specific dates, relying on the team to schedule execution using their own project management tools.
correct_answers: A) Provide the brief, specify the exact launch date, ask for a backward-scheduled timeline with dependencies and responsible teams, and request that Claude flag any unrealistic constraints.
explanations: Correct. This approach anchors the timeline to the exact launch date, uses backward scheduling, and includes dependencies and responsible teams. Flagging unrealistic constraints allows for proactive adjustments, and grounding the plan in the provided brief ensures it is comprehensive and actionable. It fully leverages Claude for structured planning.

Incorrect. Ignoring specific dates from the brief prevents the timeline from reflecting actual project constraints. A generic forward-scheduled plan based only on best practices lacks the necessary context to be actionable. Claude should incorporate the brief’s details to create a relevant and accurate timeline.

Incorrect. Rewriting the brief as a press release is an unnecessary transformation that doesn’t directly support timeline creation. Extracting a timeline from narrative prose risks losing key details and is less accurate than having Claude produce a structured schedule from the outset.

Incorrect. Listing activities by phase without specific dates does not produce a workable timeline. Relying on the team to schedule execution later shifts critical planning decisions away from Claude, missing the opportunity to integrate temporal dependencies directly into the output.

question: A hiring-assistant application uses Claude to write short candidate summaries. During review, evaluators notice that summaries for candidates from one demographic group consistently include more hedging language and fewer positive descriptors than summaries for equally qualified candidates from another group. What issue does this pattern represent?
options: A) An inconsistency, since the summaries use noticeably different sentence structures overall
B) A bias, since responses are systematically skewed by a group attribute, not qualifications
C) A hallucination, since Claude invented qualifications that the candidates do not actually have
D) A context failure, since Claude appears to have ignored the resumes provided in the prompt
correct_answers: B) A bias, since responses are systematically skewed by a group attribute, not qualifications
explanations: Incorrect. Varying sentence structure alone is not an inconsistency; the issue here is the systematic skew tied to group membership.
Correct. A systematic difference in tone or content correlated with a demographic group, rather than with actual qualifications, is the definition of bias in model output.
Incorrect. The scenario describes a skew in tone and word choice, not fabricated facts or invented credentials.
Incorrect. The scenario does not indicate that resume content was ignored, only that similarly qualified candidates were described differently based on group.

question: A team in a regulated industry is setting up a Claude Project to draft client onboarding letters. Which sequence best follows a typical organisational AI policy?
options: A) Confirm the use case and data types are permitted; get the data owner's approval; upload the material and set project instructions; pilot with a named human reviewer.
B) Upload the material and set project instructions; pilot with a named human reviewer; confirm the use case and data types are permitted; get the data owner's approval.
C) Upload the material and set project instructions; confirm the use case and data types are permitted; get the data owner's approval; pilot with a named human reviewer.
D) Get the data owner's approval; upload the material and set project instructions; confirm the use case and data types are permitted; pilot with a named human reviewer.
correct_answers: A) Confirm the use case and data types are permitted; get the data owner's approval; upload the material and set project instructions; pilot with a named human reviewer.
explanations: Correct. Policy questions come before data moves: establish that the use and the data classes are allowed, obtain the owner's approval, then configure, then prove it works under human review.
This puts client material into the workspace before anyone has confirmed the use case is permitted, which is the step the policy exists to prevent.
Uploading first means the data is already in the workspace while the permission question is still open.
Approval cannot be sought sensibly before the use case itself has been confirmed as permitted, and configuration still precedes that confirmation here.

question: A colleague realises they pasted a confidential merger document into a chat on their personal Free-plan account. What should they do first?
options: A) Delete the conversation and treat the matter as resolved without mentioning it to anyone else.
B) Switch on incognito mode for future chats and carry on working with the merger document there.
C) Ask Claude to delete the document from its memory and to confirm that nothing at all has been retained.
D) Report it through the organisation's incident or escalation process so the exposure can be assessed.
correct_answers: D) Report it through the organisation's incident or escalation process so the exposure can be assessed.
explanations: Deleting the chat hides the incident from the people responsible for assessing it.
This does nothing about the exposure that has already happened, and continues the unapproved use.
An assurance from within the conversation is not a record of containment.
Correct. A confidentiality incident has to reach the people who can assess and contain it, and quickly.

question: Explanation
options: A) Treat the ranking as one input, review the applications herself, and record that she made the decision.
B) Accept the ranking but produce it a second time, and shortlist the candidates that appear on both lists.
C) Use the ranking as the shortlist, then ask Claude to explain each position so the reasoning is on record.

correct_answers: A) Treat the ranking as one input, review the applications herself, and record that she made the decision.
explanations: Correct. A ranking drawn from writing style can disadvantage groups in ways no field names directly, so it may inform a decision about people but must not make it, and a person must own the outcome.
Agreement between two runs shows consistency, not fairness, and can simply repeat the same bias twice.
An explanation produced after the fact describes the ordering; it does not verify that the ordering was fair.
Removing names leaves plenty of signals that correlate with background, and it removes the human review as well.

question: An operations analyst asked six specific questions about a supplier's performance and received one flowing summary in reply. She is about to forward it to her manager. What should she do first?
options: A) Forward it with a note asking her manager to flag anything that looks incomplete or unclear to him.
B) Read the summary through for anything that strikes her as odd or that contradicts what she already knows.
C) Ask for the summary again in a shorter form, so her manager can take it in without a long explanation.
D) Go back to her six questions and confirm that each one is actually answered somewhere in the summary.
correct_answers: D) Go back to her six questions and confirm that each one is actually answered somewhere in the summary.
explanations: Her manager does not have her list of six questions, so he cannot tell what is missing, and the check she owns is passed to someone less able to make it.
Reading for oddities catches things she already suspects. A question that was never answered at all leaves no trace in the text, so it is exactly what this kind of reading misses.
Shortening compresses a summary whose coverage has not yet been established, and it can remove the very answers she has not verified are present.

Correct. Completeness is judged against what was asked, not against how the answer reads. A fluent summary can cover four of six questions and still feel finished, so checking question by question is what exposes the gap.

question: A team moves its live pricing sheet into a project's knowledge so every chat in the project can use it, and then changes its prices two months later. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The pricing sheet will be counted twice, once as knowledge and once in each conversation.
B) Every chat in that project will keep quoting the superseded prices with complete confidence.
C) Colleagues outside the project will be unable to see the pricing sheet in their own chats.
D) The project will refuse any further uploads until the outdated pricing sheet has been removed.
correct_answers: B) Every chat in that project will keep quoting the superseded prices with complete confidence.
explanations: Incorrect. Nothing is double-counted in that way, and this does not describe a real failure mode.
Correct. Making knowledge durable also makes staleness durable. Until the sheet is replaced, the project answers confidently from a document that no longer reflects reality.
Incorrect. That is the expected scope of a project rather than a risk created by the price change.
Incorrect. There is no such block, and framing this as an upload problem misses where the damage actually occurs.

question: An operations manager has finished a long planning chat and expects the team to revisit the same topic every month. What is the best way to keep that context available?
options: A) Rely on Claude recalling the earlier planning chat automatically whenever she opens a new conversation.
B) Keep reopening the same long chat every month so that all of the history stays inside one conversation.
C) Copy the whole transcript into the first message of every monthly chat so that nothing at all is ever left out.
D) Save the agreed decisions into a Project as knowledge, then start each monthly review as a fresh chat there.
correct_answers: D) Save the agreed decisions into a Project as knowledge, then start each monthly review as a fresh chat there.
explanations: Incorrect. Automatic recall is not a dependable store for decisions the team must rely on months later; durable context should be persisted into project knowledge deliberately.
Incorrect. A conversation that grows for a year will keep condensing its own earlier content and will draw heavily on usage allowance.
Incorrect. The transcript is mostly working discussion rather than durable fact, and re-pasting it each month wastes window space and allowance.
Correct. Persisting the durable output into project knowledge keeps the context available to every future chat without carrying months of transcript inside one conversation.

question: An operations manager writes a prompt for a weekly incident summary that the executive team reads every Monday, and a partner firm receives the same summary. Which two elements should the prompt include to make the output usable without rework? Select two.
options: A) A request that the summary be written so that it sounds authoritative and well informed.
B) A note that she is short of time this week and would appreciate a quick turnaround here.
C) The output shape she needs: one page, three headed sections, and no more than six bullets.
D) An instruction telling Claude to use its own judgment about what executives care about.
E) Why customer names must be excluded, since a partner firm also reads it.
correct_answers: C) The output shape she needs: one page, three headed sections, and no more than six bullets.
E) Why customer names must be excluded, since a partner firm also reads it.
explanations: Asking for an authoritative tone shapes how the text sounds, not what it contains, and can encourage confident phrasing over accurate reporting of the week.
Claude's output does not change because the requester is busy. This adds words to the prompt without adding any requirement the draft can be judged against.
Correct. Stating the format and its limits up front is what removes the reformatting step. "One page, three sections, six bullets" is checkable, unlike "keep it short".
Delegating the specification back to Claude is the opposite of describing intent. It guarantees a plausible guess rather than the summary this audience actually needs.
Correct. Giving the reason behind a constraint lets Claude generalise it: knowing an external partner reads the summary, it will also handle account numbers and site names sensibly.

question: A department switches all fifty of its staff to a redesigned, Claude-assisted case-handling process on the same Monday morning, with no trial group kept back. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The department's usage may rise sharply in the first week as fifty people start using Claude.
B) Some staff will need considerably longer than others to become comfortable with the new way of working.
C) Any flaw hits every case at once, and there is no unchanged group to compare results against.
D) Training all fifty staff in one week will strain the two people who designed the new process.
correct_answers: C) Any flaw hits every case at once, and there is no unchanged group to compare results against.
explanations: A jump in usage is a predictable consequence of fifty people starting at once and can be planned for. It affects cost and capacity, not the soundness of the redesigned process.
Uneven adoption is expected in any change and is managed with support and coaching. It slows the benefit rather than exposing the department to a failure it cannot see.

Correct. A full switch removes both safeguards at once: every case is exposed to a design that has never run live, and with no group still on the old process there is nothing to compare against, so the team cannot even tell whether results have got worse.
Straining the two designers is a real resourcing problem during the first week. It is a delivery pressure rather than the reason a simultaneous switch is dangerous.

question: A council's improvement team has four candidate use cases and can take only one forward this quarter. Which is the soundest first candidate for Claude?

correct_answers: C) Summarising the free-text comments on the monthly residents' survey for service leads
explanations: A budget allocation is a sole-source judgement with accountability attached, and the reasoning behind it must be owned by named people.

question: An operations manager is preparing to let her team use Claude-drafted replies across a busy customer queue. She has not yet decided who checks what. What should she do first?
options: A) Send the replies out and collect complaints, so the team learns which cases were handled badly.
B) Ask Claude to mark the replies it is least certain about so those can be routed for checking.
C) Have every reply read by two colleagues, so that nothing can reach a customer unchecked at all.

correct_answers: D) Agree what a good reply looks like and which mistakes would actually be costly to the business.
explanations: Incorrect. Learning from customer complaints puts the cost of the error onto customers, which is the outcome a review step exists to prevent.
Incorrect. A self-reported certainty score is produced by the same process as the reply, so it is not a dependable basis for routing work to a reviewer.
Incorrect. Double-reading everything is expensive and unfocused, and it is a decision about process taken before anyone has defined what reviewers are looking for.
Correct. Review only works against a standard. Naming what a correct reply contains and which failures would hurt is what tells the team where scrutiny is needed and where it is not.

question: A teacher reaches the length limit in a chat while working through a stack of graded feedback. What is the appropriate response?
options: A) Start a new chat and carry forward only the material and decisions the remaining work actually needs.
B) Buy additional usage credits, which will raise the context window available inside that conversation.
C) Wait several hours for the length limit to reset, then carry on in the same conversation thread.
D) Switch to a shorter reply style, which will free up the window space the earlier messages took.
correct_answers: A) Start a new chat and carry forward only the material and decisions the remaining work actually needs.
explanations: Correct. The length limit applies to one conversation, so a fresh chat clears it. Bringing only what is still needed keeps the new conversation lean.
Incorrect. Credits extend how much she can interact with Claude. The context window is fixed by the model and is not enlarged by buying allowance.
Incorrect. Length limits do not reset on a timer; that is how usage limits behave, and the two are easily confused.
Incorrect. Shorter future replies slow the fill rate slightly but cannot recover space already occupied by earlier messages.

question: An analyst's first draft from Claude is vague, and she wonders whether she should move up to a deeper-reasoning tier to fix it. Which two responses are sound? Select two.
options: A) Escalate to the deepest tier right away, since depth is the usual cause of a weak first draft.
B) Stay on the lightest tier no matter what, because the tier has little effect on answer quality.
C) Check first whether the request was under-specified, since a deeper tier supplies no context.
D) Escalate the tier only when the work truly needs more reasoning depth than it is now getting.
E) Split the same request across three chats on three tiers and merge whichever parts look best.
correct_answers: C) Check first whether the request was under-specified, since a deeper tier supplies no context.
D) Escalate the tier only when the work truly needs more reasoning depth than it is now getting.
explanations: Incorrect. Reaching for the deepest tier as a reflex spends quota without fixing the under-specified request underneath.
Incorrect. The tiers do differ in reasoning depth, so refusing to escalate is as unexamined as escalating by default.
Correct. Vagueness most often comes from a thin prompt, and no tier can invent the audience, format or source material you left out.
Correct. Escalating is the right move when reasoning depth is genuinely the binding constraint, and only then.
Incorrect. Running the same weak prompt three times multiplies the cost and still leaves the original specification problem in place.

question: A Claude-assisted case-summary way of working produces good results for the analyst who designed it, but two colleagues get noticeably worse results from the same written instructions. What should the designer do first?
options: A) Add examples of good summaries to the instructions so the expected standard is unmistakable.
B) Rewrite the instructions in much more detail so that less is left to the individual using them.
C) Ask the two colleagues to use the designer's own saved wording word for word every time.
D) Watch each colleague run the work once and see where their inputs differ from the designer's.
correct_answers: D) Watch each colleague run the work once and see where their inputs differ from the designer's.
explanations: Worked examples usually improve an arrangement and may well be part of the eventual fix. Adding them before the divergence has been observed is still a guess at the cause.
More detail is a plausible fix but an untargeted one. Without knowing which part of the colleagues' use diverges, the designer may add paragraphs about something that was never the problem.

Copying the designer's wording exactly hides the difference rather than explaining it, and it will not transfer to the next case. It also suggests the arrangement only works when one person operates it.

Correct. The same instructions producing different results means the difference is in what people actually do with them. Watching one run each is the quickest way to find the unstated step the designer performs without noticing, and it is what makes any later rewrite land in the right place.

question: A compliance officer must update an internal policy to reflect a new regulation. Which sequence of stages should she work through?
options: A) Pull the obligations out of the current policy; list what the regulation now requires; mark the clauses affected; draft the replacement wording.
B) Mark the clauses affected; draft the replacement wording; pull the obligations out of the current policy; list what the regulation now requires.
C) List what the regulation now requires; draft the replacement wording; pull the obligations out of the current policy; mark the clauses affected.
D) Draft the replacement wording; list what the regulation now requires; mark the clauses affected; pull the obligations out of the current policy.
correct_answers: A) Pull the obligations out of the current policy; list what the regulation now requires; mark the clauses affected; draft the replacement wording.
explanations: Correct. Establishing what the policy says today and what the regulation now demands gives the two lists that make a gap visible, the affected clauses fall out of that comparison, and only then is there something specific to redraft.
Clauses cannot be marked as affected until both the existing obligations and the new requirements have been set out to compare.
Drafting immediately after reading the regulation ignores what the policy already covers, so it produces new text that duplicates or contradicts existing clauses.
Replacement wording written before either the current position or the new requirement is known has nothing to replace and nothing to satisfy.

question: A marketing writer is about to publish a company blog post drafted with Claude. Its structure and its main claims follow a published industry study closely, and the post names no source at all. What is the most appropriate thing to do?
options: A) Leave the post as it stands, since Claude wrote the words and nothing was copied out verbatim.
B) Reword the passages that resemble the study most closely, so that the similarity is less obvious.
C) Trace the claims back to that study and credit it, rather than presenting its work as the company's.
D) Add a line stating the post was written with AI assistance, which covers where the material came from.
correct_answers: C) Trace the claims back to that study and credit it, rather than presenting its work as the company's.
explanations: Reusing another party's findings and structure needs crediting even when no sentence is copied.
Disguising the resemblance addresses how it looks rather than the missing credit to the source.
Correct. Attribution is owed to whoever did the underlying work; readers are otherwise given someone else's research as though the company had produced it.
Disclosing AI assistance says how the post was drafted, not whose research the claims rest on.

question: A project lead has twelve loosely related Claude answers gathered over a month and wants one reference document for her team. What is the most effective approach?
options: A) Decide the structure the reference needs, then have Claude assemble the answers and resolve conflicts.
B) Keep the twelve answers as they are and give the team a list of which conversation holds each one.
C) Paste all twelve of the answers into one document in the order in which they were originally produced.
D) Ask Claude to shorten each of the twelve answers so that the collection becomes quicker to read.
correct_answers: A) Decide the structure the reference needs, then have Claude assemble the answers and resolve conflicts.
explanations: Correct. Curation is more than collection: choosing the structure first and then reconciling what the answers say is what turns scattered material into something a team can rely on.
Incorrect. An index still leaves colleagues reading twelve separate answers and reconciling them individually.
Incorrect. Chronological order reflects how the questions arose, not how a reader needs the material, and it leaves conflicts in place.
Incorrect. Shortening reduces reading time but leaves twelve disconnected pieces and can remove the detail that resolves a conflict.

question: A team is choosing which slice of work to use for a two-week trial of a new Claude-assisted contract summarising arrangement. Which slice is the best choice for the trial?
options: A) The contracts causing the most delay right now, so the trial also clears the urgent backlog.
B) A random sample drawn from the whole archive, including contracts that are no longer in force.
C) A representative mix, including the awkward cases the team knows the arrangement must survive.
D) The simplest contracts, so the trial is not derailed by problems that affect only unusual cases.
correct_answers: C) A representative mix, including the awkward cases the team knows the arrangement must survive.
explanations: Using the trial to clear a backlog mixes two goals and puts urgent work in the hands of an untested arrangement. The most delayed contracts are also often the least typical, so they are a poor sample.
A random archive sample sounds rigorous but includes expired contracts the team no longer handles. Effort goes into cases that will never recur, and the awkward live cases may not appear at all.

Correct. A pilot is only useful if it is a fair rehearsal of the real work, which means deliberately including the hard cases. Two weeks on a representative mix shows both what the arrangement handles well and where it must keep a person involved.
An easy slice produces a flattering result that does not predict live performance. The arrangement would then meet its first difficult contract after the team has already committed to it.

question: An events team wants to put a Claude-drafted safety briefing for a public open day on the venue website tomorrow. Nobody has yet been named to check it. What should the team lead do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to review its own briefing and confirm that the safety guidance in it is accurate.
B) Decide who has to sign the briefing off, given that it is public and safety-related content.
C) Publish the briefing and ask staff on the day to correct anything that turns out to be wrong.
D) Circulate the briefing to the whole team so that anyone who wishes to can comment on it.
correct_answers: B) Decide who has to sign the briefing off, given that it is public and safety-related content.
explanations: Asking the same conversation to certify its own accuracy provides reassurance rather than assurance, and it does not put a person's name against the content.

Correct. Public, safety-related content sits at the top of the range where a named human must review and own the output before it goes out. Establishing who that person is comes before anything else, because it determines whether tomorrow's deadline is even achievable.

Correcting a published safety briefing after members of the public have read it does not undo the harm. High visibility and low reversibility are precisely the conditions that call for review before release, not after.
General circulation invites comment without assigning responsibility. Everyone may assume someone else has checked the safety guidance, which is how an unreviewed briefing reaches the public.

question: An analyst appends a reference list that Claude produced to her report without opening any of the items on it. What is the greatest risk?

question: A user asks Claude.ai to build a working single-page HTML landing page with embedded CSS that they can preview, tweak, and eventually export. Which output format best serves this request?
options: A) Choose an inline HTML code block because code blocks render identically to artifacts and provide the same live preview and export options.
B) Use a Mermaid diagram because diagrams are the standard way to represent the structure of a web page before writing any code.
C) Use a plain-text description of the page layout because writing prose about the design avoids the risk of embedding malformed markup.
D) Use an artifact because a single-page HTML site is self-contained, substantial, and the user previews and refines it outside the chat.
correct_answers: D) Use an artifact because a single-page HTML site is self-contained, substantial, and the user previews and refines it outside the chat.
explanations: Incorrect. Inline code blocks only display the code as text; they do not offer the live preview or one-click export features that artifacts provide, so they are not equivalent.
Incorrect. Mermaid diagrams are meant for flowcharts and diagrams, not for creating interactive web pages; they cannot fulfill the request for a working, exportable landing page.

Incorrect. A plain-text description of the page layout fails to deliver the functional, previewable HTML page the user explicitly requested, and writing prose does not mitigate markup risks better than actual code.

Correct. Artifacts are designed for self-contained, substantial content like a single-page HTML site, allowing the user to preview and refine the work in a dedicated panel and later export it for use outside the chat.

question: An operations analyst is comparing eight vendors and must decide whether to ask Claude for prose or for a structured table with fixed columns. Which two are sound reasons to choose the structured form? Select two.
options: A) The results will be moved into a tracker where every field has to line up exactly.
B) Tables remove the need to check the content, because the figures are already aligned.
C) Structured output is inherently more accurate than the same content written as prose.
D) A fixed set of columns makes it obvious when a vendor has no value for a field.
E) Producing a table takes Claude noticeably less effort than writing flowing paragraphs.
correct_answers: A) The results will be moved into a tracker where every field has to line up exactly.
D) A fixed set of columns makes it obvious when a vendor has no value for a field.
explanations: Correct. When output feeds a downstream system, a predictable field structure removes the manual re-keying that prose would force the analyst to do by hand.
Alignment is presentational. A neat table still needs the same accuracy and completeness checks as any other output before it is relied on.
Format does not change correctness. A table can hold exactly the same wrong figure as a paragraph, presented rather more convincingly.
Correct. Visible gaps are a curation benefit distinct from downstream use: prose can pass over a missing vendor detail without the omission ever showing.
Relative effort is not a reason a knowledge worker should choose a format. The decision should follow from how the information will be used.
