question: A programme manager has a Claude-drafted quarterly performance report and one hour to review it before it goes to her director. In which order should these steps be taken?
options: A) List what the original request asked the report to cover; check the draft against that list for anything missing; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.

B) List what the original request asked the report to cover; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director; check the draft against that list for anything missing.

C) Verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; check the draft against that list for anything missing; list what the original request asked the report to cover; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.

D) Check the draft against that list for anything missing; list what the original request asked the report to cover; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.
correct_answers: A) List what the original request asked the report to cover; check the draft against that list for anything missing; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.
explanations: Correct. Restating what was asked for gives her a standard; comparing the draft against it exposes missing sections cheaply and tells her where the substance actually is; verification effort then goes to the claims that matter most; recording what was checked lets the director see the limits of the review.
The draft reaches the director before the completeness check, so a missing section is discovered only after the report has already been handed over.
Verification begins before anyone has established what the report was meant to contain, so the hour is spent on whatever happens to be on the page and the coverage list arrives too late to direct it.
The draft is compared against a list that has not been written yet, so the comparison has no standard behind it and reduces to reading the report and hoping something looks absent.

question: A communications team has decided that Claude will draft its recurring stakeholder update, but the team cannot yet say how they will judge whether the arrangement is working. Which action best prepares them to delegate the task?
options: A) Write down what an acceptable draft must contain and avoid, and agree it before any drafting is handed over.
B) Agree a rota naming who will paste the source material into Claude for each reporting cycle in turn.
C) Draw up a shortlist of other tools to fall back on if the drafts disappoint during the first month.
D) Set a target for how long each draft should take compared with the time the current manual version takes today.
correct_answers: A) Write down what an acceptable draft must contain and avoid, and agree it before any drafting is handed over.
explanations: Correct. Defining what good looks like before delegating is what makes the delegation reviewable: the team gains a shared standard to check drafts against, a basis for correcting the instructions, and evidence for whether the arrangement is working rather than an argument about taste.

A rota settles who performs the task, which is useful operationally, but it does not give anyone a way to judge the output. The team would still have no agreed answer to whether a given draft is acceptable.

Planning a fallback before defining success means the team cannot tell whether the fallback is ever needed. Without a quality standard, disappointment is a matter of opinion and switching tools would not fix it.
A time target measures effort saved but says nothing about whether the drafts are fit to send. A fast draft that misses required content is worse than the slower manual version it replaced.

question: A coordinator uses Claude to draft an internal wiki page describing how to book a meeting room. Any colleague can edit the page, and a mistake would cost someone a few minutes. What is the most appropriate level of checking?
options: A) A read-through by someone who knows the booking process, then publish it to the wiki.
B) A formal review board should approve the page before it is added to the internal wiki at all.
C) Every step should be performed once by a colleague who then confirms the page in writing.
D) No checking is needed, because internal pages are not seen by customers or outside parties.
correct_answers: A) A read-through by someone who knows the booking process, then publish it to the wiki.
explanations: Correct. Verification effort should match consequence. The page is low-stakes and easily corrected, so a quick check by someone who knows the process is proportionate.
Incorrect. A standing approval body is disproportionate for a page that is trivially reversible and carries almost no consequence.
Incorrect. Physically re-performing each step and documenting it spends far more effort than the risk of a wrong booking instruction justifies.
Incorrect. Some check is still warranted; being internal reduces the stakes but does not remove the value of a quick look.

question: A benefits administrator asks Claude to answer staff questions using the benefits handbook she pastes in. Some of the questions concern situations the handbook simply does not cover. What should her request say about those?
options: A) That any question the handbook does not settle should be skipped, returning only the ones it covers clearly.
B) That every question should receive a full answer, drawing on general knowledge of employee benefits where needed.
C) That uncovered questions should still be answered, with a note attached asking the reader to confirm the details.
D) That where the handbook is silent, Claude should say so plainly instead of supplying an answer of its own.
correct_answers: D) That where the handbook is silent, Claude should say so plainly instead of supplying an answer of its own.
explanations: Silently dropping questions leaves staff with no reply and leaves her with no list of the gaps she needs to escalate.
General benefits practice is not this employer's scheme. An answer built that way looks authoritative and can commit the organisation to entitlements it does not offer.
A caveat attached to an invented answer still puts a specific figure or rule in front of the reader, and readers act on the answer rather than the caveat.
Correct. Naming the boundary of the source turns a gap into visible information she can act on, and it prevents plausible general knowledge being presented as her employer's policy.

question: An operations manager finds she hits her usage limit before lunch nearly every working day and is frustrated by the interruption. What should she do first?
options: A) Upgrade immediately to the highest plan tier available so the daily interruptions simply stop happening.
B) Review the usage view in her settings to see what recent sessions actually consumed, before changing anything.
C) Switch every task to the deepest-reasoning model so that fewer follow-up messages are needed to finish.
D) Move all of her work into brand-new chats each morning so that every conversation starts with an empty window.
correct_answers: B) Review the usage view in her settings to see what recent sessions actually consumed, before changing anything.
explanations: Incorrect. An upgrade may be justified later, but buying more allowance before understanding what consumes it is guesswork.
Correct. The fix depends on the cause, and the usage view shows how much of her session and weekly allowance has gone. Diagnosing first avoids paying for a change that would not help.
Incorrect. The deepest-reasoning tier consumes meaningfully more allowance per message, so this is likely to make matters worse.
Incorrect. A fresh window addresses a length limit, not a usage limit, which follows her across all conversations.

question: A prompt asks Claude to solve multi-step math word problems, but a review of outputs shows occasional arithmetic slips that go uncaught. The team wants to iterate on the prompt to catch these errors before the final answer is returned, without switching to a different evaluation pipeline. Which addition to the prompt best addresses this?
options: A) Ask Claude to supply only the final numeric answer without any intermediate steps, so no arithmetic is shown to check.
B) Remove all mention of the word "steps" from the prompt so Claude solves the problem in a single pass.
C) Append a step instructing Claude to verify its answer against the problem constraints before giving the final answer.
D) Instruct Claude to solve the problem twice using the exact same approach both times, then submit the first result.
correct_answers: C) Append a step instructing Claude to verify its answer against the problem constraints before giving the final answer.
explanations: Incorrect. Suppressing intermediate work hides the reasoning chain, preventing both the model and reviewers from spotting where arithmetic errors happen. It eliminates any chance for self-correction and does not add a verification mechanism.

Incorrect. Removing instruction to show steps discourages structured, step-by-step reasoning that helps maintain accuracy on multi-step math problems. Without explicit reasoning, arithmetic slips are more likely to occur and go unnoticed.

Correct. Adding an explicit self-verification step prompts Claude to check its solution against the original constraints, which can catch arithmetic errors before the final output. This technique directly addresses the need for error detection without altering the evaluation pipeline.

Incorrect. Repeating the same approach twice does not introduce a genuine check, because identical reasoning is likely to reproduce the same mistake. Since only the first result is used, the second computation provides no error-catching benefit.

question: Explanation
options: A) Drop any performance note written before the current review year, using only recent evidence.
B) Tell the candidates that AI was used to prepare the summaries the promotion panel will be reading.
C) Examine whether the rankings systematically disadvantage any group before the panel relies on them.

correct_answers: B) Tell the candidates that AI was used to prepare the summaries the promotion panel will be reading.

Correct. Performance notes carry human bias, and a ranking built on them can reproduce that bias at scale unless it is checked.
A self-reported confidence score is not a reliable measure of correctness and does not reveal systematic unfairness.
Opting out of a promotion process is not a real choice for candidates and would itself create unequal treatment.

question: An operations manager has collected about sixty requirement statements from five departments for a new supplier onboarding process. Many overlap, several contradict each other, and some are one-line wishes. She wants Claude to help her make sense of the list. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to rank all sixty statements by business value so the team can start on the top ten items.
B) Paste the full list into Claude and ask it to group related items and flag statements too vague to act on.
C) Ask Claude to estimate how long each of the sixty requirements would take to deliver before reviewing.
D) Ask Claude to draft the finished onboarding process document so the departments can react to something real.
correct_answers: B) Paste the full list into Claude and ask it to group related items and flag statements too vague to act on.
explanations: Ranking is premature while duplicates and contradictions are still in the list. A value ranking built over sixty unclean statements will rank the same need twice and score wishes that nobody can define, so the ordering would have to be redone once the list is tidied.

Correct. Analysis has to start with understanding what is actually in the list. Grouping related statements and surfacing the ones that are too vague to act on gives the manager a clean picture of overlaps, conflicts and gaps, which is exactly the work Claude accelerates well and which every later step depends on.

Effort estimates depend on requirements being unambiguous. Estimating vague one-line wishes produces numbers with no basis, and the manager would be attaching delivery figures to items that may turn out to be duplicates of one another.

Drafting the finished process before the requirements are understood invites departments to react to Claude's assumptions rather than to their own stated needs, and it makes the analysis harder because disagreements now attach to a document instead of to the underlying requirement.

question: A finance team runs an overnight batch of several thousand transaction narratives that must be finished before the six o'clock reporting cut-off. They move the batch to the deepest-reasoning tier because they want the best possible quality. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The team grows used to a higher standard of narrative and finds the earlier output unacceptable if they ever have to revert.
B) The narratives come back written in a more elaborate style than the reporting template was originally designed to accommodate.
C) The batch does not finish inside the overnight window, so the morning report goes out incomplete or does not go out at all.
D) The batch produces more detail per transaction than the finance team has time to read through before the reporting cut-off.
correct_answers: C) The batch does not finish inside the overnight window, so the morning report goes out incomplete or does not go out at all.
explanations: Raised expectations are a soft consequence and only matter if the team later reverts. They have no bearing on whether tonight's batch clears the six o'clock deadline.
An elaborate style is a formatting mismatch that can be corrected by asking for a tighter format. It does not threaten the report itself in the way a missed cut-off does.

Correct. At this volume the binding constraint is throughput against a fixed deadline. Depth that cannot complete in the window fails the task outright, which is worse than slightly plainer narratives delivered on time.
Excess detail costs reading time, but the narratives are generated per transaction and are not all read individually. The scheduling failure is the far more serious outcome here.

question: A startup has a new application idea and wants to minimize development cost and iteration time before deciding whether a more capable model is truly needed. Following Anthropic's recommended approach for this situation, which model should they implement first?
options: A) Claude Sonnet, since it should always be the first model tried regardless of budget concerns
B) Whichever model the startup's investors specify in the term sheet
C) Claude Opus, then downgrade later once prompts have been optimized for cost
D) Claude Haiku, then upgrade only if testing reveals a specific capability gap
correct_answers: D) Claude Haiku, then upgrade only if testing reveals a specific capability gap
explanations: Anthropic frames two valid starting approaches based on the use case; Sonnet being the universal first choice regardless of budget priorities is not part of that guidance.
Model selection should follow the technical criteria of capability, speed, and cost fit for the application, not external non-technical instructions unrelated to those criteria.

Starting with Opus and optimizing down over time is the recommended path for complex reasoning tasks where accuracy outweighs cost, not for a startup explicitly prioritizing low initial cost and fast iteration.

Correct. Anthropic recommends starting with a fast, cost-effective model like Haiku, testing thoroughly, and upgrading only if performance reveals a specific capability gap, which fits a startup minimizing cost and iteration time.

question: A member services officer must explain a change to membership fees. The explanation goes to members of fifteen years and to people who joined last month. Which request is most likely to produce copy she can use?
options: A) Ask for two versions of the notice, stating what each group already knows about fees and what each has to do.
B) Ask for one notice aimed at long-standing members, since newer members will accept whatever the notice tells them.
C) Ask for one notice in neutral wording, and let each reader work out for themselves which parts of it apply to them.
D) Ask for a single notice, plus a glossary at the end explaining every term that appears in the fee schedule.
correct_answers: A) Ask for two versions of the notice, stating what each group already knows about fees and what each has to do.
explanations: Correct. Naming each audience and what it already knows lets the request specify different starting points and different required actions, which is what actually separates copy that lands from copy that has to be rewritten.
Writing for the group with the most history assumes background the newest members do not have, and it treats their confusion as acceptable rather than as a cost.
A notice that serves neither group well is the usual result: long-standing members wade through explanations they do not need, and new members meet references they cannot place.
A glossary bolts definitions onto the end without changing the body of the notice, so the parts that assume familiarity still assume it.

question: A department head asks for a one-page summary of what Claude will and will not do in a redesigned review workflow. What is the most important thing for that summary to include?
options: A) A technical comparison of the model options so the department can judge the quality of the choice.
B) A ranked list of every Claude feature the department could adopt over the next financial year.
C) A statement that the outputs are reliable enough for review to be dropped once staff are trained.
D) Where Claude drafts and where a named person reviews, with the checks that stay in human hands.
correct_answers: D) Where Claude drafts and where a named person reviews, with the checks that stay in human hands.
explanations: A model comparison is not what a department head needs to understand value and limits.
A feature roadmap does not tell the department what the workflow will and will not do.
Promising that review disappears oversells the tool and removes the accountability step.
Correct. Stakeholders need the boundary between assisted work and human accountability stated plainly.

question: A new team member asks how the Claude model tiers actually differ from one another in everyday use. Which two statements are accurate? Select two.
options: A) The tiers differ only in writing style, so any of them may be used for any task at any time.
B) The deepest tier suits genuinely hard problems, and it consumes meaningfully more allowance.
C) Moving up one tier is the standard fix whenever a prompt comes back with a vague or shallow answer.
D) The mid tier is the fast, capable default, and it is the right pick for most everyday work.
E) The lightest tier gives answers of the very same depth, only more slowly than the other two.
correct_answers: B) The deepest tier suits genuinely hard problems, and it consumes meaningfully more allowance.
D) The mid tier is the fast, capable default, and it is the right pick for most everyday work.
explanations: Incorrect. The difference is reasoning depth, speed and cost, not writing style, and the tiers are not interchangeable.
Correct. The deepest tier buys reasoning depth for harder problems and costs meaningfully more of the usage allowance.
Incorrect. A vague answer usually signals an under-specified prompt, and a deeper tier cannot supply context that was never given.
Correct. The middle tier is positioned as the fast, capable default that handles most knowledge work well.
Incorrect. The lightest tier is the fastest of the three, and it trades some reasoning depth for that speed and low cost.

question: Three colleagues divide a customer research report between them. Each works on their own section in their own separate chat, and the sections are combined the day before the deadline. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Each section will be about the same length, giving the combined report an unhelpfully even balance across topics.
B) The three colleagues will each spend longer on their section than they would have spent working all together.
C) The sections will rest on different assumptions and definitions, and the combined report will not hold together.
D) The finished report will contain three different writing styles, which readers will notice as they move through it.
correct_answers: C) The sections will rest on different assumptions and definitions, and the combined report will not hold together.
explanations: Even section lengths are a cosmetic outcome, and easily adjusted once the material is in front of them.
Splitting the work reduces individual effort rather than increasing it, and effort is not what fails here.

Correct. Nothing is shared between the three chats, so each section quietly settles its own time period, customer segment definition and success measure. Those conflicts only surface at the merge, when there is a day left to resolve them.
Inconsistent voice is real and worth an editing pass, but it is visible on the surface and does not undermine the report's conclusions.

question: A bid coordinator has a Claude-assembled tender response built from the company's own past submissions, and has time to review it properly before the deadline. Which sequence is correct?
options: A) Verify the figures against the source submissions, then polish the wording, then check coverage against the tender questions, then check the response for internal contradictions.
B) Polish the wording, then check the response for internal contradictions, then check coverage against the tender questions, then verify the figures against the source submissions.
C) Check coverage against the tender questions, then verify the figures against the source submissions, then check the response for internal contradictions, then polish the wording.
D) Check the response for internal contradictions, then polish the wording, then verify the figures against the source submissions, then check coverage against the tender questions.
correct_answers: C) Check coverage against the tender questions, then verify the figures against the source submissions, then check the response for internal contradictions, then polish the wording.
explanations: Verifying figures before knowing whether every tender question is answered means checking numbers in sections that may still need rewriting, and polishing precedes both remaining content checks.
Polishing wording first invests effort in sentences that may be deleted, and leaves the coverage check, the most decisive step for a tender, until after two rounds of editing have already been done.

Correct. Coverage comes first because a missing answer is the costliest defect and changes what else needs checking; accuracy of figures and internal consistency come next; wording is polished last, once the content is settled.
Internal consistency is a useful check but cannot be conclusive while sections are still missing, and coverage, the step that determines whether the bid is even compliant, is left to the very end.

question: A communications lead is drafting an announcement in a chat that is close to its length limit, and the announcement is due in an hour. What should she do first?
options: A) Upgrade to a higher plan tier straight away so that the conversation gains a larger context window.
B) Delete the earliest messages in the conversation so that the newer content has more room to work with.
C) Switch the conversation to a faster, cheaper model so the remaining exchanges take up less of the window.
D) Capture the current draft and the outstanding decisions outside the chat before she does anything else.
correct_answers: D) Capture the current draft and the outstanding decisions outside the chat before she does anything else.
explanations: Incorrect. The context window is fixed by the model in use, so buying more allowance does not enlarge the window inside that chat.
Incorrect. Removing earlier messages by hand is slow, destroys the record, and is not how room is reclaimed in a chat.
Incorrect. Lighter models generally come with smaller context windows, so this shrinks the room she has left rather than extending it.
Correct. With a deadline close, the priority is making the work durable. Once the draft and open points are safely out of the conversation, restarting or continuing becomes a low-risk choice.

question: A researcher has checked most of a twenty-claim brief but two claims could not be confirmed against any source before her deadline. What should she do with those two?
options: A) Delete them quietly, on the basis that a brief containing only verified claims is the safest thing to circulate.
B) Keep them but mark them clearly as unconfirmed, so readers know which parts rest on nothing she could check.
C) Leave them in the brief unchanged, since they were not shown to be wrong and removing them would weaken it.
D) Soften their wording so they read as more tentative, which lowers the risk without drawing attention to them.
correct_answers: B) Keep them but mark them clearly as unconfirmed, so readers know which parts rest on nothing she could check.
explanations: Silent deletion hides that a question was raised and not resolved, and a later reader may reintroduce the same claim having no idea it was doubted.

Correct. Marking them preserves information the reader needs and shows exactly where the evidence stops, which lets anyone relying on the brief decide whether those two points matter to their decision.
Presented alongside verified claims and in the same voice, unconfirmed claims inherit the credibility of the ones that were checked.
Hedged wording signals mild uncertainty rather than absent verification, and it deliberately avoids making the gap visible.

question: A new joiner asks how the Claude model tiers differ from the point of view of someone using the Claude app. Which description is accurate?
options: A) Sonnet reasons most deeply, Opus is the everyday default option, and Haiku handles only images.
B) Haiku gives the deepest reasoning, Sonnet is the fastest option, and Opus suits routine bulk work.
C) Opus reasons most deeply and uses more allowance, Sonnet is the capable default, Haiku is fastest.
D) The tiers produce identical answers and differ only in how quickly those answers come back to you.
correct_answers: C) Opus reasons most deeply and uses more allowance, Sonnet is the capable default, Haiku is fastest.
explanations: Incorrect. Sonnet is the capable default rather than the deepest tier, and Haiku is a general fast model, not an image-only one.
Incorrect. This inverts the tiers. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest rather than the deepest-reasoning option.
Correct. As an end user experiences them, the tiers trade reasoning depth against speed and how much of the usage allowance each message consumes.
Incorrect. Speed is one axis, but reasoning depth genuinely differs, which is why the choice matters on hard work.

options: A) Ask Claude to respond twice and then manually pick whichever version happens to avoid LaTeX notation on that particular occasion.

question: A user is hesitant to connect Gmail to Claude over privacy concerns. Which statement accurately describes how Anthropic handles connector data?

B) Anthropic trains its models on connector data by default, unless the user opts out.
C) Connector data is processed only in memory and never stored on any server.

question: A researcher uploaded a single industry report and asked for a summary of it. Web search was switched off throughout. Which observation is the strongest sign that a detail in the summary was fabricated rather than drawn from the report?
options: A) The summary opens with general background about the industry before it turns to the specific findings the report contains.
B) The summary is noticeably longer than the researcher expected for a report of this size, and repeats one point in two places.
C) The summary states a precise figure, with a named source and a year, that appears nowhere in the uploaded report itself.
D) The summary uses phrasing of its own rather than reusing the exact sentences that appear in the uploaded industry report.
correct_answers: C) The summary states a precise figure, with a named source and a year, that appears nowhere in the uploaded report itself.
explanations: General framing before the specifics is a stylistic choice and is easy to remove. It becomes a concern only if the background contains checkable claims, which is not what this observation describes.
Length and repetition point to a shape-and-quality problem rather than an invention problem. A verbose or redundant summary can still be entirely faithful to the document it was built from.

Correct. With no web search and a single uploaded document, everything factual should trace back to that document. A precise, confidently attributed figure that is absent from the source is the classic signature of fabricated detail.

Paraphrasing is normal and often desirable in a summary; different wording says nothing about whether the underlying content came from the report. This would flag almost every competent summary as suspect.

question: A department head tells an analyst, "I want Claude to handle our client onboarding." The analyst has been given no other detail. What should the analyst do first?
options: A) Draw up a list of onboarding steps that Claude could not perform, and send that list to the department head.
B) Set up a shared project workspace and upload the current onboarding documents so Claude has background.
C) Ask the department head which onboarding outcome is failing today, and for whom, before naming any tool.
D) Run a series of trial prompts to see how well Claude drafts onboarding emails, then share the results.
correct_answers: C) Ask the department head which onboarding outcome is failing today, and for whom, before naming any tool.
explanations: Cataloguing limitations before the goal is known produces an answer to an unasked question. Some of those steps may be irrelevant to the department head's actual concern, and the list reads as resistance rather than analysis.

Loading the current documents is useful eventually, but doing it first assumes the existing process is the thing worth automating. If the real problem is that onboarding starts too late or asks clients for the wrong information, the documents encode the problem rather than the solution.

Correct. The request names a tool, not a problem. Establishing which onboarding outcome is failing and who feels it defines the problem to be solved, and that definition determines which steps are worth delegating at all and how success would later be judged.

Trial prompts show what Claude can produce, not what the department needs. Demonstrating a capability before the problem is defined tends to anchor everyone on whichever step happens to demo well rather than on the step that is actually hurting.

question: An operations manager wants Claude to help with the files in one shared folder and is about to connect the company's Google Drive. Which two actions best limit unnecessary exposure? Select two.

correct_answers: B) Check what the connecting account can already open in Drive, because Claude inherits that same reach.

explanations: Incognito affects whether chats are kept and used for improvement; it does not limit what a connected Drive exposes.

Correct on separate grounds: connecting a corporate data source is a governance decision, and most policies require approval before it happens.

question: A research lab needs help with a scientific analysis task involving nuanced multi-step reasoning, where correctness matters far more than response time or token cost. Which model tier does Anthropic's guidance point to?

correct_answers: A) Select Claude Opus, because scientific and mathematical tasks where accuracy outweighs cost are core use cases.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic explicitly recommends Claude Opus for complex reasoning, scientific, and mathematical tasks where accuracy outweighs cost and speed, exactly matching this scenario.

Incorrect. Sonnet is a strong general-purpose model, but when nuanced, multi-step reasoning and accuracy are paramount, Anthropic points to the most capable tier (Opus) rather than a general-purpose default.

Incorrect. Haiku is optimized for cost and latency sensitivity; Anthropic's guidance reserves it for tasks where speed or economy is the priority, not nuanced scientific work demanding maximum correctness.
Incorrect. Lowering the effort parameter limits reasoning depth to reduce latency and cost; it does not improve accuracy and would undermine performance on a task requiring nuanced reasoning.

question: A finance officer pasted eighty rows of expense data into a chat and asked Claude to total them by cost centre. Which two verifications should she perform on the returned figures? Select two.
options: A) Look over the totals to see whether they seem about right for a month of this kind.
B) Ask Claude to check its own arithmetic and proceed once it reports that all is correct.
C) Confirm that all eighty of the rows are counted in exactly one of the totals.
D) Recalculate a sample of the cost centre totals herself and compare them with the output.
E) Check that currency symbols and decimal places are applied consistently across the table.
correct_answers: C) Confirm that all eighty of the rows are counted in exactly one of the totals.
D) Recalculate a sample of the cost centre totals herself and compare them with the output.
explanations: A plausibility glance catches only large errors. A total that is wrong by one misfiled row looks entirely normal, which is what makes this check weak on its own.
Self-checking produces another generated answer, not an independent verification, and it can confidently confirm a figure that was wrong to begin with.
Correct. This is a coverage test rather than an arithmetic one: totals can each be added correctly while several rows were skipped or double-counted.
Correct. An independent recalculation is direct evidence about accuracy, and it catches a total that is internally consistent but simply computed wrongly.
Consistent formatting says nothing about whether the numbers are right. Tidy presentation is often what makes an incorrect total feel trustworthy.

question: A city communications team drafts a public road-construction notice, but the first draft uses formal legal phrasing like 'aforementioned thoroughfare' that is likely to confuse residents. What is the best refinement for this audience?
options: A) Keep the legal phrasing exactly as written but enlarge the font of the notice.
B) Translate the phrase 'aforementioned thoroughfare' into another commonly spoken local language.
C) Replace legal jargon with plain language, and ensure all facts remain accurate and complete.
D) Add a formal cover letter from city officials before the notice to provide necessary context.
correct_answers: C) Replace legal jargon with plain language, and ensure all facts remain accurate and complete.
explanations: Incorrect. Enlarging the font does not make the phrasing any easier to understand; the notice would still contain confusing legal terms. The core issue is word choice, not visibility.

Incorrect. Translating jargon into another language does not guarantee it becomes plain or accessible; it may remain just as formal and confusing. The goal is to replace complex terms with clear, everyday language, not merely translate them.

Correct. Plain language makes the notice understandable to all residents, not just those familiar with legal jargon. Accuracy must be maintained so the public receives correct and complete information about the road construction.
Incorrect. A formal cover letter would introduce even more official language, failing to simplify the confusing terms in the notice itself. Residents would still encounter the same unclear phrasing.

question: A project manager's prompt says only "never use the word delay in the status report". Claude complies literally but the reports still alarm the sponsor. Which two revisions would make the instruction work as intended? Select two.
options: A) Say how slipped dates should be reported, such as a revised date and the cause.
B) Explain that the sponsor escalates on schedule language, so Claude applies the intent widely.
C) Ask Claude to confirm that it has understood the instruction before it writes anything.
D) Add the phrase "this is extremely important" directly in front of the existing sentence.
E) Repeat the banned word instruction three times so that Claude treats it as a firm rule.
correct_answers: A) Say how slipped dates should be reported, such as a revised date and the cause.
B) Explain that the sponsor escalates on schedule language, so Claude applies the intent widely.
explanations: Correct. A prohibition alone leaves Claude to guess a substitute. Defining the positive replacement is an independent fix that specifies the desired output rather than the reason for it.
Correct. Supplying the reason turns a single banned word into a general principle, so Claude also handles "slippage", "behind plan" and similar phrasing the way the sponsor needs.
A confirmation step surfaces the same literal reading back to the manager and consumes a turn without improving the specification behind it.
Emphasis phrases do not clarify intent. The word was already avoided, so raising the stakes on an obeyed rule changes nothing about the report.
Repetition adds emphasis, not information. The instruction was already followed; the problem is that following it literally does not achieve the underlying goal.

question: A software team wants a coding assistant for daily feature development: reviewing pull requests, generating unit tests, and answering questions about the codebase. They want strong code quality and agentic tool use without paying premium enterprise pricing. Which model tier fits best?
options: A) Claude Opus delivers the highest accuracy for pull request reviews and test generation, essential for daily feature development.

correct_answers: C) Claude Sonnet delivers frontier-level coding and agentic tool use at a mid-range price, ideal for daily dev tasks.
explanations: Incorrect. While Claude Opus may offer the highest accuracy, it is designed for the most complex, large-scale agentic coding challenges and comes with premium pricing. For routine daily development work, Sonnet provides sufficient accuracy at a more appropriate cost, making Opus unnecessary for this scenario.

Incorrect. While Claude Haiku offers extended thinking that can facilitate step-by-step reasoning, the team requires strong general code quality and agentic tool use for daily development. Haiku's primary strength is speed and cost efficiency, not the frontier-level coding capability needed for thorough pull request reviews and test generation.

Correct. Claude Sonnet provides frontier-level coding performance and agentic tool use at a price point that balances cost and capability, making it ideal for daily development tasks like code review and test generation. This matches the team's need for strong code quality without enterprise premium pricing.

Incorrect. Fast mode on Claude Opus improves output speed but does not reduce pricing to Sonnet's level. Opus fast mode still operates at a premium price point, so it does not meet the team's requirement to avoid premium enterprise pricing.

question: A communications officer asks Claude for balanced talking points on a contested planning decision. The draft states one side's arguments plainly and introduces the other side's with repeated hedging. How should this be classified?
options: A) A hallucination, because the arguments on one side must therefore have been invented.
B) A bias, because the response treats comparable arguments unevenly through its choice of framing.
C) A formatting problem, because the hedging simply reflects a different paragraph style in use.
D) An inconsistency, because the two halves of the response use rather different sentence constructions.
correct_answers: B) A bias, because the response treats comparable arguments unevenly through its choice of framing.
explanations: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the arguments are fabricated. The issue is how comparable arguments are framed, not whether they exist.
Correct. Systematically softer language for one side skews the reader's impression even where every individual statement is accurate, which is what bias in an output looks like.
Incorrect. Hedging changes how strongly a claim is asserted, which is a matter of substance rather than presentation.
Incorrect. An inconsistency is a conflict between statements about the same fact, not a difference in phrasing between sections.

question: A charity's donation-thank-you process works well overall but is slow only at the drafting step. Which integration approach is most appropriate?

B) Redesign the process so donors receive whatever Claude drafts straight away

correct_answers: A) Augment the process by having Claude draft, with the same person signing off
explanations: Correct. When one step is the constraint and the rest of the process is sound, augment that step and leave the controls in place. The sign-off is not what was slow.
Sending unreviewed drafts to donors is an outward-facing, effectively irreversible step and should not be delegated unchecked.
Optional, unstructured use leaves the bottleneck exactly where it was and produces inconsistent letters to donors.
Removing the sign-off removes the check that makes the process safe, in exchange for time that was not being lost there.

question: A game designer asks Claude to build a playable HTML5 prototype of a simple puzzle game with score tracking, and wants to keep tweaking the mechanics over the next hour based on playtesting. Which feature keeps the running prototype visible and editable throughout that session?
options: A) A shared team workspace is necessary because individual accounts cannot render and tweak HTML5 prototypes.
B) Research mode is required because its engine renders and updates interactive content during iterative tweaks.
C) A Project is needed since project knowledge alone renders the HTML5 prototype and supports iterative tweaks.
D) The artifact panel keeps the prototype rendered separately while accepting live iterative edits.
correct_answers: D) The artifact panel keeps the prototype rendered separately while accepting live iterative edits.
explanations: Incorrect. Individual accounts can render artifacts including HTML5 prototypes without a shared team workspace. The artifact panel works within a single user’s session to display and iteratively edit the prototype.

Incorrect. Research mode performs web searches and has no engine for rendering or updating interactive HTML5 content. That rendering and iterative edit capability comes from artifacts, not research mode.

Incorrect. Project knowledge bases store reference documents and do not render live interactive content. Artifacts—not a Project—are required to render the HTML5 prototype and support iterative tweaks within the conversation.

Correct. The artifact panel is designed to render self-contained content like an HTML5 game prototype separately from the chat, allowing the designer to see a live view while requesting iterative edits to the mechanics. It explicitly supports this interactive, visible feedback loop.

question: A prompt for a tone-sensitive customer email generator gives Claude no persona or role, just the raw task instructions. Emails come back with an inconsistent, generic tone that doesn't match the brand voice. What is a lightweight change likely to help?
options: A) Increase the max_tokens limit so Claude has more space to naturally settle into a consistent tone over a longer response.
B) Add a system prompt sentence establishing Claude's role, such as being a customer service specialist for the brand.
C) Remove the existing task instructions entirely and rely only on examples to communicate the desired tone.
D) Ask Claude to write each email in a different language and then translate it back, hoping tone carries over more consistently.
correct_answers: B) Add a system prompt sentence establishing Claude's role, such as being a customer service specialist for the brand.
explanations: Incorrect. A larger token budget affects available response length, not tone consistency, and is not the documented lever for brand voice.

Correct. Anthropic notes that setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for a given use case, and that even a single sentence establishing a role makes a noticeable difference in output consistency.
Incorrect. Removing the task instructions would leave Claude without clear direction on what to actually write, which is a separate problem from tone and likely to make output worse.
Incorrect. Round-tripping through translation is not a documented technique for tone control and introduces unnecessary risk of meaning drift.

question: A researcher writing an executive summary wants Claude's analysis of a quarterly report to note both the strongest supporting evidence and the weakest counterpoints, rather than a one-sided take. Which instruction best supports this balanced analysis?

B) Ask Claude only for evidence supporting the report's existing headline conclusion

correct_answers: C) Explicitly ask for both the strongest evidence and the weakest counterpoints
explanations: Incorrect. Listing every sentence without judgment does not distinguish the strongest evidence from the weakest counterpoints as asked.
Incorrect. Asking only for supporting evidence produces a one-sided analysis and ignores the counterpoints the researcher explicitly wants surfaced.

Correct. Being clear and direct about wanting both the strongest evidence and the weakest counterpoints tells Claude exactly what balanced analytical output is expected, rather than leaving the balance to inference.
Incorrect. A plain summary without evaluating evidence does not perform the comparative analysis of strengths and weaknesses that was requested.

question: A pilot has worked well, and the team wants the new way of working to survive the departure of the person who created it. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; capture the working instructions in one shared place; write down what a good result looks like.

B) Write down what a good result looks like; capture the working instructions in one shared place; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck.

C) Capture the working instructions in one shared place; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; write down what a good result looks like; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone.

D) Have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; write down what a good result looks like; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; capture the working instructions in one shared place.
correct_answers: B) Write down what a good result looks like; capture the working instructions in one shared place; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck.
explanations: This begins by correcting instructions that do not yet exist in a shared place and ends by defining the standard, so every earlier step was taken without knowing what success meant.

Correct. The quality standard has to exist before anyone can tell whether a handover succeeded, the instructions must be captured somewhere shared to be handed over at all, a second person running from them alone is the real test, and their sticking points show precisely what to correct.
Correcting the instructions before anyone has tried to follow them means correcting imagined problems, and the standard for a good result is written after the corrections it should have guided.
The second person cannot run the work from instructions that have not yet been captured, and writing down what good looks like after the test leaves them no way to judge their own output.

question: A product team compares two Claude-drafted release notes for the same feature, one for a public changelog and one for an internal engineering wiki. What is a key factor to check for each draft's fit?
options: A) Whether the public draft includes internal ticket numbers so support staff can reference them
B) Whether the internal draft is written with the same marketing tone as the public changelog
C) Whether both drafts are published to the same location so all readers see identical content
D) Whether the public draft avoids internal codenames and detail that the engineering draft can include
correct_answers: D) Whether the public draft avoids internal codenames and detail that the engineering draft can include
explanations: Incorrect. Internal ticket numbers are meaningful to engineers but are not something a general public audience needs or can act on.
Incorrect. A marketing tone suits the public draft but is not a meaningful fit for an internal wiki meant for precise technical reference.
Incorrect. Publishing both drafts to the same location defeats the purpose of tailoring one for public users and one for internal engineers.
Correct. A public changelog should be free of internal codenames and implementation detail, while the internal wiki draft can appropriately retain that detail for engineers.

question: A team plans to bring Claude into a workflow that three other departments feed into. Which step is most important before the change goes live?
options: A) Wait until the other departments adopt the same arrangement themselves
B) Tell the feeding departments what changes for them and what does not
C) Give each department its own version of the new written instructions
D) Ask the departments to stop sending work until the change is settled
correct_answers: B) Tell the feeding departments what changes for them and what does not
explanations: Making the change conditional on three other departments adopting it first blocks a workflow improvement that is entirely within this team's control.
Correct. Integration touches everyone who feeds the workflow. Being explicit about what changes for them, and what stays the same, is what stops the redesign breaking at its handovers.
Separate instruction versions per department guarantee that the workflow behaves differently depending on who fed it.
Halting incoming work to make an internal change imposes the cost on other departments unnecessarily.

question: Explanation
options: A) Move the background that stays true across tasks into a project, so it need not be repeated.
B) Begin a fresh conversation containing only the material that the current piece of work needs.
C) Repeat the correction every single time details from the earlier tender reappear in the answers.
D) Ask Claude to read the whole conversation again from the very top before it answers each question.
E) Paste the previous answer back in each morning to remind Claude of what it said before.
correct_answers: A) Move the background that stays true across tasks into a project, so it need not be repeated.
B) Begin a fresh conversation containing only the material that the current piece of work needs.
explanations: Correct for an independent reason: it stops the problem returning, by giving durable context a home outside any single conversation.
Correct. A conversation this long has accumulated superseded material, and a clean start removes what is confusing the answers.
Fixing each recurrence by hand treats the symptom and leaves the overloaded conversation exactly as it was.
Re-reading the conversation reinforces the mixed-up history rather than clearing it, and consumes more allowance.
Adding the earlier output back in makes the conversation longer still, which is the condition causing the drift.
